paragraphs: Annealing methods search for good network configurations by controlling how freely units change, often through a temperature schedule chosen in advance. This paper replaces that global schedule with local decisions. Each unit determines its own temperature when it updates, based on how well nearby constraints are satisfied.

The resulting behavior lets poorly satisfied regions continue searching while already satisfactory regions remain stable. Search in a difficult region also continues as long as its constraints remain unsatisfied, rather than ending after a predetermined number of cycles. All processing occurs at the unit level, making the mechanism computationally simple.

The reported comparison finds global maxima more quickly and consistently than externally scheduled systems, including the referenced Boltzmann-machine approach. The contribution is a locally adaptive search process for constraint-satisfaction networks. Its central insight is that different parts of a network can need different amounts of continued exploration at the same moment.
summary.tldr: Automatic local annealing lets each unit adjust its own search temperature, keeping difficult regions active while stable regions settle.

title: Automatic Local Annealing

abstract: We have designed, fabricated, and tested a series of compact CMOS integrated circuits that realize the winner-take-all function. These analog, continuous-time circuits use only O(n) of interconnect to perform this function. We have also modified the winner-take-all circuit, realizing a circuit that computes local nonlinear inhibition.
originalAbstract: We have designed, fabricated, and tested a series of compact CMOS integrated circuits that realize the winner-take-all function. These analog, continuous-time circuits use only O(n) of interconnect to perform this function. We have also modified the winner-take-all circuit, realizing a circuit that computes local nonlinear inhibition.

paragraphs: The paper presents compact integrated circuits that implement a winner-take-all function, selecting a winning response from competing inputs. The authors designed, fabricated, and tested a series of these circuits using CMOS technology. The contribution therefore includes physical circuit realization, taking the neural computation through implementation and testing.

The circuits are analog and operate continuously in time. Their central scaling property is that the amount of interconnect grows linearly with the number of inputs. This is the meaning of the O(n) claim: increasing the size of the competition requires proportionally more wiring. It describes interconnection complexity rather than establishing a corresponding bound on the time required to select a winner.

The authors also modify the winner-take-all circuit to compute local nonlinear inhibition. This extends the circuit approach from selecting a winner to a related form of local suppression. Together, the designs show how compact analog hardware can implement competitive neural operations while keeping interconnection requirements linear for the winner-take-all function.
summary.tldr: Fabricated analog CMOS circuits implement winner-take-all selection with linear interconnect complexity and can be adapted for local nonlinear inhibition.

title: Winner-Take-All Networks of O(N) Complexity

abstract: The development of projections from the retinas to the cortex is mathematically analyzed according to the previously proposed thermodynamic formulation of the self-organization of neural networks. Three types of submodality included in the visual afferent pathways are assumed in two models: model (A), in which the ocularity and retinotopy are considered separately, and model (B), in which on-center/off-center pathways are considered in addition to ocularity and retinotopy. Model (A) shows striped ocular dominance spatial patterns and, in ocular dominance histograms, reveals a dip in the binocular bin. Model (B) displays spatially modulated irregular patterns and shows single-peak behavior in the histograms. When we compare the simulated results with the observed results, it is evident that the ocular dominance spatial patterns and histograms for models (A) and (B) agree very closely with those seen in monkeys and cats.

paragraphs: The paper mathematically studies how projections from the retinas to the cortex develop through self-organization. It uses a previously proposed thermodynamic formulation and compares two models containing different combinations of visual-pathway properties. The question is how those interacting properties affect the spatial organization and distribution of ocular dominance.

Model A considers ocularity and retinotopy separately: the eye supplying information and the organization associated with retinal position. It produces striped ocular-dominance patterns and a histogram with a dip in the binocular category. Model B additionally includes on-center and off-center pathways. Its patterns are irregular but spatially modulated, and its histogram has a single peak.

The authors report close agreement between these simulated patterns and histograms and observations in monkeys and cats. Considering both spatial appearance and the distribution of ocular dominance provides two descriptions of the modeled organization. The comparison shows that adding another pathway distinction changes the resulting organization substantially, making interactions among visual submodalities central to the proposed developmental explanation.
summary.tldr: Self-organization models produce different ocular-dominance patterns depending on whether on-center and off-center pathways are included.

title: Interaction Among Ocularity, Retinotopy and On-center/Off-center Pathways During Development

abstract: We develop a sequential adaptation algorithm for radial basis function (RBF) neural networks of Gaussian nodes, based on the method of succes(cid:173) sive F-Projections. This method makes use of each observation efficiently in that the network mapping function so obtained is consistent with that information and is also optimal in the least L 2-norm sense. The RBF network with the F-Projections adaptation algorithm was used for pre(cid:173) dicting a chaotic time-series. We compare its performance to an adapta(cid:173) tion scheme based on the method of stochastic approximation, and show that the F-Projections algorithm converges to the underlying model much faster.

This method makes use of each observation efficiently in that the network mapping function so obtained is consistent with that information and is also optimal in the least L 2-norm sense. The RBF network with the F-Projections adaptation algorithm was used for pre(cid:173) dicting a chaotic time-series. We compare its performance to an adapta(cid:173) tion scheme based on the method of stochastic approximation, and show that the F-Projections algorithm converges to the underlying model much faster.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to update a radial basis function network as observations arrive one after another. The network uses Gaussian nodes, and the adaptation method is based on successive F-Projections. The focus is on extracting useful information from each observation while updating the function represented by the network.

The proposed procedure produces a mapping consistent with the information in an observation and optimal according to a least L2-norm criterion. That criterion gives the update a defined mathematical objective. Rather than treating efficient use of data only as an empirical goal, the method builds a particular notion of consistency and optimality into the adaptation procedure.

The researchers apply the network to prediction of a chaotic time series and compare it with an adaptation method based on stochastic approximation. They report much faster convergence toward the underlying model with F-Projections. The stated result concerns the rate at which the learned mapping approaches that model, showing the practical importance of the adaptation rule alongside the choice of network representation.
summary.tldr: Successive F-Projections adapt Gaussian RBF networks sequentially and converge faster than stochastic approximation in the reported chaotic time-series task.

title: Sequential Adaptation of Radial Basis Function Neural Networks and its Application to Time-series Prediction

abstract: One method proposed for improving the generalization capability of a feed(cid:173) forward network trained with the backpropagation algorithm is to use artificial training vectors which are obtained by adding noise to the orig(cid:173) inal training vectors. We discuss the connection of such backpropagation training with noise to kernel density and kernel regression estimation. We compare by simulated examples (1) backpropagation, (2) backpropagation with noise, and (3) kernel regression in mapping estimation and pattern classification contexts.
originalAbstract: One method proposed for improving the generalization capability of a feed(cid:173) forward network trained with the backpropagation algorithm is to use artificial training vectors which are obtained by adding noise to the orig(cid:173) inal training vectors. We discuss the connection of such backpropagation training with noise to kernel density and kernel regression estimation. We compare by simulated examples (1) backpropagation, (2) backpropagation with noise, and (3) kernel regression in mapping estimation and pattern classification contexts.

paragraphs: The paper studies a proposed way to improve neural-network generalization: create artificial training examples by adding noise to the original training vectors. A feed-forward network then learns using backpropagation with these perturbed examples. The central question is how this training procedure relates to established statistical methods for estimating relationships from data.

The authors connect noisy backpropagation training to kernel density estimation and kernel regression. These connections provide a statistical perspective on what happens when training data are spread into nearby variations. The focus is therefore both a practical training modification and an interpretation of that modification through another family of estimation methods.

Simulated examples compare ordinary backpropagation, backpropagation with added noise, and kernel regression. The comparisons cover both mapping estimation, where the task is to predict a relationship, and pattern classification, where the task is to assign categories. The stated contribution is the connection and comparative investigation across these settings; the abstract does not identify one method as the overall winner.
summary.tldr: The paper connects noise-augmented backpropagation to kernel estimation and compares the methods on prediction and classification tasks.

title: Kernel Regression and Backpropagation Training With Noise

abstract: The most commonly used neural network models are not well suited to direct digital implementations because each node needs to per(cid:173) form a large number of operations between floating point values. Fortunately, the ability to learn from examples and to generalize is not restricted to networks ofthis type. Indeed, networks where each node implements a simple Boolean function (Boolean networks) can be designed in such a way as to exhibit similar properties. Two algorithms that generate Boolean networks from examples are pre(cid:173) sented. The results show that these algorithms generalize very well in a class of problems that accept compact Boolean network descriptions. The techniques described are general and can be ap(cid:173) plied to tasks that are not known to have that characteristic. Two examples of applications are presented: image reconstruction and hand-written character recognition.

paragraphs: The paper explores learning systems suited to direct digital implementation. Many neural network nodes require numerous floating-point operations, which motivates considering networks whose individual nodes instead compute simple Boolean functions. The authors investigate whether such networks can retain the ability to learn from examples and generalize.

They present two algorithms that construct Boolean networks from training examples. The reported results show strong generalization for a class of problems that can be described by compact Boolean networks. This condition matters because the favorable finding is tied to problems with an economical representation in the proposed form.

The methods are general enough to be applied even when compact Boolean structure is not known beforehand. The paper demonstrates applications to image reconstruction and handwritten character recognition. Its contribution is to connect simple digital operations with learned network behavior, showing that learning need not depend on the usual floating-point node computations. The application examples broaden the discussion beyond problems whose Boolean structure is already established.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms learn Boolean networks from examples, generalizing well on compactly representable problems and supporting image and handwriting applications.

title: Learning Complex Boolean Functions: Algorithms and Applications

abstract: In order to grasp an object, we need to solve the inverse kine(cid:173) matics problem, i.e., the coordinate transformation from the visual coordinates to the joint angle vector coordinates of the arm. Al(cid:173) though several models of coordinate transformation learning have been proposed, they suffer from a number of drawbacks. In human motion control, the learning of the hand position error feedback controller in the inverse kinematics solver is important. This paper proposes a novel model of the coordinate transformation learning of the human visual feedback controller that uses the change of the joint angle vector and the corresponding change of the square of the hand position error norm. The feasibility of the proposed model is illustrated using numerical simulations.
originalAbstract: In order to grasp an object, we need to solve the inverse kine(cid:173) matics problem, i.e., the coordinate transformation from the visual coordinates to the joint angle vector coordinates of the arm. Al(cid:173) though several models of coordinate transformation learning have been proposed, they suffer from a number of drawbacks. In human motion control, the learning of the hand position error feedback controller in the inverse kinematics solver is important. This paper proposes a novel model of the coordinate transformation learning of the human visual feedback controller that uses the change of the joint angle vector and the corresponding change of the square of the hand position error norm. The feasibility of the proposed model is illustrated using numerical simulations.

paragraphs: Reaching to grasp an object requires relating its visually observed position to the arm's joint angles. This is an inverse kinematics problem: a desired hand location must be translated into the coordinates that describe the arm's configuration. The paper focuses on learning the hand-position feedback controller involved in solving that transformation.

The proposed model uses two linked changes: a change in the joint-angle vector and the corresponding change in the squared magnitude of the hand-position error. The latter measures how far the hand is from its target. Relating these quantities gives the learning process information about how a joint movement changes the size of the positioning error.

This approach matters because it places changes in task error at the center of learning the visual feedback transformation. The learning signal connects movement in joint coordinates with progress toward the visible target. Numerical simulations illustrate the model's feasibility, supporting the claim that the proposed relationship can be used to learn the controller within the simulated setting.
summary.tldr: A simulated hand-position controller learns coordinate transformations by relating joint movements to changes in squared positioning error.

title: Coordinate Transformation Learning of Hand Position Feedback Controller by Using Change of Position Error Norm

abstract: The responses of cortical sensory neurons are notoriously variable, with the number of spikes evoked by identical stimuli varying signiﬁcantly from trial to trial. This variability is most often interpreted as ‘noise’, purely detrimental to the sensory system. In this paper, we propose an al- ternative view in which the variability is related to the uncertainty, about world parameters, which is inherent in the sensory stimulus. Speciﬁ- cally, the responses of a population of neurons are interpreted as stochas- tic samples from the posterior distribution in a latent variable model. In addition to giving theoretical arguments supporting such a representa- tional scheme, we provide simulations suggesting how some aspects of response variability might be understood in this framework.

This variability is most often interpreted as ‘noise’, purely detrimental to the sensory system. In this paper, we propose an al- ternative view in which the variability is related to the uncertainty, about world parameters, which is inherent in the sensory stimulus. Speciﬁ- cally, the responses of a population of neurons are interpreted as stochas- tic samples from the posterior distribution in a latent variable model. In addition to giving theoretical arguments supporting such a representa- tional scheme, we provide simulations suggesting how some aspects of response variability might be understood in this framework.

paragraphs: Sensory neurons can produce different numbers of spikes across repeated presentations of the same stimulus. This variability is commonly treated as noise that interferes with sensory processing. The paper proposes another interpretation: some variability may reflect uncertainty about the world that remains even when the sensory stimulus is fixed.

In the proposed account, population responses are stochastic samples from a posterior distribution in a latent-variable model. The posterior describes possible hidden world parameters given the sensory evidence. Different responses can therefore represent different possibilities supported by that evidence, connecting variable activity with the representation of uncertainty.

The authors provide theoretical arguments for this representation and simulations suggesting how it could explain some aspects of neural response variability. The claim is a proposed interpretation supported by modeling, rather than a demonstration that all variability has this role. Its significance is that trial-to-trial differences may contain information about sensory uncertainty, giving those differences a potential computational meaning within the model.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes that variable neural responses may encode sensory uncertainty by sampling from a posterior distribution.

title: Interpreting Neural Response Variability as Monte Carlo Sampling of the Posterior

abstract: In this paper we show that it is possible to model sensory impressions of consumers about beef meat. This is not a straightforward task; the reason is that when we are aiming to induce a function that maps object descriptions into ratings, we must consider that consumers' ratings are just a way to express their preferences about the products presented in the same testing session. Therefore, we had to use a special purpose SVM polynomial kernel. The training data set used collects the ratings of panels of experts and consumers; the meat was provided by 103 bovines of 7 Spanish breeds with different carcass weights and aging periods. Additionally, to gain insight into consumer preferences, we used feature subset selection tools. The result is that aging is the most important trait for improving consumers' appreciation of beef meat.

Therefore, we had to use a special purpose SVM polynomial kernel. The training data set used collects the ratings of panels of experts and consumers; the meat was provided by 103 bovines of 7 Spanish breeds with different carcass weights and aging periods. Additionally, to gain insight into consumer preferences, we used feature subset selection tools. The result is that aging is the most important trait for improving consumers' appreciation of beef meat.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether a model can predict consumers’ sensory impressions of beef from descriptions of the meat. A key complication is that ratings express preferences among products encountered in the same testing session. The learning problem therefore needs to account for the comparative context in which those judgments are made.

The authors use a support vector machine with a specially designed polynomial kernel for this task. Their training data include ratings from expert and consumer panels, using meat from 103 cattle across seven Spanish breeds. The samples vary in carcass weight and aging period, giving the model several traits to relate to appreciation.

The study also uses feature-subset selection to identify which traits matter for consumer preferences. Aging emerges as the most important trait for improving appreciation in the reported analysis. The contribution combines prediction with interpretation: the model addresses the structure of sensory ratings, while selecting traits yields an actionable finding about what distinguishes more appreciated beef in this study.
summary.tldr: A specialized nonlinear SVM models beef preferences, and feature selection identifies aging as the most important trait in the study.

title: Trait Selection for Assessing Beef Meat Quality Using Non-linear SVM

abstract: There has been a surge of interest in learning non-linear manifold models to approximate high-dimensional data. Both for computational complexity reasons and for generalization capability, sparsity is a desired feature in such models. This usually means dimensionality reduction, which naturally implies estimating the intrinsic dimension, but it can also mean selecting a subset of the data to use as landmarks, which is especially important because many existing algorithms have quadratic complexity in the number of observations. This paper presents an algorithm for selecting landmarks, based on LASSO regression, which is well known to favor sparse approximations because it uses regularization with an l1 norm. As an added benefit, a continuous manifold parameterization, based on the landmarks, is also found. Experimental results with synthetic and real data illustrate the algorithm.

This usually means dimensionality reduction, which naturally implies estimating the intrinsic dimension, but it can also mean selecting a subset of the data to use as landmarks, which is especially important because many existing algorithms have quadratic complexity in the number of observations. This paper presents an algorithm for selecting landmarks, based on LASSO regression, which is well known to favor sparse approximations because it uses regularization with an l1 norm. As an added benefit, a continuous manifold parameterization, based on the landmarks, is also found. Experimental results with synthetic and real data illustrate the algorithm.

paragraphs: Manifold learning seeks nonlinear representations of high-dimensional data. Sparsity can mean reducing the number of dimensions, but it can also mean representing the data through a selected subset of observations. This paper focuses on that second form: choosing landmark points that can support a compact manifold model.

The proposed algorithm selects landmarks using LASSO regression. Its l1 regularization encourages sparse approximations, making it suitable for choosing a subset rather than relying on every observation. Landmark selection addresses a computational concern because many manifold-learning methods have costs that grow quadratically with the number of observations.

The procedure also produces a continuous parameterization of the manifold based on the selected landmarks. It therefore supplies both representative points and a way to describe the manifold through them. Experiments on synthetic and real data illustrate the algorithm. The contribution connects a sparsity-promoting regression method with manifold representation, addressing the desire for compact models motivated by computational cost and generalization.
summary.tldr: LASSO-based landmark selection builds sparse manifold representations and also yields a continuous parameterization from the chosen points.

title: Selecting Landmark Points for Sparse Manifold Learning

abstract: Graph clustering methods such as spectral clustering are defined for general weighted graphs. In machine learning, however, data often is not given in form of a graph, but in terms of similarity (or distance) values between points. In this case, first a neighborhood graph is constructed using the similarities between the points and then a graph clustering algorithm is applied to this graph. In this paper we investigate the influence of the construction of the similarity graph on the clustering results. We first study the convergence of graph clustering criteria such as the normalized cut (Ncut) as the sample size tends to infinity. We find that the limit expressions are different for different types of graph, for example the r-neighborhood graph or the k -nearest neighbor graph. In plain words: Ncut on a kNN graph does something systematically different than Ncut on an r-neighborhood graph! This finding shows that graph clustering criteria cannot be studied independently of the kind of graph they are applied to. We also provide examples which show that these differences can be observed for toy and real data already for rather small sample sizes.

paragraphs: Graph clustering often begins with data that are not already a graph. Similarities or distances between observations must first be converted into connections. This paper investigates whether that preliminary construction changes what the clustering method does. It focuses on criteria such as normalized cut, which can be applied to several different kinds of neighborhood graph.

The authors analyze what these criteria approach as the sample size grows. They find different limiting expressions for different graph constructions, including radius-based neighborhood graphs and nearest-neighbor graphs. Consequently, applying the same normalized-cut criterion to these graphs can lead to systematically different clustering behavior even in the large-sample limit.

The distinction also appears in examples using toy and real data with relatively small samples. Graph construction therefore affects more than a finite-sample implementation detail: it helps determine the effective clustering objective. The paper's central implication is that understanding or comparing a graph clustering criterion requires considering the type of graph on which that criterion is evaluated.
summary.tldr: The same graph clustering criterion can have systematically different behavior depending on how the neighborhood graph is constructed.

title: Influence of graph construction on graph-based clustering measures

abstract: Multi-class classification becomes challenging at test time when the number of classes is very large and testing against every possible class can become computationally infeasible. This problem can be alleviated by imposing (or learning) a structure over the set of classes. We propose an algorithm for learning a tree-structure of classifiers which, by optimizing the overall tree loss, provides superior accuracy to existing tree labeling methods. We also propose a method that learns to embed labels in a low dimensional space that is faster than non-embedding approaches and has superior accuracy to existing embedding approaches. Finally we combine the two ideas resulting in the label embedding tree that outperforms alternative methods including One-vs-Rest while being orders of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Classification becomes expensive at prediction time when a system must consider a very large number of possible classes. Testing every class can become computationally impractical. This paper tackles that cost by learning structure over the labels, using both a tree of classifiers and a low-dimensional representation of labels.

The tree-learning algorithm optimizes the loss of the overall tree, and the authors report better accuracy than existing tree labeling methods. Separately, their label-embedding method represents labels in a lower-dimensional space. It is faster than approaches without embeddings and more accurate than existing embedding approaches in the reported comparisons.

The final method combines the two ideas into a label embedding tree. The authors report that it outperforms alternatives, including One-vs-Rest, while making predictions orders of magnitude faster. The contribution is therefore both computational and predictive: organizing a large label set and compressing its representation can work together to reduce test-time cost while improving accuracy in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Combining learned classifier trees with label embeddings improves accuracy and delivers orders-of-magnitude prediction speedups in the reported comparisons.

title: Label Embedding Trees for Large Multi-Class Tasks

abstract: The group Lasso is an extension of the Lasso for feature selection on (predefined) non-overlapping groups of features. The non-overlapping group structure limits its applicability in practice. There have been several recent attempts to study a more general formulation, where groups of features are given, potentially with overlaps between the groups. The resulting optimization is, however, much more challenging to solve due to the group overlaps. In this paper, we consider the efficient optimization of the overlapping group Lasso penalized problem. We reveal several key properties of the proximal operator associated with the overlapping group Lasso, and compute the proximal operator by solving the smooth and convex dual problem, which allows the use of the gradient descent type of algorithms for the optimization. We have performed empirical evaluations using both synthetic and the breast cancer gene expression data set, which consists of 8,141 genes organized into (overlapping) gene sets. Experimental results show that the proposed algorithm is more efficient than existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

There have been several recent attempts to study a more general formulation, where groups of features are given, potentially with overlaps between the groups. In this paper, we consider the efficient optimization of the overlapping group Lasso penalized problem. We have performed empirical evaluations using both synthetic and the breast cancer gene expression data set, which consists of 8,141 genes organized into (overlapping) gene sets. paragraphs: Group Lasso selects features using predefined groups, making it useful when variables have a known organization. Allowing a feature to belong to several groups expands the kinds of structure the method can represent. However, these overlaps also couple the groups during optimization and make the resulting problem harder to solve efficiently.

This paper studies the proximal operator associated with the overlapping group penalty, an optimization component needed to handle that penalty. The authors establish properties of the operator and compute it by solving a dual problem that is both smooth and convex. That reformulation enables gradient-descent-type algorithms.

The method is evaluated on synthetic data and breast cancer gene-expression data containing 8,141 genes arranged into overlapping gene sets. The reported experiments find it more efficient than existing state-of-the-art algorithms. The contribution therefore addresses the computational cost of using overlapping groups, making this more flexible feature organization easier to use in the tested problems.
summary.tldr: A smooth convex dual formulation enables more efficient optimization of overlapping group Lasso in the reported experiments.

title: Efficient Methods for Overlapping Group Lasso

abstract: We present an efficient algorithm for the problem of online multiclass prediction with bandit feedback in the fully adversarial setting. We measure its regret with respect to the log-loss defined in \cite{AbernethyR09}, which is parameterized by a scalar (\alpha). We prove that the regret of \newtron is (O(\log T)) when (\alpha) is a constant that does not vary with horizon (T), and at most (O(T^{2/3})) if (\alpha) is allowed to increase to infinity with (T). For (\alpha) = (O(\log T)), the regret is bounded by (O(\sqrt{T})), thus solving the open problem of \cite{KST08, AbernethyR09}. Our algorithm is based on a novel application of the online Newton method \cite{HAK07}. We test our algorithm and show it to perform well in experiments, even when (\alpha) is a small constant.

Our algorithm is based on a novel application of the online Newton method \cite{HAK07}. We test our algorithm and show it to perform well in experiments, even when (\alpha) is a small constant.

paragraphs: Newtron addresses online prediction among multiple classes when feedback is limited to the bandit setting. The analysis allows a fully adversarial sequence rather than assuming a favorable data-generating process. The authors evaluate regret using a particular log-loss family controlled by a scalar parameter, alpha, so the guarantees depend on how that parameter is chosen.

The algorithm uses a new application of the online Newton method. For a constant alpha that does not change with the prediction horizon T, the authors prove regret of O(log T). When alpha may increase toward infinity with T, they establish an upper bound of O(T^(2/3)). These statements describe different parameter regimes.

For alpha of order O(log T), the regret bound is O(sqrt(T)), resolving the open problem identified in the paper. Experimental tests also show good performance even with a small constant alpha. The contribution combines an efficient algorithm with explicit theoretical guarantees under limited feedback, while making clear that the rate depends on the parameterized loss used for comparison.
summary.tldr: Newtron efficiently handles adversarial multiclass prediction with bandit feedback and provides regret bounds that depend on its log-loss parameter.

title: Newtron: an Efficient Bandit algorithm for Online Multiclass Prediction

abstract: This paper explores unsupervised learning of parsing models along two directions. First, which models are identifiable from infinite data? We use a general technique for numerically checking identifiability based on the rank of a Jacobian matrix, and apply it to several standard constituency and dependency parsing models. Second, for identifiable models, how do we estimate the parameters efficiently? EM suffers from local optima, while recent work using spectral methods cannot be directly applied since the topology of the parse tree varies across sentences. We develop a strategy, unmixing, which deals with this additional complexity for restricted classes of parsing models.

Second, if the parameters are identifiable in that sense, can they be estimated efficiently? This paper separates those questions to study both the information available in the data and the computational difficulty of learning.

This provides a way to investigate whether a model can in principle be recovered before considering the behavior of a particular estimation algorithm.

The proposed unmixing strategy deals with that additional structural variation for restricted classes of parsing models. Its scope is therefore specific, while its motivation connects recoverability and efficient parameter learning.
summary.tldr: The paper investigates parsing-model identifiability and introduces unmixing to support efficient estimation for restricted model classes.

title: Identifiability and Unmixing of Latent Parse Trees

abstract: Residue-residue contact prediction is a fundamental problem in protein structure prediction. Hower, despite considerable research efforts, contact prediction methods are still largely unreliable. Here we introduce a novel deep machine-learning architecture which consists of a multidimensional stack of learning modules. For contact prediction, the idea is implemented as a three-dimensional stack of Neural Networks NN^k_{ij}, where i and j index the spatial coordinates of the contact map and k indexes ''time''. The temporal dimension is introduced to capture the fact that protein folding is not an instantaneous process, but rather a progressive refinement. Networks at level k in the stack can be trained in supervised fashion to refine the predictions produced by the previous level, hence addressing the problem of vanishing gradients, typical of deep architectures. Increased accuracy and generalization capabilities of this approach are established by rigorous comparison with other classical machine learning approaches for contact prediction. The deep approach leads to an accuracy for difficult long-range contacts of about 30%, roughly 10% above the state-of-the-art. Many variations in the architectures and the training algorithms are possible, leaving room for further improvements. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to other problems with strong underlying spatial and temporal components.

Each stage can be trained with supervision to improve the predictions produced by the preceding stage. The temporal organization is motivated by protein folding being a progressive process. Providing supervision at successive levels also addresses the vanishing-gradient problem associated with deep architectures, giving the intermediate prediction stages their own training role.

They also identify possible architectural and training variations and suggest applicability to other problems with strong spatial and temporal structure. The central contribution is a deep prediction process organized around successive, supervised improvements.
summary.tldr: A spatially organized stack of supervised neural networks progressively refines protein contact predictions and improves reported long-range contact accuracy.

title: Deep Spatio-Temporal Architectures and Learning for Protein Structure Prediction

abstract: Sparse high-dimensional data vectors are common in many application domains where a very large number of rarely non-zero features can be devised. Unfortunately, this creates a computational bottleneck for unsupervised feature learning algorithms such as those based on auto-encoders and RBMs, because they involve a reconstruction step where the whole input vector is predicted from the current feature values. An algorithm was recently developed to successfully handle the case of auto-encoders, based on an importance sampling scheme stochastically selecting which input elements to actually reconstruct during training for each particular example. To generalize this idea to RBMs, we propose a stochastic ratio-matching algorithm that inherits all the computational advantages and unbiasedness of the importance sampling scheme. We show that stochastic ratio matching is a good estimator, allowing the approach to beat the state-of-the-art on two bag-of-word text classification benchmarks (20 Newsgroups and RCV1), while keeping computational cost linear in the number of non-zeros.

paragraphs: Sparse data may contain extremely many possible features even though only a few are nonzero in each example. This creates a bottleneck for feature-learning methods that reconstruct an entire input vector during training. Restricted Boltzmann machines face this problem because reconstructing all coordinates can remain expensive even when the observed input is sparse.

The paper adapts an importance-sampling idea previously developed for auto-encoders. Instead of handling every input element during each training example, sampling selects which elements receive computation. The authors introduce stochastic ratio matching for RBMs, retaining the computational advantages and unbiasedness of the importance-sampling scheme.

The authors show that stochastic ratio matching provides a good estimator and report results on the 20 Newsgroups and RCV1 bag-of-words text-classification benchmarks. Their approach beats the state of the art on those two benchmarks while keeping computation linear in the number of nonzero entries. This connects learning quality with a cost measure that reflects actual input sparsity rather than the full feature vocabulary.
summary.tldr: Stochastic ratio matching trains RBMs on sparse inputs with unbiased sampling and computation linear in the number of nonzero features.

title: Stochastic Ratio Matching of RBMs for Sparse High-Dimensional Inputs

abstract: In real-world action recognition problems, low-level features cannot adequately characterize the rich spatial-temporal structures in action videos. In this work, we encode actions based on attributes that describes actions as high-level concepts: \textit{e.g.}, jump forward and motion in the air. We base our analysis on two types of action attributes. One type of action attributes is generated by humans. The second type is data-driven attributes, which is learned from data using dictionary learning methods. Attribute-based representation may exhibit high variance due to noisy and redundant attributes. We propose a discriminative and compact attribute-based representation by selecting a subset of discriminative attributes from a large attribute set. Three attribute selection criteria are proposed and formulated as a submodular optimization problem. A greedy optimization algorithm is presented and guaranteed to be at least (1-1/e)-approximation to the optimum. Experimental results on the Olympic Sports and UCF101 datasets demonstrate that the proposed attribute-based representation can significantly boost the performance of action recognition algorithms and outperform most recently proposed recognition approaches.

The second type is data-driven attributes, which is learned from data using dictionary learning methods. Attribute-based representation may exhibit high variance due to noisy and redundant attributes. paragraphs: Action videos contain spatial and temporal structure that low-level features may characterize inadequately. This paper represents actions through higher-level attributes, such as moving forward during a jump or being in the air. It considers both attributes supplied by people and attributes learned from data using dictionary-learning methods.

A large attribute vocabulary can contain noise and redundancy, making its representation variable and unnecessarily large. The authors therefore select a compact subset of discriminative attributes. They introduce three selection criteria and formulate the resulting problem as submodular optimization. A greedy algorithm comes with a guarantee of achieving at least a 1−1/e fraction of the optimum.

That guarantee concerns the attribute-selection objective. Recognition performance is assessed separately through experiments on Olympic Sports and UCF101. The results show substantial improvements to action-recognition algorithms and performance exceeding most of the recently proposed approaches considered. The paper's contribution links a high-level representation of actions with principled subset selection, using a theoretical approximation result to support selection and experiments to establish its recognition benefits.
summary.tldr: Submodular selection produces compact action-attribute representations with an approximation guarantee and improved video-recognition results.

title: Submodular Attribute Selection for Action Recognition in Video

abstract: State-of-the-art object detection networks depend on region proposal algorithms to hypothesize object locations. Advances like SPPnet and Fast R-CNN have reduced the running time of these detection networks, exposing region proposal computation as a bottleneck. In this work, we introduce a Region Proposal Network (RPN) that shares full-image convolutional features with the detection network, thus enabling nearly cost-free region proposals. An RPN is a fully-convolutional network that simultaneously predicts object bounds and objectness scores at each position. RPNs are trained end-to-end to generate high-quality region proposals, which are used by Fast R-CNN for detection. With a simple alternating optimization, RPN and Fast R-CNN can be trained to share convolutional features. For the very deep VGG-16 model, our detection system has a frame rate of 5fps (including all steps) on a GPU, while achieving state-of-the-art object detection accuracy on PASCAL VOC 2007 (73.2% mAP) and 2012 (70.4% mAP) using 300 proposals per image. Code is available at https://github.com/ShaoqingRen/faster_rcnn.

paragraphs: Object detection systems need candidate regions indicating where objects might be. As detection networks became faster, generating those proposals emerged as a major remaining computational cost. Faster R-CNN addresses that bottleneck by making proposal generation a neural-network component that shares image features with the detector.

The Region Proposal Network is fully convolutional and predicts both object boundaries and objectness scores at each position. It is trained end to end to produce proposals that Fast R-CNN then uses for detection. A simple alternating optimization procedure trains the two networks to share convolutional features, allowing proposal generation to reuse computation already needed for detecting objects.

With the very deep VGG-16 model, the complete system runs at five frames per second on a GPU, including all processing steps. Using 300 proposals per image, it reports 73.2% mean average precision on PASCAL VOC 2007 and 70.4% on 2012, described as state-of-the-art accuracy. The contribution is the combination of effective detection and nearly cost-free proposals through shared full-image features.
summary.tldr: Faster R-CNN shares convolutional features between region proposal and detection networks to reduce proposal cost while maintaining strong detection accuracy.

title: Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks

abstract: We present a data-driven stochastic optimal control framework that is derived using the path integral (PI) control approach. We find iterative control laws analytically without a priori policy parameterization based on probabilistic representation of the learned dynamics model. The proposed algorithm operates in a forward-backward sweep manner which differentiate it from other PI-related methods that perform forward sampling to find open-loop optimal controls. Our method uses significantly less sampled data to find analytic control laws compared to other approaches within the PI control family that rely on extensive sampling from given dynamics models or trials on physical systems in a model-free fashion. In addition, the learned controllers can be generalized to new tasks without re-sampling based on the compositionality theory for the linearly-solvable optimal control framework.We provide experimental results on three different systems and comparisons with state-of-the-art model-based methods to demonstrate the efficiency and generalizability of the proposed framework.

The proposed algorithm operates in a forward-backward sweep manner which differentiate it from other PI-related methods that perform forward sampling to find open-loop optimal controls. Our method uses significantly less sampled data to find analytic control laws compared to other approaches within the PI control family that rely on extensive sampling from given dynamics models or trials on physical systems in a model-free fashion. In addition, the learned controllers can be generalized to new tasks without re-sampling based on the compositionality theory for the linearly-solvable optimal control framework.We provide experimental results on three different systems and comparisons with state-of-the-art model-based methods to demonstrate the efficiency and generalizability of the proposed framework.

paragraphs: The paper develops stochastic optimal control from a learned probabilistic model of system dynamics. Using the path-integral approach, it derives iterative control laws analytically without requiring a policy parameterization in advance. Uncertainty in the learned dynamics is part of the representation used to construct the controller.

Its computation proceeds through a forward-backward sweep. This distinguishes it from path-integral methods that use forward sampling to obtain open-loop controls. The authors report needing significantly less sampled data than approaches in that family that depend on extensive simulation from dynamics models or repeated model-free trials on physical systems.

The learned controllers can also be generalized to new tasks without resampling through compositionality in the linearly solvable optimal-control framework. That framework provides the basis for the transfer claim. Experiments on three systems, including comparisons with state-of-the-art model-based methods, demonstrate the proposed method’s efficiency and generalizability. The contribution combines analytical controller construction, a probabilistic dynamics model, and a way to reuse learned control information across tasks.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic path-integral control method derives analytical controllers with fewer samples and supports task reuse through linearly solvable control compositionality.

title: Sample Efficient Path Integral Control under Uncertainty

abstract: The well known maximum-entropy principle due to Jaynes, which states that given mean parameters, the maximum entropy distribution matching them is in an exponential family has been very popular in machine learning due to its “Occam’s razor” interpretation. Unfortunately, calculating the potentials in the maximum entropy distribution is intractable [BGS14]. We provide computationally efficient versions of this principle when the mean parameters are pairwise moments: we design distributions that approximately match given pairwise moments, while having entropy which is comparable to the maximum entropy distribution matching those moments. We additionally provide surprising applications of the approximate maximum entropy principle to designing provable variational methods for partition function calculations for Ising models without any assumptions on the potentials of the model. More precisely, we show that we can get approximation guarantees for the log-partition function comparable to those in the low-temperature limit, which is the setting of optimization of quadratic forms over the hypercube. ([AN06])

paragraphs: The maximum-entropy principle selects a distribution that matches specified averages while retaining as much uncertainty as possible. Although the resulting distribution belongs to an exponential family, finding its parameters can be computationally intractable. This paper develops an efficient approximate version when the supplied information consists of pairwise moments.

The constructed distributions approximately reproduce those moments while achieving entropy comparable to that of the exact maximum-entropy solution. Both parts matter: matching the statistics alone would not preserve the uncertainty objective, while high entropy alone would not respect the observed relationships. The result provides a computationally accessible way to pursue these requirements together.

The authors apply this principle to variational calculations for the log-partition function of Ising models. Their approximation guarantees require no assumptions on the models' potentials. They obtain guarantees comparable to those available in the low-temperature limit, where the related problem becomes optimization of quadratic forms over the hypercube. This connects an approximate distribution-construction principle to provable methods for a difficult probabilistic calculation.
summary.tldr: Efficient approximate maximum-entropy constructions yield provable variational guarantees for Ising log-partition functions without restrictions on model potentials.

title: Approximate maximum entropy principles via Goemans-Williamson with applications to provable variational methods

abstract: We consider convex-concave saddle-point problems where the objective functions may be split in many components, and extend recent stochastic variance reduction methods (such as SVRG or SAGA) to provide the first large-scale linearly convergent algorithms for this class of problems which are common in machine learning. While the algorithmic extension is straightforward, it comes with challenges and opportunities: (a) the convex minimization analysis does not apply and we use the notion of monotone operators to prove convergence, showing in particular that the same algorithm applies to a larger class of problems, such as variational inequalities, (b) there are two notions of splits, in terms of functions, or in terms of partial derivatives, (c) the split does need to be done with convex-concave terms, (d) non-uniform sampling is key to an efficient algorithm, both in theory and practice, and (e) these incremental algorithms can be easily accelerated using a simple extension of the "catalyst" framework, leading to an algorithm which is always superior to accelerated batch algorithms.

While the algorithmic extension is straightforward, it comes with challenges and opportunities: (a) the convex minimization analysis does not apply and we use the notion of monotone operators to prove convergence, showing in particular that the same algorithm applies to a larger class of problems, such as variational inequalities, (b) there are two notions of splits, in terms of functions, or in terms of partial derivatives, (c) the split does need to be done with convex-concave terms, (d) non-uniform sampling is key to an efficient algorithm, both in theory and practice, and (e) these incremental algorithms can be easily accelerated using a simple extension of the "catalyst" framework, leading to an algorithm which is always superior to accelerated batch algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper extends stochastic variance-reduction methods such as SVRG and SAGA to convex-concave saddle-point problems with objectives split into many components. It presents large-scale algorithms with linear convergence for the class studied. The aim is to bring incremental optimization techniques to problems involving both minimization and maximization.

Although the algorithmic extension is straightforward, the analysis used for convex minimization does not transfer directly. The authors instead use monotone operators to establish convergence, also extending the algorithm's applicability to problems such as variational inequalities. They distinguish splitting an objective into functions from splitting it through partial derivatives and discuss the convex-concave requirement on the terms.

Nonuniform sampling is identified as important for efficiency in both the theoretical analysis and practical results. The methods can also be accelerated through an extension of the catalyst framework. The authors report that the resulting accelerated algorithm is superior to accelerated batch algorithms in their comparison. Together, these contributions combine a new convergence analysis with choices that improve incremental saddle-point optimization.
summary.tldr: Variance-reduced incremental algorithms extend to saddle-point problems, with monotone-operator convergence proofs and catalyst-based acceleration.

title: Stochastic Variance Reduction Methods for Saddle-Point Problems

abstract: Estimators of information theoretic measures such as entropy and mutual information from samples are a basic workhorse for many downstream applications in modern data science. State of the art approaches have been either geometric (nearest neighbor (NN) based) or kernel based (with bandwidth chosen to be data independent and vanishing sub linearly in the sample size). In this paper we combine both these approaches to design new estimators of entropy and mutual information that strongly outperform all state of the art methods. Our estimator uses bandwidth choice of fixed $k$-NN distances; such a choice is both data dependent and linearly vanishing in the sample size and necessitates a bias cancellation term that is universal and independent of the underlying distribution. As a byproduct, we obtain a unified way of obtaining both kernel and NN estimators. The corresponding theoretical contribution relating the geometry of NN distances to asymptotic order statistics is of independent mathematical interest.

In this paper we combine both these approaches to design new estimators of entropy and mutual information that strongly outperform all state of the art methods. Our estimator uses bandwidth choice of fixed $k$-NN distances; such a choice is both data dependent and linearly vanishing in the sample size and necessitates a bias cancellation term that is universal and independent of the underlying distribution. As a byproduct, we obtain a unified way of obtaining both kernel and NN estimators. The corresponding theoretical contribution relating the geometry of NN distances to asymptotic order statistics is of independent mathematical interest.

paragraphs: Entropy and mutual information summarize uncertainty and statistical dependence, but estimating them from samples requires handling the geometry of the observed data. Existing approaches have largely used either nearest neighbor geometry or kernel smoothing. This paper combines those two approaches to build new estimators of both quantities.

The key choice is to set the kernel bandwidth using distances to a fixed number of nearest neighbors. That makes the smoothing scale depend on the data rather than selecting it independently. The abstract describes this bandwidth as shrinking linearly with sample size. Such a choice requires a bias cancellation term, which the authors show is universal and does not depend on the underlying distribution.

The paper reports that the resulting estimators substantially outperform existing methods. Its framework also offers a unified route to both kernel and nearest neighbor estimators, connecting approaches usually presented separately. On the theoretical side, it relates nearest neighbor distance geometry to asymptotic order statistics. Thus, the contribution concerns both estimator performance and the mathematical explanation of how local sample geometry supports information estimation.
summary.tldr: Data-dependent nearest neighbor bandwidths and a universal bias correction unite kernel and geometric approaches to entropy and mutual information estimation.

title: Breaking the Bandwidth Barrier: Geometrical Adaptive Entropy Estimation

abstract: Clustering is a fundamental step in many information-retrieval and data-mining applications. Detecting clusters in graphs is also a key tool for finding the community structure in social and behavioral networks. In many of these applications, the input graph evolves over time in a continual and decentralized manner, and, to maintain a good clustering, the clustering algorithm needs to repeatedly probe the graph. Furthermore, there are often limitations on the frequency of such probes, either imposed explicitly by the online platform (e.g., in the case of crawling proprietary social networks like twitter) or implicitly because of resource limitations (e.g., in the case of crawling the web). In this paper, we study a model of clustering on evolving graphs that captures this aspect of the problem. Our model is based on the classical stochastic block model, which has been used to assess rigorously the quality of various static clustering methods. In our model, the algorithm is supposed to reconstruct the planted clustering, given the ability to query for small pieces of local information about the graph, at a limited rate. We design and analyze clustering algorithms that work in this model, and show asymptotically tight upper and lower bounds on their accuracy. Finally, we perform simulations, which demonstrate that our main asymptotic results hold true also in practice.

paragraphs: Finding communities becomes harder when a network keeps changing and an algorithm cannot inspect it continuously. The paper studies this setting, where maintaining a useful clustering requires repeated observations but access is limited by platform rules or available resources. The key issue is how accurately communities can be tracked with a restricted rate of information gathering.

The authors formulate an evolving graph model based on the stochastic block model. Within it, the algorithm tries to reconstruct a planted clustering while querying only small pieces of local graph information. This makes the observation constraint part of the mathematical problem, alongside the graph's community structure and its evolution.

They design and analyze clustering algorithms and derive asymptotically tight upper and lower bounds on accuracy. The paired bounds characterize attainable performance and the limits imposed by this model at the asymptotic scale. Simulations also support the relevance of the main theoretical findings in the tested settings, connecting the analysis to behavior beyond the asymptotic statements.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how accurately communities can be recovered in evolving graphs when local observations arrive at a limited rate.

title: Community Detection on Evolving Graphs

abstract: Many machine learning applications involve jointly predicting multiple mutually dependent output variables. Learning to search is a family of methods where the complex decision problem is cast into a sequence of decisions via a search space. Although these methods have shown promise both in theory and in practice, implementing them has been burdensomely awkward. In this paper, we show the search space can be defined by an arbitrary imperative program, turning learning to search into a credit assignment compiler. Altogether with the algorithmic improvements for the compiler, we radically reduce the complexity of programming and the running time. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach on multiple joint prediction tasks. In all cases, we obtain accuracies as high as alternative approaches, at drastically reduced execution and programming time.

paragraphs: Joint prediction tasks require several outputs to be chosen together because their values depend on one another. Learning to search handles this by turning a structured prediction into a sequence of decisions. Although the approach has theoretical and practical promise, defining the necessary search machinery has made implementations cumbersome.

This paper allows the search space to be specified by an arbitrary imperative program. The surrounding learning system becomes a credit-assignment compiler that supports learning over the program’s decisions. Algorithmic improvements to that compiler aim to reduce both execution cost and the amount of programming required.

Evaluations on multiple joint-prediction tasks obtain accuracy comparable to alternative approaches while substantially reducing programming and execution time. The abstract does not identify exact tasks, runtimes, or code-size measurements. The practical contribution is a programming interface and learning mechanism that make structured decision problems easier to express without sacrificing the reported predictive performance.
summary.tldr: A credit-assignment compiler makes learning-to-search systems easier and faster to implement.

title: A Credit Assignment Compiler for Joint Prediction

abstract: An important problem in sequential decision-making under uncertainty is to use limited data to compute a safe policy, i.e., a policy that is guaranteed to perform at least as well as a given baseline strategy. In this paper, we develop and analyze a new model-based approach to compute a safe policy when we have access to an inaccurate dynamics model of the system with known accuracy guarantees. Our proposed robust method uses this (inaccurate) model to directly minimize the (negative) regret w.r.t. the baseline policy. Contrary to the existing approaches, minimizing the regret allows one to improve the baseline policy in states with accurate dynamics and seamlessly fall back to the baseline policy, otherwise. We show that our formulation is NP-hard and propose an approximate algorithm. Our empirical results on several domains show that even this relatively simple approximate algorithm can significantly outperform standard approaches.
originalAbstract: An important problem in sequential decision-making under uncertainty is to use limited data to compute a safe policy, i.e., a policy that is guaranteed to perform at least as well as a given baseline strategy. In this paper, we develop and analyze a new model-based approach to compute a safe policy when we have access to an inaccurate dynamics model of the system with known accuracy guarantees. Our proposed robust method uses this (inaccurate) model to directly minimize the (negative) regret w.r.t. the baseline policy. Contrary to the existing approaches, minimizing the regret allows one to improve the baseline policy in states with accurate dynamics and seamlessly fall back to the baseline policy, otherwise. Our empirical results on several domains show that even this relatively simple approximate algorithm can significantly outperform standard approaches.

It studies how to pursue that goal using an inaccurate dynamics model whose accuracy guarantees are known.

The proposed robust formulation directly optimizes performance relative to the baseline through a regret objective. This allows improvement in states where the dynamics are accurately modeled while falling back to the baseline elsewhere. The baseline therefore guides how the method responds to uneven knowledge about the system.

The authors show that their formulation is NP-hard and develop an approximate algorithm to make the approach usable. Experiments across several domains show that even this relatively simple approximation can substantially outperform standard approaches. The theoretical formulation and empirical approximation serve distinct roles: the formulation captures robust baseline-relative improvement, while the experiments demonstrate the practical promise of the proposed approximation under model uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Robust baseline-regret optimization targets policy improvements where dynamics are accurate and fallback behavior where they are uncertain.

title: Safe Policy Improvement by Minimizing Robust Baseline Regret

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new image representation based on a multilayer kernel machine. Unlike traditional kernel methods where data representation is decoupled from the prediction task, we learn how to shape the kernel with supervision. We proceed by first proposing improvements of the recently-introduced convolutional kernel networks (CKNs) in the context of unsupervised learning; then, we derive backpropagation rules to take advantage of labeled training data. The resulting model is a new type of convolutional neural network, where optimizing the filters at each layer is equivalent to learning a linear subspace in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). We show that our method achieves reasonably competitive performance for image classification on some standard ``deep learning'' datasets such as CIFAR-10 and SVHN, and also for image super-resolution, demonstrating the applicability of our approach to a large variety of image-related tasks.

This paper develops a multilayer image representation in which supervision can shape the kernel itself. The aim is to let the representation respond to what the model is being trained to predict.

The authors first improve convolutional kernel networks in an unsupervised setting, then derive backpropagation rules that allow labeled examples to guide learning. The resulting architecture is a form of convolutional neural network with a kernel interpretation. summary.tldr: Supervised convolutional kernel networks learn task-dependent image representations through backpropagation while retaining a kernel-space interpretation.

title: End-to-End Kernel Learning with Supervised Convolutional Kernel Networks

abstract: Equipping machine learning models with ethical and legal constraints is a serious issue; without this, the future of machine learning is at risk. This paper takes a step forward in this direction and focuses on ensuring machine learning models deliver fair decisions. In legal scholarships, the notion of fairness itself is evolving and multi-faceted. We set an overarching goal to develop a unified machine learning framework that is able to handle any definitions of fairness, their combinations, and also new definitions that might be stipulated in the future. To achieve our goal, we recycle two well-established machine learning techniques, privileged learning and distribution matching, and harmonize them for satisfying multi-faceted fairness definitions. We consider protected characteristics such as race and gender as privileged information that is available at training but not at test time; this accelerates model training and delivers fairness through unawareness. Further, we cast demographic parity, equalized odds, and equality of opportunity as a classical two-sample problem of conditional distributions, which can be solved in a general form by using distance measures in Hilbert Space. We show several existing models are special cases of ours. Finally, we advocate returning the Pareto frontier of multi-objective minimization of error and unfairness in predictions. This will facilitate decision makers to select an operating point and to be accountable for it.

This paper pursues a unified framework for accommodating such definitions and their combinations. It brings together privileged learning and distribution matching, treating fairness as something that can influence training and be evaluated alongside predictive error.

The authors describe this as accelerating training and providing fairness through unawareness. summary.tldr: A fairness framework combines protected information during training with distribution matching and exposes tradeoffs between predictive error and unfairness.

title: Recycling Privileged Learning and Distribution Matching for Fairness

abstract: Optimizing distributed learning systems is an art of balancing between computation and communication. There have been two lines of research that try to deal with slower networks: {\em communication compression} for low bandwidth networks, and {\em decentralization} for high latency networks. In this paper, We explore a natural question: {\em can the combination of both techniques lead to a system that is robust to both bandwidth and latency?} Although the system implication of such combination is trivial, the underlying theoretical principle and algorithm design is challenging: unlike centralized algorithms, simply compressing {\rc exchanged information, even in an unbiased stochastic way, within the decentralized network would accumulate the error and cause divergence.} In this paper, we develop a framework of quantized, decentralized training and propose two different strategies, which we call {\em extrapolation compression} and {\em difference compression}. We analyze both algorithms and prove both converge at the rate of $O(1/\sqrt{nT})$ where $n$ is the number of workers and $T$ is the number of iterations, matching the convergence rate for full precision, centralized training. We validate our algorithms and find that our proposed algorithm outperforms the best of merely decentralized and merely quantized algorithm significantly for networks with {\em both} high latency and low bandwidth.

paragraphs: Distributed learning must balance calculation time against the cost of exchanging information. Compression addresses limited network bandwidth, while decentralized training addresses high communication latency. This paper investigates how to combine the two so that training can work well when both network problems occur together.

The combination requires more than simply reducing the precision of messages. In decentralized training, compression errors can accumulate and cause divergence, even when the compression is unbiased. The authors introduce a quantized decentralized training framework with two strategies, extrapolation compression and difference compression. Both are designed to make compressed communication compatible with a convergent learning process.

The analysis proves a convergence rate of O(1/sqrt(nT)) for both algorithms, where n is the worker count and T is the iteration count. This matches the stated rate for full-precision centralized training. Empirical validation finds significant improvements over approaches using only decentralization or only quantization on networks with both high latency and low bandwidth, supporting the value of addressing the two communication constraints together.
summary.tldr: Two compressed decentralized training strategies achieve the stated centralized convergence rate and improve performance on networks with both low bandwidth and high latency.

title: Communication Compression for Decentralized Training

abstract: Back-propagation (BP) is the foundation for successfully training deep neural networks. However, BP sometimes has difficulties in propagating a learning signal deep enough effectively, e.g., the vanishing gradient phenomenon. Meanwhile, BP often works well when combining with ``designing tricks'' like orthogonal initialization, batch normalization and skip connection. There is no clear understanding on what is essential to the efficiency of BP. In this paper, we take one step towards clarifying this problem. We view BP as a solution of back-matching propagation which minimizes a sequence of back-matching losses each corresponding to one block of the network. We study the Hessian of the local back-matching loss (local Hessian) and connect it to the efficiency of BP. It turns out that those designing tricks facilitate BP by improving the spectrum of local Hessian. In addition, we can utilize the local Hessian to balance the training pace of each block and design new training algorithms. Based on a scalar approximation of local Hessian, we propose a scale-amended SGD algorithm. We apply it to train neural networks with batch normalization, and achieve favorable results over vanilla SGD. This corroborates the importance of local Hessian from another side.

This paper seeks a common explanation for that improvement. It views back-propagation through back-matching propagation, which minimizes a sequence of losses associated with individual network blocks.

They connect the spectrum of this local Hessian to the effectiveness of back-propagation and explain the listed design choices through improvements to that spectrum. summary.tldr: Local curvature helps explain effective back-propagation design choices and motivates an SGD variant that balances learning across network blocks.

title: On the Local Hessian in Back-propagation

abstract: Many modern machine learning models are trained to achieve zero or near-zero training error in order to obtain near-optimal (but non-zero) test error. This phenomenon of strong generalization performance for ``overfitted'' / interpolated classifiers appears to be ubiquitous in high-dimensional data, having been observed in deep networks, kernel machines, boosting and random forests. Their performance is consistently robust even when the data contain large amounts of label noise. Very little theory is available to explain these observations. The vast majority of theoretical analyses of generalization allows for interpolation only when there is little or no label noise. This paper takes a step toward a theoretical foundation for interpolated classifiers by analyzing local interpolating schemes, including geometric simplicial interpolation algorithm and singularly weighted $k$-nearest neighbor schemes. Consistency or near-consistency is proved for these schemes in classification and regression problems. Moreover, the nearest neighbor schemes exhibit optimal rates under some standard statistical assumptions. Finally, this paper suggests a way to explain the phenomenon of adversarial examples, which are seemingly ubiquitous in modern machine learning, and also discusses some connections to kernel machines and random forests in the interpolated regime.
