paragraphs: A model can fit its training examples perfectly and still perform well on new data, even when training labels contain substantial noise. This challenges the idea that interpolation necessarily indicates harmful overfitting. The paper develops theory for specific local prediction rules to help explain how exact fitting can coexist with good generalization.

The analysis covers geometric simplicial interpolation and nearest-neighbor methods with singular weights. For these schemes, the authors prove consistency or near-consistency in classification and regression. These results concern how prediction risk behaves as more data become available. They establish that fitting the observations exactly need not prevent the analyzed procedures from approaching good population-level performance.

Under some standard statistical assumptions, the nearest-neighbor schemes also achieve optimal rates. The scope of those guarantees is the particular schemes and assumptions studied, rather than every interpolating model. The paper additionally suggests an explanation for adversarial examples and discusses connections to kernel methods and random forests. Those connections position the local analysis as a step toward understanding a broader empirical phenomenon.
summary.tldr: Theory for local interpolating predictors shows that exact training fit can coexist with consistency and, under stated assumptions, optimal statistical rates.

title: Overfitting or perfect fitting? Risk bounds for classification and regression rules that interpolate

abstract: The Equalized Odds (for short, EO) is one of the most popular measures of discrimination used in the supervised learning setting. It ascertains fairness through the balance of the misclassification rates (false positive and negative) across the protected groups -- e.g., in the context of law enforcement, an African-American defendant who would not commit a future crime will have an equal opportunity of being released, compared to a non-recidivating Caucasian defendant. Despite this noble goal, it has been acknowledged in the literature that statistical tests based on the EO are oblivious to the underlying causal mechanisms that generated the disparity in the first place (Hardt et al. 2016). This leads to a critical disconnect between statistical measures readable from the data and the meaning of discrimination in the legal system, where compelling evidence that the observed disparity is tied to a specific causal process deemed unfair by society is required to characterize discrimination. The goal of this paper is to develop a principled approach to connect the statistical disparities characterized by the EO and the underlying, elusive, and frequently unobserved, causal mechanisms that generated such inequality. We start by introducing a new family of counterfactual measures that allows one to explain the misclassification disparities in terms of the underlying mechanisms in an arbitrary, non-parametric structural causal model. This will, in turn, allow legal and data analysts to interpret currently deployed classifiers through causal lens, linking the statistical disparities found in the data to the corresponding causal processes. Leveraging the new family of counterfactual measures, we develop a learning procedure to construct a classifier that is statistically efficient, interpretable, and compatible with the basic human intuition of fairness. We demonstrate our results through experiments in both real (COMPAS) and synthetic datasets.

Experiments use both synthetic data and the COMPAS dataset. The contribution connects evaluation and model construction: the same causal perspective that helps explain errors also informs how a classifier is learned.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual measures connect unequal classification errors to causal mechanisms and support a learning procedure informed by that causal account.

title: Equality of Opportunity in Classification: A Causal Approach

abstract: We study the multi-channel sparse blind deconvolution (MCS-BD) problem, whose task is to simultaneously recover a kernel $\mathbf a$ and multiple sparse inputs $\{\mathbf x_i\}_{i=1}^p$ from their circulant convolution $\mathbf y_i = \mb a \circledast \mb x_i $ ($i=1,\cdots,p$). We formulate the task as a nonconvex optimization problem over the sphere. Under mild statistical assumptions of the data, we prove that the vanilla Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) method, with random initializations, provably recovers both the kernel $\mathbf a$ and the signals $\{\mathbf x_i\}_{i=1}^p$ up to a signed shift ambiguity. In comparison with state-of-the-art results, our work shows significant improvements in terms of sample complexity and computational efficiency. Our theoretical results are corroborated by numerical experiments, which demonstrate superior performance of the proposed approach over the previous methods on both synthetic and real datasets.

We formulate the task as a nonconvex optimization problem over the sphere. Under mild statistical assumptions of the data, we prove that the vanilla Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) method, with random initializations, provably recovers both the kernel $\mathbf a$ and the signals $\{\mathbf x_i\}_{i=1}^p$ up to a signed shift ambiguity. paragraphs: Multichannel sparse blind deconvolution seeks to recover a shared kernel and several sparse input signals from their observed convolutions. Both the kernel and the original inputs are unknown. This paper studies the circulant convolution setting and formulates recovery as a nonconvex optimization problem constrained to a sphere.

The proposed solver is ordinary Riemannian gradient descent, which performs gradient-based optimization while respecting that spherical constraint. Under mild statistical assumptions on the data, the authors prove that random initialization followed by this method recovers both the kernel and the signals. Recovery is qualified by a signed shift ambiguity, so the guarantee allows that remaining equivalence between recovered solutions.

Compared with prior state-of-the-art results, the paper reports improvements in sample complexity and computational efficiency. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the theory and show superior performance over earlier methods. The significance is that a relatively direct optimization procedure has a recovery guarantee under the stated assumptions, despite the nonconvex formulation and the need to estimate multiple unknown components jointly.
summary.tldr: Under statistical assumptions, Riemannian gradient descent recovers a shared convolution kernel and sparse signals up to a signed shift ambiguity.

title: A Nonconvex Approach for Exact and Efficient Multichannel Sparse Blind Deconvolution

abstract: This paper studies the online optimal control problem with time-varying convex stage costs for a time-invariant linear dynamical system, where a finite lookahead window of accurate predictions of the stage costs are available at each time. We design online algorithms, Receding Horizon Gradient-based Control (RHGC), that utilize the predictions through finite steps of gradient computations. We study the algorithm performance measured by dynamic regret: the online performance minus the optimal performance in hindsight. It is shown that the dynamic regret of RHGC decays exponentially with the size of the lookahead window. In addition, we provide a fundamental limit of the dynamic regret for any online algorithms by considering linear quadratic tracking problems. The regret upper bound of one RHGC method almost reaches the fundamental limit, demonstrating the effectiveness of the algorithm. Finally, we numerically test our algorithms for both linear and nonlinear systems to show the effectiveness and generality of our RHGC.

paragraphs: The paper studies online control for a time-invariant linear system with convex costs that change over time. At each decision, the controller has accurate predictions of those costs over a finite future window. The question is how effectively a computationally limited controller can use that lookahead.

The proposed Receding Horizon Gradient-based Control algorithms use a finite number of gradient computations to incorporate predictions. Performance is measured by dynamic regret: the difference between the online controller's cost and the best cost achievable with hindsight. The authors show that RHGC's regret decreases exponentially as the prediction window grows in the analyzed setting.

The paper also derives a fundamental regret limit for online algorithms using linear quadratic tracking problems. One RHGC method has an upper bound that nearly reaches that limit, indicating that its use of predictions is close to the theoretical benchmark. Numerical tests on both linear and nonlinear systems provide further evidence of effectiveness. The nonlinear experiments broaden the empirical demonstration beyond the linear dynamics assumed in the stated theoretical problem.
summary.tldr: Gradient-based receding-horizon controllers achieve exponentially decreasing dynamic regret as accurate cost lookahead grows in the analyzed linear setting.

title: Online Optimal Control with Linear Dynamics and Predictions: Algorithms and Regret Analysis

abstract: How should a player who repeatedly plays a game against a no-regret learner strategize to maximize his utility? We study this question and show that under some mild assumptions, the player can always guarantee himself a utility of at least what he would get in a Stackelberg equilibrium. When the no-regret learner has only two actions, we show that the player cannot get any higher utility than the Stackelberg equilibrium utility. But when the no-regret learner has more than two actions and plays a mean-based no-regret strategy, we show that the player can get strictly higher than the Stackelberg equilibrium utility. We construct the optimal game-play for the player against a mean-based no-regret learner who has three actions. When the no-regret learner's strategy also guarantees him a no-swap regret, we show that the player cannot get anything higher than a Stackelberg equilibrium utility.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a strategic player should act when repeatedly facing an opponent that uses a no-regret learning algorithm. Its benchmark is the player’s utility in a Stackelberg equilibrium. Under mild assumptions, the authors show that the strategic player can guarantee at least that much utility against a no-regret learner.

Whether the player can do better depends on the learner’s available actions and learning strategy. With only two actions for the learner, the Stackelberg utility is an upper bound as well. With more than two actions and a mean-based no-regret strategy, the player can obtain strictly more. The paper constructs optimal play against a mean-based learner with three actions.

A stronger learning guarantee changes that conclusion: if the learner also has no swap regret, the strategic player cannot exceed the Stackelberg benchmark. The results therefore distinguish several forms of protection against strategic opponents. Ordinary no-regret behavior permits different outcomes depending on the action set and strategy class, while the additional no-swap-regret guarantee restores the stated utility ceiling.
summary.tldr: A strategic player’s achievable utility against a no-regret learner depends on the learner’s action count and whether it also guarantees no swap regret.

title: Strategizing against No-regret Learners

abstract: Computing expected predictions of discriminative models is a fundamental task in machine learning that appears in many interesting applications such as fairness, handling missing values, and data analysis. Unfortunately, computing expectations of a discriminative model with respect to a probability distribution defined by an arbitrary generative model has been proven to be hard in general. In fact, the task is intractable even for simple models such as logistic regression and a naive Bayes distribution. In this paper, we identify a pair of generative and discriminative models that enables tractable computation of expectations, as well as moments of any order, of the latter with respect to the former in case of regression. Specifically, we consider expressive probabilistic circuits with certain structural constraints that support tractable probabilistic inference. Moreover, we exploit the tractable computation of high-order moments to derive an algorithm to approximate the expectations for classification scenarios in which exact computations are intractable. Our framework to compute expected predictions allows for handling of missing data during prediction time in a principled and accurate way and enables reasoning about the behavior of discriminative models. We empirically show our algorithm to consistently outperform standard imputation techniques on a variety of datasets. Finally, we illustrate how our framework can be used for exploratory data analysis.

This operation is useful for missing data, fairness, and model analysis, but it can be computationally intractable even when combining logistic regression with a naive Bayes distribution. The paper asks which model structures make the calculation manageable.

The authors identify a pairing of generative and discriminative models that permits tractable expectations and moments of any order for regression. Their construction uses expressive probabilistic circuits subject to particular structural constraints. These constraints are central: efficient inference comes from the selected model pairing, rather than from an unrestricted ability to combine arbitrary predictors and distributions.

For classification cases where exact expectations remain intractable, the authors use higher-order moments to develop an approximation algorithm. The framework also handles missing inputs at prediction time by accounting for their uncertainty. Experiments report consistent improvements over standard imputation techniques across a variety of datasets. An exploratory data analysis application further illustrates how expected predictions can support reasoning about model behavior.
summary.tldr: Structurally constrained model pairs enable exact expected regression predictions and moment-based approximations for classification, improving missing-data prediction in experiments.

title: On Tractable Computation of Expected Predictions

abstract: We introduce a framework for inference in general state-space hidden Markov models (HMMs) under likelihood misspecification. In particular, we leverage the loss-theoretic perspective of Generalized Bayesian Inference (GBI) to define generalised filtering recursions in HMMs, that can tackle the problem of inference under model misspecification. In doing so, we arrive at principled procedures for robust inference against observation contamination by utilising the $\beta$-divergence. Operationalising the proposed framework is made possible via sequential Monte Carlo methods (SMC), where the standard particle methods, and their associated convergence results, are readily adapted to the new setting. We demonstrate our approach to object tracking and Gaussian process regression problems, and observe improved performance over standard filtering algorithms.

In doing so, we arrive at principled procedures for robust inference against observation contamination by utilising the $\beta$-divergence. Operationalising the proposed framework is made possible via sequential Monte Carlo methods (SMC), where the standard particle methods, and their associated convergence results, are readily adapted to the new setting. We demonstrate our approach to object tracking and Gaussian process regression problems, and observe improved performance over standard filtering algorithms.

paragraphs: Filtering estimates a changing hidden state from observations arriving over time. In a hidden Markov model, this inference depends on an assumed observation likelihood. This paper considers what happens when that likelihood is misspecified, meaning the model’s description of observations does not adequately match the data-generating process.

The authors build filtering recursions using the loss-based perspective of generalized Bayesian inference. In particular, they use beta-divergence to obtain principled procedures designed to resist contamination in observations. This changes how observations contribute to inference, giving the framework a way to address mismatch in the observation model rather than simply applying the usual likelihood-based update.

Sequential Monte Carlo makes the framework computationally usable: standard particle methods and their convergence results can be adapted to the generalized setting. The authors demonstrate the approach on object tracking and Gaussian process regression, observing improvements over standard filtering algorithms. The contribution combines a robust inference formulation with an established computational approach, making the proposed updates practical while carrying over relevant convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: Generalized Bayesian updates and particle methods provide robust filtering under misspecified observation likelihoods.

title: Generalised Bayesian Filtering via Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: Applying image processing algorithms independently to each video frame often leads to temporal inconsistency in the resulting video. To address this issue, we present a novel and general approach for blind video temporal consistency. Our method is only trained on a pair of original and processed videos directly instead of a large dataset. Unlike most previous methods that enforce temporal consistency with optical flow, we show that temporal consistency can be achieved by training a convolutional network on a video with the Deep Video Prior. Moreover, a carefully designed iteratively reweighted training strategy is proposed to address the challenging multimodal inconsistency problem. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on 7 computer vision tasks on videos. Extensive quantitative and perceptual experiments show that our approach obtains superior performance than state-of-the-art methods on blind video temporal consistency.

Moreover, a carefully designed iteratively reweighted training strategy is proposed to address the challenging multimodal inconsistency problem. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on 7 computer vision tasks on videos. Extensive quantitative and perceptual experiments show that our approach obtains superior performance than state-of-the-art methods on blind video temporal consistency.

paragraphs: Processing a video one frame at a time can produce results that look reasonable individually but change inconsistently across time. This paper addresses that mismatch through a general method for improving temporal consistency. It trains directly on a pair consisting of the original video and its processed version, rather than requiring a large training dataset.

The central approach uses a convolutional network and what the authors call the Deep Video Prior. They show that training on the video itself can produce temporal consistency without the optical-flow enforcement used by most previous methods. The paper also introduces an iteratively reweighted training strategy to address multimodal inconsistency, a more challenging form of variation in the processed output.

The authors evaluate the method across seven video vision tasks, reporting stronger quantitative and perceptual performance than existing state-of-the-art approaches to blind temporal consistency. This breadth supports its intended role as a general way to improve processed videos. Its practical distinction is that the training signal comes from the specific original-and-processed video pair, making the method applicable without collecting a separate large dataset for this purpose.
summary.tldr: Training a convolutional network on an original-and-processed video pair improves temporal consistency across several video tasks.

title: Blind Video Temporal Consistency via Deep Video Prior

abstract: The design of voting rules is traditionally guided by desirable axioms. Recent work shows that, surprisingly, the axiomatic approach can also support the generation of explanations for voting outcomes. However, no bounds on the size of these explanations is given; for all we know, they may be unbearably tedious. We prove, however, that outcomes of the important Borda rule can be explained using $O(m^2)$ steps, where $m$ is the number of alternatives. Our main technical result is a general lower bound that, in particular, implies that the foregoing bound is asymptotically tight. We discuss the significance of our results for AI and machine learning, including their potential to bolster an emerging paradigm of automated decision making called virtual democracy.

paragraphs: Voting rules are often justified through axioms expressing desirable properties of collective decisions. Those same axioms can also be used to explain why a particular voting outcome follows. This paper examines a practical obstacle for that approach: even a logically valid explanation could be too long to be useful.

For the Borda voting rule, the authors prove that outcomes can be explained in O(m²) steps, where m is the number of alternatives. This supplies a concrete upper bound on explanation length. It establishes how the required number of steps scales as the set of alternatives grows, addressing the previously unresolved possibility of excessively lengthy explanations.

The paper’s main technical result is a general lower bound that makes the Borda upper bound asymptotically tight. Thus, in the analyzed framework, the quadratic scaling cannot generally be improved in its order of growth. The authors discuss possible implications for AI and machine learning, including virtual democracy. Their contribution establishes limits on the length of axiom-based explanations, giving a mathematical basis for assessing their potential practicality.
summary.tldr: Borda voting outcomes admit axiom-based explanations of quadratic length, and a matching lower bound establishes that scaling as asymptotically tight.

title: Explainable Voting

abstract: The vast majority of deep models use multiple gradient signals, typically corresponding to a sum of multiple loss terms, to update a shared set of trainable weights. However, these multiple updates can impede optimal training by pulling the model in conflicting directions. We present Gradient Sign Dropout (GradDrop), a probabilistic masking procedure which samples gradients at an activation layer based on their level of consistency. GradDrop is implemented as a simple deep layer that can be used in any deep net and synergizes with other gradient balancing approaches. We show that GradDrop outperforms the state-of-the-art multiloss methods within traditional multitask and transfer learning settings, and we discuss how GradDrop reveals links between optimal multiloss training and gradient stochasticity.

paragraphs: Many neural networks train shared weights using several loss terms. Each term supplies a gradient signal, and these signals can push the shared model in conflicting directions. The paper focuses on this conflict as an obstacle to effective training, particularly when multiple tasks or objectives must be learned together.

Gradient Sign Dropout, or GradDrop, addresses the problem through probabilistic masking. At an activation layer, it samples gradient signals according to their consistency. This makes agreement between update directions part of how training information is selected. The method is implemented as a simple layer that can be used in deep networks and combined with other approaches for balancing gradients.

The authors report that GradDrop outperforms the compared state-of-the-art multiloss methods in traditional multitask and transfer-learning settings. They also use the method to examine connections between effective multiloss optimization and randomness in gradient updates. The contribution therefore combines a practical training component with a perspective on why carefully structured stochasticity can help when shared parameters receive competing learning signals.
summary.tldr: GradDrop probabilistically masks conflicting gradient signals and improves multiloss training in the reported multitask and transfer-learning evaluations.

title: Just Pick a Sign: Optimizing Deep Multitask Models with Gradient Sign Dropout

abstract: Modern large-scale kernel-based tests such as maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) and kernelized Stein discrepancy (KSD) optimize kernel hyperparameters on a held-out sample via data splitting to obtain the most powerful test statistics. While data splitting results in a tractable null distribution, it suffers from a reduction in test power due to smaller test sample size. Inspired by the selective inference framework, we propose an approach that enables learning the hyperparameters and testing on the full sample without data splitting. Our approach can correctly calibrate the test in the presence of such dependency, and yield a test threshold in closed form. At the same significance level, our approach’s test power is empirically larger than that of the data-splitting approach, regardless of its split proportion.

paragraphs: Kernel-based statistical tests can become more powerful when their hyperparameters are chosen using data. Common approaches separate the sample into a portion for tuning and a portion for testing. This makes the behavior of the test under the null hypothesis easier to handle, but leaves fewer observations for the actual test and can reduce its ability to detect a difference.

This paper proposes using the full sample for both hyperparameter learning and testing. Inspired by selective inference, the method accounts for the dependence created when the same observations serve both purposes. The authors show that the test can be correctly calibrated despite this dependence and provide a test threshold in closed form.

The approach applies to the setting of modern kernel tests such as maximum mean discrepancy and kernelized Stein discrepancy. At the same significance level, experiments show greater test power than data splitting across all split proportions considered. The result demonstrates that accounting for data reuse can preserve calibration while recovering power otherwise lost to splitting.
summary.tldr: A selectively calibrated kernel-testing method reuses the full sample for tuning and testing, improving empirical power over data splitting.

title: Learning Kernel Tests Without Data Splitting

abstract: Rather than performing inefficient local iterative routing between adjacent capsule layers, we propose an alternative global view based on representing the inherent uncertainty in part-object assignment. In our formulation, the local routing iterations are replaced with variational inference of part-object connections in a probabilistic capsule network, leading to a significant speedup without sacrificing performance. In this way, global context is also considered when routing capsules by introducing global latent variables that have direct influence on the objective function, and are updated discriminatively in accordance with the minimum description length (MDL) principle. We focus on enhancing capsule network properties, and perform a thorough evaluation on pose-aware tasks, observing improvements in performance over previous approaches whilst being more computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Capsule networks need to determine how represented parts connect to represented objects. This paper replaces repeated local routing between adjacent capsule layers with a probabilistic treatment of uncertainty in those connections. The goal is to make routing more computationally efficient while allowing it to use a broader view of the input.

The proposed network uses variational inference to estimate part-object connections. Global latent variables bring information beyond adjacent layers into the routing process and directly influence the objective being optimized. These variables are updated discriminatively according to the minimum description length principle, making global context part of the learning formulation.

The authors report a significant speedup without sacrificing performance and evaluate the method on tasks that require awareness of pose. In those evaluations, they observe performance improvements over previous approaches alongside greater computational efficiency. The findings support modeling routing uncertainty explicitly as a way to improve capsule networks, with the stated evidence focused on preserving and enhancing their pose-related capabilities.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic capsule routing uses global context and variational inference to improve computational efficiency and reported pose-aware performance.

title: Introducing Routing Uncertainty in Capsule Networks

abstract: We present novel information-theoretic limits on detecting sparse changes in Isingmodels, a problem that arises in many applications where network changes canoccur due to some external stimuli. We show that the sample complexity fordetecting sparse changes, in a minimax sense, is no better than learning the entiremodel even in settings with local sparsity. This is a surprising fact in light of priorwork rooted in sparse recovery methods, which suggest that sample complexityin this context scales only with the number of network changes. To shed light onwhen change detection is easier than structured learning, we consider testing ofedge deletion in forest-structured graphs, and high-temperature ferromagnets ascase studies. We show for these that testing of small changes is similarly hard, buttesting oflargechanges is well-separated from structure learning. These resultsimply that testing of graphical models may not be amenable to concepts such asrestricted strong convexity leveraged for sparsity pattern recovery, and algorithmdevelopment instead should be directed towards detection of large changes.

paragraphs: Detecting whether a network has changed might seem easier than learning its entire structure, particularly when only a few connections change. This paper examines that intuition for Ising models. It derives information-theoretic limits on the number of samples needed to detect sparse structural changes, including settings where the underlying network has local sparsity.

The central result is a worst-case, minimax statement: detecting sparse changes can require as many samples as learning the whole model. This challenges the expectation, suggested by earlier sparse-recovery approaches, that the required data should scale only with the number of changed connections. A small change set does not by itself ensure an easier testing problem.

The authors also study edge deletions in forest-structured graphs and high-temperature ferromagnets. In these cases, small-change testing remains similarly difficult, while large-change testing is distinctly easier than structure learning. The findings suggest that tools successful for recovering sparse structures may not transfer directly to change detection, and motivate algorithm development aimed at detecting larger changes.
summary.tldr: Detecting sparse changes in Ising models can be as sample-demanding as learning the whole structure, while larger changes can be easier in studied cases.

title: Limits on Testing Structural Changes in Ising Models

abstract: Under distribution shift (DS) where the training data distribution differs from the test one, a powerful technique is importance weighting (IW) which handles DS in two separate steps: weight estimation (WE) estimates the test-over-training density ratio and weighted classification (WC) trains the classifier from weighted training data. However, IW cannot work well on complex data, since WE is incompatible with deep learning. In this paper, we rethink IW and theoretically show it suffers from a circular dependency: we need not only WE for WC, but also WC for WE where a trained deep classifier is used as the feature extractor (FE). To cut off the dependency, we try to pretrain FE from unweighted training data, which leads to biased FE. To overcome the bias, we propose an end-to-end solution dynamic IW that iterates between WE and WC and combines them in a seamless manner, and hence our WE can also enjoy deep networks and stochastic optimizers indirectly. Experiments with two representative types of DS on three popular datasets show that our dynamic IW compares favorably with state-of-the-art methods.

However, IW cannot work well on complex data, since WE is incompatible with deep learning. In this paper, we rethink IW and theoretically show it suffers from a circular dependency: we need not only WE for WC, but also WC for WE where a trained deep classifier is used as the feature extractor (FE). paragraphs: Importance weighting addresses differences between training and test distributions by changing how much influence each training example receives. The usual procedure first estimates the ratio between test and training densities, then trains a classifier using those weights. This paper examines why that separation becomes problematic when deep representations are needed for complex data.

The authors identify a circular dependency: weighted classification needs estimated weights, but estimating useful weights needs features from a trained deep classifier. Pretraining the feature extractor on unweighted training data breaks the immediate circle but introduces bias into the features. The paper’s theoretical analysis makes this dependency central to understanding the difficulty.

Dynamic importance weighting addresses it by repeatedly alternating weight estimation and weighted classification within an end-to-end solution. This connects improvements to the classifier with the features used for subsequent weighting, allowing weight estimation to benefit indirectly from deep networks and stochastic optimization. Experiments covering two representative distribution shifts on three datasets compare favorably with state-of-the-art methods, supporting the coupled approach in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Dynamic importance weighting alternates weight estimation and classifier training to address their circular dependency under distribution shift.

title: Rethinking Importance Weighting for Deep Learning under Distribution Shift

abstract: Data poisoning---the process by which an attacker takes control of a model by making imperceptible changes to a subset of the training data---is an emerging threat in the context of neural networks. Existing attacks for data poisoning neural networks have relied on hand-crafted heuristics, because solving the poisoning problem directly via bilevel optimization is generally thought of as intractable for deep models. We propose MetaPoison, a first-order method that approximates the bilevel problem via meta-learning and crafts poisons that fool neural networks. MetaPoison is effective: it outperforms previous clean-label poisoning methods by a large margin. MetaPoison is robust: poisoned data made for one model transfer to a variety of victim models with unknown training settings and architectures. MetaPoison is general-purpose, it works not only in fine-tuning scenarios, but also for end-to-end training from scratch, which till now hasn't been feasible for clean-label attacks with deep nets. MetaPoison can achieve arbitrary adversary goals---like using poisons of one class to make a target image don the label of another arbitrarily chosen class. Finally, MetaPoison works in the real-world. We demonstrate for the first time successful data poisoning of models trained on the black-box Google Cloud AutoML API.

paragraphs: Clean-label data poisoning alters training examples while retaining their labels, aiming to influence the model learned from them. The paper addresses the difficulty of directly optimizing such attacks against deep networks. The underlying problem has two linked levels: changes to training data affect training, which in turn affects the attacker’s desired model behavior.

MetaPoison uses a first-order meta-learning method to approximate this bilevel optimization. The authors report substantially stronger attacks than previous clean-label methods. They also find that poisoned data designed for one model transfer to victim models with different architectures and unknown training settings, showing that the attack can extend beyond the model used to construct it.

The authors demonstrate flexible target outcomes, including making a target image receive an arbitrarily selected class label through poisons from another class. They additionally report successful poisoning of models trained through the black-box Google Cloud AutoML API. Together, these results show practical reach across several training arrangements and a deployed training service.
summary.tldr: MetaPoison approximates bilevel optimization with meta-learning to create transferable clean-label poisoning attacks, including against models trained from scratch.

title: MetaPoison: Practical General-purpose Clean-label Data Poisoning

abstract: Kernel methods augmented with random features give scalable algorithms for learning from big data. But it has been computationally hard to sample random features according to a probability distribution that is optimized for the data, so as to minimize the required number of features for achieving the learning to a desired accuracy. Here, we develop a quantum algorithm for sampling from this optimized distribution over features, in runtime O(D) that is linear in the dimension D of the input data. Our algorithm achieves an exponential speedup in D compared to any known classical algorithm for this sampling task. In contrast to existing quantum machine learning algorithms, our algorithm circumvents sparsity and low-rank assumptions and thus has wide applicability. We also show that the sampled features can be combined with regression by stochastic gradient descent to achieve the learning without canceling out our exponential speedup. Our algorithm based on sampling optimized random features leads to an accelerated framework for machine learning that takes advantage of quantum computers.

paragraphs: Random features make kernel learning more scalable, but the choice of sampling distribution matters. A distribution optimized for the data can reduce the number of features needed to reach a desired accuracy. The obstacle addressed here is the computational difficulty of drawing features from that optimized distribution.

The authors develop a quantum sampling algorithm with runtime linear in the input dimension D. For this sampling task, they report an exponential speedup in D over every known classical algorithm. The comparison is specifically to known classical methods, and the stated advantage concerns optimized feature sampling. The algorithm also avoids the sparsity and low-rank assumptions used by existing quantum learning approaches discussed in the abstract.

The paper then connects the sampling procedure to regression trained with stochastic gradient descent. It shows that this downstream learning stage can be performed without eliminating the exponential speedup. That connection matters because a faster sampling subroutine is useful for learning only if later computation preserves its benefit. The result is a quantum-assisted learning framework built around data-adapted random features.
summary.tldr: A quantum algorithm samples optimized random features in linear input dimension, exponentially faster than known classical samplers, with a regression stage that preserves the advantage.

title: Learning with Optimized Random Features: Exponential Speedup by Quantum Machine Learning without Sparsity and Low-Rank Assumptions

abstract: Image-based 3D shape retrieval (IBSR) aims to find the corresponding 3D shape of a given 2D image from a large 3D shape database. The common routine is to map 2D images and 3D shapes into an embedding space and define (or learn) a shape similarity measure. While metric learning with some adaptation techniques seems to be a natural solution to shape similarity learning, the performance is often unsatisfactory for fine-grained shape retrieval. In the paper, we identify the source of the poor performance and propose a practical solution to this problem. We find that the shape difference between a negative pair is entangled with the texture gap, making metric learning ineffective in pushing away negative pairs. To tackle this issue, we develop a geometry-focused multi-view metric learning framework empowered by texture synthesis. The synthesis of textures for 3D shape models creates hard triplets, which suppress the adverse effects of rich texture in 2D images, thereby push the network to focus more on discovering geometric characteristics. Our approach shows state-of-the-art performance on a recently released large-scale 3D-FUTURE [1] repository, as well as three widely studied benchmarks, including Pix3D [2], Stanford Cars [3], and Comp Cars [4]. Codes will be made publicly available at: https://github.com/3D-FRONT-FUTURE/IBSR-texture.

Fine-grained retrieval remains difficult because small geometric differences must be distinguished across these different forms of visual input.

The paper identifies an obstacle in metric learning: differences in shape become entangled with differences in texture. This can make learning to separate nonmatching pairs ineffective. The proposed framework synthesizes textures for 3D models to create difficult training triplets and combines them with geometry-focused, multi-view metric learning.

These examples suppress the distracting influence of rich image textures and encourage the network to discover geometric characteristics. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on 3D-FUTURE, Pix3D, Stanford Cars, and Comp Cars. The finding supports deliberately shaping training difficulty around the desired similarity criterion: here, the training examples push the learned representation toward geometry when appearance differences would otherwise interfere.
summary.tldr: Synthesized textures create difficult training examples that help image-to-3D retrieval models focus on geometry.

title: Hard Example Generation by Texture Synthesis for Cross-domain Shape Similarity Learning

abstract: Label-free alignment between datasets collected at different times, locations, or by different instruments is a fundamental scientific task. Hyperbolic spaces have recently provided a fruitful foundation for the development of informative representations of hierarchical data. Here, we take a purely geometric approach for label-free alignment of hierarchical datasets and introduce hyperbolic Procrustes analysis (HPA). HPA consists of new implementations of the three prototypical Procrustes analysis components: translation, scaling, and rotation, based on the Riemannian geometry of the Lorentz model of hyperbolic space. We analyze the proposed components, highlighting their useful properties for alignment. The efficacy of HPA, its theoretical properties, stability and computational efficiency are demonstrated in simulations. In addition, we showcase its performance on three batch correction tasks involving gene expression and mass cytometry data. Specifically, we demonstrate high-quality unsupervised batch effect removal from data acquired at different sites and with different technologies that outperforms recent methods for label-free alignment in hyperbolic spaces.

In addition, we showcase its performance on three batch correction tasks involving gene expression and mass cytometry data. paragraphs: Datasets measuring related phenomena can differ because they were collected at different sites, times, or with different instruments. Aligning them without labels is particularly relevant when their representations capture hierarchical structure. This paper introduces hyperbolic Procrustes analysis, a geometric alignment method designed for representations in hyperbolic space.

The approach reconstructs the three familiar components of Procrustes alignment—translation, scaling, and rotation—using the Riemannian geometry of the Lorentz model. These operations must respect the geometry of the representation space. The authors analyze properties that make the proposed transformations useful for alignment and examine their behavior through simulations.

The simulations demonstrate efficacy, stability, computational efficiency, and the theoretical properties of the method. The paper also evaluates three batch-correction tasks involving gene expression and mass cytometry measurements. It reports high-quality unsupervised removal of differences associated with collection sites and technologies, outperforming recent hyperbolic label-free alignment methods. These findings support geometry-aware alignment as a way to bring hierarchical datasets into correspondence while addressing acquisition-related differences.
summary.tldr: Hyperbolic Procrustes analysis uses geometry-aware translation, scaling, and rotation to align hierarchical datasets without labels.

title: Hyperbolic Procrustes Analysis Using Riemannian Geometry

abstract: Contrastive learning approaches have achieved great success in learning visual representations with few labels of the target classes. That implies a tantalizing possibility of scaling them up beyond a curated “seed" benchmark, to incorporating more unlabeled images from the internet-scale external sources to enhance its performance. However, in practice, larger amount of unlabeled data will require more computing resources due to the bigger model size and longer training needed. Moreover, open-world unlabeled data usually follows an implicit long-tail class or attribute distribution, many of which also do not belong to the target classes. Blindly leveraging all unlabeled data hence can lead to the data imbalance as well as distraction issues. This motivates us to seek a principled approach to strategically select unlabeled data from an external source, in order to learn generalizable, balanced and diverse representations for relevant classes. In this work, we present an open-world unlabeled data sampling framework called Model-Aware K-center (MAK), which follows three simple principles: (1) tailness, which encourages sampling of examples from tail classes, by sorting the empirical contrastive loss expectation (ECLE) of samples over random data augmentations; (2) proximity, which rejects the out-of-distribution outliers that may distract training; and (3) diversity, which ensures diversity in the set of sampled examples. Empirically, using ImageNet-100-LT (without labels) as the seed dataset and two “noisy” external data sources, we demonstrate that MAK can consistently improve both the overall representation quality and the class balancedness of the learned features, as evaluated via linear classifier evaluation on full-shot and few-shot settings. Thecode is available at: https://github.com/VITA-Group/MAK.

paragraphs: Adding internet images to contrastive learning does not automatically improve the representation. External collections can contain many examples from common classes, few from rare ones, and images unrelated to the target task. Processing everything also increases computational demands. This paper studies how to select useful unlabeled examples instead of indiscriminately expanding the training collection.

The proposed Model-Aware K-center framework combines three selection principles. Tailness encourages examples from underrepresented classes, using a sample's expected contrastive loss across random augmentations as a ranking signal. Proximity filters out outliers that could distract learning. Diversity encourages the selected set to cover different examples rather than repeatedly adding similar content.

Experiments start with an unlabeled ImageNet-100-LT seed dataset and use two noisy external sources. Linear-classifier evaluations in full-shot and few-shot settings show consistent improvements in overall representation quality and balance across classes. The findings indicate that model-informed selection can make external unlabeled data more useful, with gains assessed both in aggregate performance and in how evenly the learned features serve different classes.
summary.tldr: Model-Aware K-center selects external unlabeled images for rarity, relevance, and diversity to improve contrastive representations on imbalanced data.

title: Improving Contrastive Learning on Imbalanced Data via Open-World Sampling

abstract: In the predict-then-optimize framework, the objective is to train a predictive model, mapping from environment features to parameters of an optimization problem, which maximizes decision quality when the optimization is subsequently solved. Recent work on decision-focused learning shows that embedding the optimization problem in the training pipeline can improve decision quality and help generalize better to unseen tasks compared to relying on an intermediate loss function for evaluating prediction quality. We study the predict-then-optimize framework in the context of sequential decision problems (formulated as MDPs) that are solved via reinforcement learning. In particular, we are given environment features and a set of trajectories from training MDPs, which we use to train a predictive model that generalizes to unseen test MDPs without trajectories. Two significant computational challenges arise in applying decision-focused learning to MDPs: (i) large state and action spaces make it infeasible for existing techniques to differentiate through MDP problems, and (ii) the high-dimensional policy space, as parameterized by a neural network, makes differentiating through a policy expensive. We resolve the first challenge by sampling provably unbiased derivatives to approximate and differentiate through optimality conditions, and the second challenge by using a low-rank approximation to the high-dimensional sample-based derivatives. We implement both Bellman-based and policy gradient-based decision-focused learning on three different MDP problems with missing parameters, and show that decision-focused learning performs better in generalization to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: Predict-then-optimize systems estimate the parameters of a decision problem and then solve it. This paper applies that idea to sequential decisions modeled as Markov decision processes. Training uses environment features and recorded trajectories, while the predictor must generalize to new environments for which trajectories are unavailable.

The learning objective emphasizes the quality of the decisions produced from predicted parameters. Making this practical requires differentiating through the decision-solving process, which is difficult with large state and action spaces and neural-network policies. The authors use provably unbiased derivative samples to approximate and differentiate optimality conditions, then apply a low-rank approximation to the high-dimensional sample-based derivatives.

The framework is implemented through both Bellman-based and policy-gradient-based decision-focused learning. Experiments on three MDP problems with missing parameters show better generalization to unseen tasks. The contribution connects the predictor's training signal to downstream decision quality while addressing the computational obstacles that otherwise make this connection expensive in sequential settings.
summary.tldr: Decision-focused training learns MDP parameters from environment features using sampled derivatives and low-rank approximations to improve generalization to unseen tasks.

title: Learning MDPs from Features: Predict-Then-Optimize for Sequential Decision Making by Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Invariance under symmetry is an important problem in machine learning. Our paper looks specifically at equivariant neural networks where transformations of inputs yield homomorphic transformations of outputs. Here, steerable CNNs have emerged as the standard solution. An inherent problem of steerable representations is that general nonlinear layers break equivariance, thus restricting architectural choices. Our paper applies harmonic distortion analysis to illuminate the effect of nonlinearities on Fourier representations of SO(2). We develop a novel FFT-based algorithm for computing representations of non-linearly transformed activations while maintaining band-limitation. It yields exact equivariance for polynomial (approximations of) nonlinearities, as well as approximate solutions with tunable accuracy for general functions. We apply the approach to build a fully E(3)-equivariant network for sampled 3D surface data. In experiments with 2D and 3D data, we obtain results that compare favorably to the state-of-the-art in terms of accuracy while permitting continuous symmetry and exact equivariance.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks are designed so that transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation of the output. In steerable convolutional networks, however, general nonlinear layers can disrupt that relationship. This restricts which activation functions an architecture can use. The paper studies how to expand those choices while preserving controlled behavior under continuous symmetries.

The authors analyze how nonlinearities affect Fourier representations of planar rotations using harmonic distortion analysis. They then develop an algorithm based on the fast Fourier transform that computes representations of transformed activations while maintaining a bounded frequency range. For polynomial nonlinearities, including polynomial approximations, the method gives exact equivariance; for general functions, it offers approximations with adjustable accuracy.

The approach also supports a fully E(3)-equivariant network for sampled three-dimensional surfaces. Experiments on two-dimensional and three-dimensional data compare favorably with state-of-the-art methods in accuracy. The contribution links broader nonlinear architectural choices with symmetry preservation, while retaining the distinction between exact polynomial constructions and approximate handling of general functions.
summary.tldr: An FFT-based method expands nonlinear activation choices in equivariant networks, giving exact polynomial constructions and tunable approximations for general functions.

title: General Nonlinearities in SO(2)-Equivariant CNNs

abstract: The existing literature on deep learning for tabular data proposes a wide range of novel architectures and reports competitive results on various datasets. However, the proposed models are usually not properly compared to each other and existing works often use different benchmarks and experiment protocols. As a result, it is unclear for both researchers and practitioners what models perform best. Additionally, the field still lacks effective baselines, that is, the easy-to-use models that provide competitive performance across different problems.In this work, we perform an overview of the main families of DL architectures for tabular data and raise the bar of baselines in tabular DL by identifying two simple and powerful deep architectures. The first one is a ResNet-like architecture which turns out to be a strong baseline that is often missing in prior works. The second model is our simple adaptation of the Transformer architecture for tabular data, which outperforms other solutions on most tasks. Both models are compared to many existing architectures on a diverse set of tasks under the same training and tuning protocols. We also compare the best DL models with Gradient Boosted Decision Trees and conclude that there is still no universally superior solution. The source code is available at https://github.com/yandex-research/rtdl.

paragraphs: Comparing neural networks for tabular data is difficult when papers use different datasets, training procedures, and tuning protocols. This paper reviews major architecture families and evaluates models under shared conditions. Its goal is to identify useful baselines and make performance comparisons easier to interpret.

The study highlights two relatively simple architectures. A ResNet-like model provides a strong baseline that earlier work often omitted. The authors also introduce a straightforward adaptation of the Transformer for tabular inputs, which outperforms other solutions on most evaluated tasks. Both models are compared with many existing architectures across a diverse collection of tasks using the same training and tuning protocols.

The paper further compares the strongest deep learning models with gradient boosted decision trees. That comparison finds no universally superior solution. The practical message is therefore twofold: tabular deep learning benefits from stronger, accessible reference models, and model choice still depends on the problem. The Transformer’s success across most tasks does not establish that neural networks dominate every tabular setting.
summary.tldr: Consistent comparisons identify strong ResNet-like and Transformer baselines for tabular data, while finding no universal winner over boosted trees.

title: Revisiting Deep Learning Models for Tabular Data

abstract: Anderson mixing (AM) is an acceleration method for fixed-point iterations. Despite its success and wide usage in scientific computing, the convergence theory of AM remains unclear, and its applications to machine learning problems are not well explored. In this paper, by introducing damped projection and adaptive regularization to the classical AM, we propose a Stochastic Anderson Mixing (SAM) scheme to solve nonconvex stochastic optimization problems. Under mild assumptions, we establish the convergence theory of SAM, including the almost sure convergence to stationary points and the worst-case iteration complexity. Moreover, the complexity bound can be improved when randomly choosing an iterate as the output. To further accelerate the convergence, we incorporate a variance reduction technique into the proposed SAM. We also propose a preconditioned mixing strategy for SAM which can empirically achieve faster convergence or better generalization ability. Finally, we apply the SAM method to train various neural networks including the vanilla CNN, ResNets, WideResNet, ResNeXt, DenseNet and LSTM. Experimental results on image classification and language model demonstrate the advantages of our method.

paragraphs: Anderson mixing accelerates fixed-point iterations and has a history of use in scientific computing. This paper adapts it to nonconvex stochastic optimization, where noisy updates and a complex objective make convergence analysis challenging. The proposed Stochastic Anderson Mixing method adds damped projection and adaptive regularization to the classical procedure.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove almost sure convergence to stationary points and establish a worst-case iteration-complexity bound. Stationary-point convergence is the stated target; it does not assert that every run reaches a global optimum. The complexity bound improves when the algorithm returns a randomly chosen iterate rather than using the output choice considered in the original bound.

The paper also incorporates variance reduction to accelerate convergence and proposes a preconditioned mixing strategy. The latter empirically offers faster convergence or better generalization. Experiments train several convolutional network families and an LSTM on image classification and language modeling tasks, demonstrating advantages of the approach alongside its conditional theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Anderson Mixing adapts an acceleration method to noisy nonconvex optimization with convergence guarantees and neural-network training benefits.

title: Stochastic Anderson Mixing for Nonconvex Stochastic Optimization

abstract: We study Bayesian automated mechanism design in unstructured dynamic environments, where a principal repeatedly interacts with an agent, and takes actions based on the strategic agent's report of the current state of the world. Both the principal and the agent can have arbitrary and potentially different valuations for the actions taken, possibly also depending on the actual state of the world. Moreover, at any time, the state of the world may evolve arbitrarily depending on the action taken by the principal. The goal is to compute an optimal mechanism which maximizes the principal's utility in the face of the self-interested strategic agent.We give an efficient algorithm for computing optimal mechanisms, with or without payments, under different individual-rationality constraints, when the time horizon is constant. Our algorithm is based on a sophisticated linear program formulation, which can be customized in various ways to accommodate richer constraints. For environments with large time horizons, we show that the principal's optimal utility is hard to approximate within a certain constant factor, complementing our algorithmic result. These results paint a relatively complete picture for automated dynamic mechanism design in unstructured environments. We further consider a special case of the problem where the agent is myopic, and give a refined efficient algorithm whose time complexity scales linearly in the time horizon. In the full version of the paper, we show that memoryless mechanisms, which are without loss of generality optimal in Markov decision processes without strategic behavior, do not provide a good solution for our problem, in terms of both optimality and computational tractability. Moreover, we present experimental results where our algorithms are applied to synthetic dynamic environments with different characteristics, which not only serve as a proof of concept for our algorithms, but also exhibit intriguing phenomena in dynamic mechanism design.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated decisions involving a principal and a strategic agent. The principal acts using the agent's reports about the world, but their interests may differ. Actions can also change future states, so designing a good mechanism requires accounting for both incentives and the consequences of decisions over time.

The authors formulate mechanism design as a linear program that can accommodate different constraints. When the time horizon is constant, they give an efficient algorithm for optimal mechanisms, both with and without payments and under different participation requirements. The paper also finds that memoryless mechanisms can perform poorly in this strategic setting, despite their usefulness in ordinary Markov decision processes. Experiments in synthetic dynamic environments demonstrate the algorithms and illustrate additional behavior arising from repeated strategic interaction.
summary.tldr: The paper gives efficient dynamic mechanism-design algorithms for constant horizons and myopic agents, alongside hardness results for longer strategic interactions.

title: Automated Dynamic Mechanism Design

abstract: Combination therapy refers to the use of multiple treatments -- such as surgery, medication, and behavioral therapy - to cure a single disease, and has become a cornerstone for treating various conditions including cancer, HIV, and depression. All possible combinations of treatments lead to a collection of treatment regimens (i.e., policies) with mixed scopes, or what physicians could observe and which actions they should take depending on the context. In this paper, we investigate the online reinforcement learning setting for optimizing the policy space with mixed scopes. In particular, we develop novel online algorithms that achieve sublinear regret compared to an optimal agent deployed in the environment. The regret bound has a dependency on the maximal cardinality of the induced state-action space associated with mixed scopes. We further introduce a canonical representation for an arbitrary subset of interventional distributions given a causal diagram, which leads to a non-trivial, minimal representation of the model parameters.

paragraphs: Different decision policies may have access to different observations and control different actions. The paper calls these differences mixed policy scopes. Combination therapy motivates the setting: different treatment regimens combine interventions and specify which information a physician can observe and which actions can be taken in context.

The authors study online reinforcement learning over such policy spaces and develop algorithms with sublinear regret relative to an optimal agent in the environment. Sublinear regret means that the accumulated performance gap grows more slowly than the number of interactions. The bound depends on the largest induced state-action space associated with the mixed scopes.

The paper also introduces a canonical representation for an arbitrary subset of intervention distributions specified through a causal diagram. This yields a nontrivial minimal representation of model parameters. Together, the contributions address both learning across policies with different observation and action scopes and representing the causal quantities involved. The treatment example motivates the mathematical setting; the stated findings concern algorithms, regret guarantees, and model representation.
summary.tldr: Online learning algorithms achieve sublinear regret over policies with differing observation and action scopes, alongside a minimal causal parameter representation.

title: Online Reinforcement Learning for Mixed Policy Scopes

abstract: We propose a model for online graph problems where algorithms are given access to an oracle that predicts (e.g., based on modeling assumptions or past data) the degrees of nodes in the graph. Within this model, we study the classic problem of online bipartite matching, and a natural greedy matching algorithm called MinPredictedDegree, which uses predictions of the degrees of offline nodes. For the bipartite version of a stochastic graph model due to Chung, Lu, and Vu where the expected values of the offline degrees are known and used as predictions, we show that MinPredictedDegree stochastically dominates any other online algorithm, i.e., it is optimal for graphs drawn from this model. Since the "symmetric" version of the model, where all online nodes are identical, is a special case of the well-studied "known i.i.d. model", it follows that the competitive ratio of MinPredictedDegree on such inputs is at least 0.7299. For the special case of graphs with power law degree distributions, we show that MinPredictedDegree frequently produces matchings almost as large as the true maximum matching on such graphs. We complement these results with an extensive empirical evaluation showing that MinPredictedDegree compares favorably to state-of-the-art online algorithms for online matching.

paragraphs: Online bipartite matching requires choosing matches as graph information arrives. This paper studies algorithms that additionally receive predictions of node degrees, potentially derived from prior data or modeling assumptions. Its proposed greedy rule, MinPredictedDegree, uses predicted degrees of the offline nodes to guide matching decisions.

The strongest result applies to a specific stochastic graph model: the bipartite Chung–Lu–Vu model with known expected offline degrees used as predictions. Within this setting, MinPredictedDegree stochastically dominates every other online algorithm. summary.tldr: MinPredictedDegree uses degree predictions for online matching and is optimal under a specified stochastic graph model with known expected degrees.

title: (Optimal) Online Bipartite Matching with Degree Information

abstract: From optimal transport to robust dimensionality reduction, many machine learning applicationscan be cast into the min-max optimization problems over Riemannian manifolds. Though manymin-max algorithms have been analyzed in the Euclidean setting, it has been elusive how theseresults translate to the Riemannian case. Zhang et al. (2022) have recently identified that geodesic convexconcave Riemannian problems admit always Sion’s saddle point solutions. Immediately, an importantquestion that arises is if a performance gap between the Riemannian and the optimal Euclidean spaceconvex concave algorithms is necessary. Our work is the first to answer the question in the negative:We prove that the Riemannian corrected extragradient (RCEG) method achieves last-iterate at alinear convergence rate at the geodesically strongly convex concave case, matching the euclidean one.Our results also extend to the stochastic or non-smooth case where RCEG & Riemanian gradientascent descent (RGDA) achieve respectively near-optimal convergence rates up to factors dependingon curvature of the manifold. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of RCEG insolving robust PCA.

paragraphs: Some machine-learning optimization problems involve competing minimization and maximization objectives on curved spaces. Algorithms for ordinary Euclidean spaces are well studied, but their guarantees do not automatically transfer to Riemannian manifolds. This paper asks whether curved geometry necessarily imposes a worse convergence rate for convex-concave problems.

The authors analyze Riemannian corrected extragradient, or RCEG. For geodesically strongly convex-concave problems, they prove linear convergence of the last iterate, matching the Euclidean rate. A last-iterate guarantee concerns the algorithm's current solution directly. The result establishes that a convergence-rate gap is not unavoidable in this setting.

The work also extends to stochastic and nonsmooth cases. RCEG and Riemannian gradient ascent-descent respectively achieve near-optimal rates, with factors that depend on manifold curvature. Experiments on robust principal component analysis demonstrate RCEG's effectiveness for a concrete application. The findings therefore combine a matching rate under strong geometric convexity-concavity with broader guarantees that still explicitly account for the influence of curved geometry.
summary.tldr: Riemannian corrected extragradient matches Euclidean linear convergence in the geodesically strongly convex-concave setting.

title: First-Order Algorithms for Min-Max Optimization in Geodesic Metric Spaces

abstract: We explore the connection between outlier-robust high-dimensional statistics and non-convex optimization in the presence of sparsity constraints, with a focus on the fundamental tasks of robust sparse mean estimation and robust sparse PCA. We develop novel and simple optimization formulations for these problems such that any approximate stationary point of the associated optimization problem yields a near-optimal solution for the underlying robust estimation task. As a corollary, we obtain that any first-order method that efficiently converges to stationarity yields an efficient algorithm for these tasks. The obtained algorithms are simple, practical, and succeed under broader distributional assumptions compared to prior work.

paragraphs: High-dimensional estimation becomes difficult when observations include outliers and the desired answer must satisfy sparsity constraints. This paper studies two central examples: estimating a sparse mean and performing sparse principal component analysis robustly. It asks how these statistical goals can be expressed as optimization problems that are practical to solve.

The authors construct simple nonconvex formulations with a strong connection between optimization progress and statistical quality. For these formulations, any approximate stationary point yields a near-optimal solution to the corresponding robust estimation problem. Stationarity is therefore sufficient for the stated statistical result; an optimization method does not need to establish that it has found a global optimum.

A consequence is that any first-order method that efficiently reaches stationarity provides an efficient algorithm for these estimation tasks. That qualification matters: the result transfers efficiency from a suitable optimization method rather than asserting it for every possible procedure. The resulting algorithms are described as practical and successful under broader distributional assumptions than previous work, connecting robust sparse statistics with accessible nonconvex optimization.
summary.tldr: New nonconvex formulations make approximate stationarity sufficient for near-optimal robust sparse mean estimation and sparse PCA.

title: Outlier-Robust Sparse Estimation via Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: Artificial neural networks for motor control usually adopt generic architectures like fully connected MLPs. While general, these tabula rasa architectures rely on large amounts of experience to learn, are not easily transferable to new bodies, and have internal dynamics that are difficult to interpret. In nature, animals are born with highly structured connectivity in their nervous systems shaped by evolution; this innate circuitry acts synergistically with learning mechanisms to provide inductive biases that enable most animals to function well soon after birth and learn efficiently. Convolutional networks inspired by visual circuitry have encoded useful biases for vision. However, it is unknown the extent to which ANN architectures inspired by neural circuitry can yield useful biases for other AI domains. In this work, we ask what advantages biologically inspired ANN architecture can provide in the domain of motor control. Specifically, we translate C. elegans locomotion circuits into an ANN model controlling a simulated Swimmer agent. On a locomotion task, our architecture achieves good initial performance and asymptotic performance comparable with MLPs, while dramatically improving data efficiency and requiring orders of magnitude fewer parameters. Our architecture is interpretable and transfers to new body designs. An ablation analysis shows that constrained excitation/inhibition is crucial for learning, while weight initialization contributes to good initial performance. Our work demonstrates several advantages of biologically inspired ANN architecture and encourages future work in more complex embodied control.

summary.tldr: A network inspired by worm locomotion circuitry learns simulated swimming efficiently with far fewer parameters than generic networks.

title: Neural Circuit Architectural Priors for Embodied Control

abstract: Test-time adversarial attacks have posed serious challenges to the robustness of machine-learning models, and in many settings the adversarial perturbation need not be bounded by small $\ell_p$-norms. Motivated by attacks in program analysis and security tasks, we investigate $\textit{relational adversaries}$, a broad class of attackers who create adversarial examples in a reflexive-transitive closure of a logical relation. We analyze the conditions for robustness against relational adversaries and investigate different levels of robustness-accuracy trade-off due to various patterns in a relation. Inspired by the insights, we propose $\textit{normalize-and-predict}$, a learning framework that leverages input normalization to achieve provable robustness. The framework solves the pain points of adversarial training against relational adversaries and can be combined with adversarial training for the benefits of both approaches. Guided by our theoretical findings, we apply our framework to source code authorship attribution and malware detection. Results of both tasks show our learning framework significantly improves the robustness of models against relational adversaries. In the process, it outperforms adversarial training, the most noteworthy defense mechanism, by a wide margin.

This paper formalizes such relational adversaries using all inputs reachable through zero or more applications of a specified logical relation.

The authors analyze conditions for robustness and how different patterns in the relation affect the trade-off between robustness and accuracy. Their resulting framework, normalize-and-predict, uses input normalization to obtain provable robustness. It addresses difficulties encountered by adversarial training in this setting and can also be combined with adversarial training to draw on both approaches.

The work therefore expands the kind of transformations a robustness framework can address, while connecting its defense mechanism to a theoretical analysis of the permitted relationships between inputs.
summary.tldr: Normalize-and-predict provides provable robustness against relational transformations and improves defenses in code attribution and malware detection.

title: Robust Learning against Relational Adversaries

abstract: Deep topic models have been proven as a promising way to extract hierarchical latent representations from documents represented as high-dimensional bag-of-words vectors.However, the representation capability of existing deep topic models is still limited by the phenomenon of "posterior collapse", which has been widely criticized in deep generative models, resulting in the higher-level latent representations exhibiting similar or meaningless patterns.To this end, in this paper, we first develop a novel deep-coupling generative process for existing deep topic models, which incorporates skip connections into the generation of documents, enforcing strong links between the document and its multi-layer latent representations.After that, utilizing data augmentation techniques, we reformulate the deep-coupling generative process as a Markov decision process and develop a corresponding Policy Gradient (PG) based training algorithm, which can further alleviate the information reduction at higher layers.Extensive experiments demonstrate that our developed methods can effectively alleviate "posterior collapse" in deep topic models, contributing to providing higher-quality latent document representations.
