paragraphs: Deep topic models aim to represent documents at several levels of abstraction, starting from counts of the words they contain. Their higher layers can suffer from posterior collapse: instead of capturing useful distinctions, the latent representations become repetitive or uninformative. This paper addresses the resulting loss of representational capacity.

The first contribution changes how documents are generated from the model’s hidden representations. The authors add skip connections that create stronger links between the document and multiple latent layers. This gives the higher layers a more direct connection to the information that the model must explain.

The second contribution combines data augmentation with a reformulation of that generative process as a Markov decision process. This allows the authors to develop a policy-gradient training algorithm intended to further reduce information loss at higher layers. Experiments show that these changes alleviate posterior collapse and produce higher-quality document representations. The stated result is an improvement in the usefulness of the hierarchy, rather than a claim that collapse is eliminated.
summary.tldr: Skip connections and policy-gradient training help deep topic models retain useful information in their higher latent layers.

title: Alleviating "Posterior Collapse'' in Deep Topic Models via Policy Gradient

abstract: According to World Health Organization, there is an estimated 2.2 billion people with a near or distance vision impairment worldwide. Difficulty in self-navigation is one of the greatest challenges to independence for the blind and low vision (BLV) people. Through consultations with several BLV service providers, we realized that negotiating surface discontinuities is one of the very prominent challenges when navigating an outdoor environment within the urban. Surface discontinuities are commonly formed by rises and drop-offs along a pathway. They could be a threat to balancing during a walk and perceiving such a threat is highly challenging to the BLVs. In this paper, we introduce SurDis, a novel dataset of depth maps and stereo images that exemplifies the issue of surface discontinuity in the urban areas of Klang Valley, Malaysia. We seek to address the limitation of existing datasets of such nature in these areas. Current mobility tools for the BLVs predominantly focus on furniture, indoor built environments, traffic signs, vehicles, humans and various types of objects' detection above the surface of a pathway. We emphasize a specific purpose for SurDis – to support the development of assistive wearable technology for the BLVs to negotiate surface discontinuity. We consulted BLV volunteers on the specifications of surface condition that could become hazardous for navigation using 3D printed replicas of actual scaled-down scenes, and identified locations that are frequented by the BLVs as our target data collection fields. With feedback from these volunteers, we developed a lightweight, small and unobtrusive prototype equipped with a tiny stereo camera and an embedded system on a single board computer to capture the samples from 10 different locations. We describe instrument development, data collection, preprocessing, annotation, and experiments conducted. The dataset contains: (1) more than 17000 depth maps generated from 200 sets of stereo image sequences, (2) annotations of surface discontinuity in the depth maps, and (3) bitmap stereo image pairs corresponding to the depth maps in (1).

title: SurDis: A Surface Discontinuity Dataset for Wearable Technology to Assist Blind Navigation in Urban Environments

abstract: It is common for data structures such as images and shapes of 2D objects to be represented as points on a manifold. The utility of a mechanism to produce sanitized differentially private estimates from such data is intimately linked to how compatible it is with the underlying structure and geometry of the space. In particular, as recently shown, utility of the Laplace mechanism on a positively curved manifold, such as Kendall’s 2D shape space, is significantly influenced by the curvature. Focusing on the problem of sanitizing the Fr\'echet mean of a sample of points on a manifold, we exploit the characterization of the mean as the minimizer of an objective function comprised of the sum of squared distances and develop a K-norm gradient mechanism on Riemannian manifolds that favors values that produce gradients close to the the zero of the objective function. For the case of positively curved manifolds, we describe how using the gradient of the squared distance function offers better control over sensitivity than the Laplace mechanism, and demonstrate this numerically on a dataset of shapes of corpus callosa. Further illustrations of the mechanism’s utility on a sphere and the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices are also presented.

paragraphs: Images and object shapes can be represented as points on curved mathematical spaces called manifolds. Producing a private estimate from such data requires attention to that geometry because the usefulness of the result depends on compatibility with the space. This paper focuses on privately estimating the Fréchet mean, which minimizes the sum of squared distances to sample points.

The authors develop a K-norm gradient mechanism on Riemannian manifolds. It favors candidate outputs whose objective gradients are close to zero, connecting the private estimate to the optimization condition defining the mean. For positively curved manifolds, using gradients of squared distances provides better control of sensitivity than the Laplace mechanism considered in the paper.

Numerical results on shapes of corpus callosa illustrate that positive-curvature comparison. Further examples examine the mechanism on a sphere and on the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices. The contribution is a geometry-aware route to private averaging, with the stated sensitivity advantage tied specifically to the positively curved setting and utility illustrated across several structured spaces.
summary.tldr: A gradient-based privacy mechanism estimates means on manifolds, offering better sensitivity control in the positively curved setting studied.

title: Shape And Structure Preserving Differential Privacy

abstract: Contrastive learning (CL) has been the de facto technique for self-supervised representation learning (SSL), with impressive empirical success such as multi-modal representation learning. However, traditional CL loss only considers negative samples from a minibatch, which could cause biased gradients due to the non-decomposibility of the loss. For the first time, we consider optimizing a more generalized contrastive loss, where each data sample is associated with an infinite number of negative samples. We show that directly using minibatch stochastic optimization could lead to gradient bias. To remedy this, we propose an efficient Bayesian data augmentation technique to augment the contrastive loss into a decomposable one, where standard stochastic optimization can be directly applied without gradient bias. Specifically, our augmented loss defines a joint distribution over the model parameters and the augmented parameters, which can be conveniently optimized by a proposed stochastic expectation-maximization algorithm. Our framework is more general and is related to several popular SSL algorithms. We verify our framework on both small scale models and several large foundation models, including SSL of ImageNet and SSL for vision-language representation learning. Experiment results indicate the existence of gradient bias in all cases, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on improving previous state of the arts. Remarkably, our method can outperform the strong MoCo-v3 under the same hyper-parameter setting with only around half of the minibatch size; and also obtains strong results in the recent public benchmark ELEVATER for few-shot image classification.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning commonly uses negative examples drawn from the current minibatch. This paper examines how that practice can bias training gradients because the loss does not decompose into independent sample contributions. The authors formulate a more general objective with infinitely many negative samples associated with each example and show that direct minibatch optimization can produce biased gradients.

Their remedy is Bayesian data augmentation that converts the objective into a decomposable form. The augmented loss defines a joint distribution over model parameters and additional parameters, which the authors optimize with a stochastic expectation-maximization algorithm. This formulation allows standard stochastic optimization without the gradient bias identified for the original objective.

Experiments cover small models, ImageNet self-supervision, and vision-language representation learning, finding gradient bias throughout the tested settings. The proposed method improves previous results and outperforms MoCo-v3 under the same hyperparameter setting with roughly half the minibatch size. It also achieves strong ELEVATER few-shot classification results. These findings support gradient bias as a useful perspective on contrastive learning's dependence on batch size.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian augmentation removes an identified source of contrastive-learning gradient bias and enables strong results with smaller minibatches.

title: Why do We Need Large Batchsizes in Contrastive Learning? A Gradient-Bias Perspective

abstract: We consider contextual bandits with knapsacks, with an underlying structure between rewards generated and cost vectors suffered. We do so motivated by sales with commercial discounts. At each round, given the stochastic i.i.d.\ context $\mathbf{x}_t$ and the arm picked $a_t$ (corresponding, e.g., to a discount level), a customer conversion may be obtained, in which case a reward $r(a,\mathbf{x}_t)$ is gained and vector costs $\mathbf{c}(a_t,\mathbf{x}_t)$ are suffered (corresponding, e.g., to losses of earnings). Otherwise, in the absence of a conversion, the reward and costs are null. The reward and costs achieved are thus coupled through the binary variable measuring conversion or the absence thereof. This underlying structure between rewards and costs is different from the linear structures considered by Agrawal and Devanur [2016] (but we show that the techniques introduced in the present article may also be applied to the case of these linear structures). The adaptive policies exhibited in this article solve at each round a linear program based on upper-confidence estimates of the probabilities of conversion given $a$ and $\mathbf{x}$. This kind of policy is most natural and achieves a regret bound of the typical order $(\mathrm{OPT}/B) \smash{\sqrt{T}}$, where $B$ is the total budget allowed, $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the optimal expected reward achievable by a static policy, and $T$ is the number of rounds.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated decisions that earn rewards while spending limited resources, motivated by choosing commercial discounts. A customer’s context is observed, a discount or other action is selected, and a conversion may occur. Both the reward and resource costs are incurred only if that conversion happens; otherwise, both are zero.

This shared conversion event creates a particular dependence between reward and cost. The authors design adaptive policies that estimate conversion probabilities for actions and contexts, then solve a linear program at each round using optimistic confidence estimates. The method therefore builds its decisions around the conversion structure while accounting for the available budget.

Under the stated assumption that contexts are independent and identically distributed, the policies achieve regret of the typical order (OPT/B)√T. Here OPT is the best expected reward of a static policy, B is the budget, and T is the number of rounds. The result gives a learning guarantee for this coupled reward-and-cost model, and the authors also show that their techniques apply to previously studied linear structures.
summary.tldr: Optimistic conversion estimates and repeated linear programming yield regret guarantees for contextual decisions with conversion-dependent rewards and costs.

title: Contextual Bandits with Knapsacks for a Conversion Model

abstract: Training neural networks sequentially in time to approximate solution fields of time-dependent partial differential equations can be beneficial for preserving causality and other physics properties; however, the sequential-in-time training is numerically challenging because training errors quickly accumulate and amplify over time. This work introduces Neural Galerkin schemes that update randomized sparse subsets of network parameters at each time step. The randomization avoids overfitting locally in time and so helps prevent the error from accumulating quickly over the sequential-in-time training, which is motivated by dropout that addresses a similar issue of overfitting due to neuron co-adaptation. The sparsity of the update reduces the computational costs of training without losing expressiveness because many of the network parameters are redundant locally at each time step. In numerical experiments with a wide range of evolution equations, the proposed scheme with randomized sparse updates is up to two orders of magnitude more accurate at a fixed computational budget and up to two orders of magnitude faster at a fixed accuracy than schemes with dense updates.

paragraphs: Neural networks can approximate solutions to time-dependent partial differential equations by advancing sequentially through time. This can help preserve causality and physical properties, but errors made during training may accumulate and grow at later steps. The paper introduces a Neural Galerkin approach designed to reduce both this error growth and the cost of updates.

At each time step, the method updates a randomly selected sparse subset of network parameters. Randomization reduces local overfitting in time, drawing motivation from dropout's role in limiting neuron co-adaptation. Sparse updates reduce computation because many parameters are locally redundant, allowing fewer parameters to change without sacrificing the network's expressive capacity.

Across numerical experiments involving a wide range of evolution equations, randomized sparse updates achieve up to two orders of magnitude greater accuracy at a fixed computational budget. They also achieve up to two orders of magnitude faster computation at a fixed accuracy than dense updates. These findings show that selective updates can improve numerical behavior as well as computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: Randomized sparse parameter updates improve the efficiency and accuracy of neural methods that solve evolution equations sequentially in time.

title: Randomized Sparse Neural Galerkin Schemes for Solving Evolution Equations with Deep Networks

abstract: Despite a great deal of research, it is still not well-understood why trained neural networks are highly vulnerable to adversarial examples.In this work we focus on two-layer neural networks trained using data which lie on a low dimensional linear subspace.We show that standard gradient methods lead to non-robust neural networks, namely, networks which have large gradients in directions orthogonal to the data subspace, and are susceptible to small adversarial $L_2$-perturbations in these directions.Moreover, we show that decreasing the initialization scale of the training algorithm, or adding $L_2$ regularization, can make the trained network more robust to adversarial perturbations orthogonal to the data.

paragraphs: This paper investigates adversarial vulnerability in two-layer ReLU networks under a specific geometric assumption: the training data lie within a low-dimensional linear subspace. This setting lets the authors distinguish changes that stay within the space occupied by the data from changes that move away from it.

The authors show that standard gradient training methods produce networks with large gradients in directions orthogonal to the data subspace. A large gradient means that a small movement in such a direction can substantially change the network's output. They connect this behavior to susceptibility to adversarial perturbations that are small in Euclidean, or L2, distance.

The analysis also identifies two ways to improve robustness in these orthogonal directions: reducing the scale of the initial parameters or adding L2 regularization during training. These results connect vulnerability to choices made by the training algorithm. Their scope is the stated network and data setting, with robustness improvements specifically concerning perturbations orthogonal to the data; they do not establish universal protection against adversarial changes.
summary.tldr: For two-layer ReLU networks trained on a low-dimensional linear subspace, the paper explains vulnerability to orthogonal perturbations and identifies training choices that can improve robustness.

title: Adversarial Examples Exist in Two-Layer ReLU Networks for Low Dimensional Linear Subspaces

abstract: Reconstructing 3D clothed human avatars from single images is a challenging task, especially when encountering complex poses and loose clothing. Current methods exhibit limitations in performance, largely attributable to their dependence on insufficient 2D image features and inconsistent query methods. Owing to this, we present the Global-correlated 3D-decoupling Transformer for clothed Avatar reconstruction (GTA), a novel transformer-based architecture that reconstructs clothed human avatars from monocular images. Our approach leverages transformer architectures by utilizing a Vision Transformer model as an encoder for capturing global-correlated image features. Subsequently, our innovative 3D-decoupling decoder employs cross-attention to decouple tri-plane features, using learnable embeddings as queries for cross-plane generation. To effectively enhance feature fusion with the tri-plane 3D feature and human body prior, we propose a hybrid prior fusion strategy combining spatial and prior-enhanced queries, leveraging the benefits of spatial localization and human body prior knowledge. Comprehensive experiments on CAPE and THuman2.0 datasets illustrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both geometry and texture reconstruction, exhibiting high robustness to challenging poses and loose clothing, and producing higher-resolution textures. Codes are available at https://github.com/River-Zhang/GTA.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a clothed person in three dimensions from one image is especially difficult when poses are complicated or clothing hangs loosely. The paper attributes weaknesses in existing approaches partly to limited image features and inconsistent ways of querying them. GTA addresses these issues with a transformer architecture designed to connect global image information with a structured three-dimensional representation.

A Vision Transformer first extracts features that capture relationships across the image. A decoder then uses cross-attention and learned queries to produce tri-plane features, representing three-dimensional information across three planes. The method also combines spatial queries with queries enhanced by a human-body prior. This fusion brings together information about location and prior knowledge of body structure.

Experiments on CAPE and THuman2.0 show improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods in both reconstructed geometry and texture. The reported results include robustness to challenging poses and loose clothing, alongside higher-resolution textures. The approach matters because it coordinates global visual context, three-dimensional features, and body knowledge within one reconstruction system, with empirical support for those difficult image conditions.
summary.tldr: GTA combines global image features, tri-plane decoding, and body priors to improve single-image reconstruction of clothed human avatars.

title: Global-correlated 3D-decoupling Transformer for Clothed Avatar Reconstruction

abstract: We develop an approach to efficiently grow neural networks, within which parameterization and optimization strategies are designed by considering their effects on the training dynamics. Unlike existing growing methods, which follow simple replication heuristics or utilize auxiliary gradient-based local optimization, we craft a parameterization scheme which dynamically stabilizes weight, activation, and gradient scaling as the architecture evolves, and maintains the inference functionality of the network. To address the optimization difficulty resulting from imbalanced training effort distributed to subnetworks fading in at different growth phases, we propose a learning rate adaption mechanism that rebalances the gradient contribution of these separate subcomponents. Experiments show that our method achieves comparable or better accuracy than training large fixed-size models, while saving a substantial portion of the original training computation budget. We demonstrate that these gains translate into real wall-clock training speedups.

paragraphs: Training a large network from the beginning spends computation on its full architecture throughout training. This paper studies a different approach: start with a smaller network and grow it incrementally. The central challenge is making those architectural changes compatible with learning, so that adding capacity does not disrupt the network’s behavior or create poorly balanced updates.

The authors design a parameterization that stabilizes the scales of weights, activations, and gradients as the network grows, while preserving its inference functionality. They also address a second problem: components introduced at different stages receive different amounts of training. A learning-rate adaptation mechanism rebalances the gradient contributions of these components to account for that uneven training effort.

In the reported experiments, growing networks achieve accuracy comparable to or better than large networks trained at a fixed size, while using substantially less training computation. The savings also translate into measured wall-clock speedups. Together, the findings support coordinating network growth with optimization, rather than treating expansion as an architectural operation alone.
summary.tldr: Carefully stabilizing network growth and adapting learning rates reduces training computation while preserving or improving accuracy in experiments.

title: Accelerated Training via Incrementally Growing Neural Networks using Variance Transfer and Learning Rate Adaptation

abstract: Gradient-based sampling algorithms have demonstrated their effectiveness in text generation, especially in the context of controlled text generation. However, there exists a lack of theoretically grounded and principled approaches for this task. In this paper, we take an important step toward building a principled approach for sampling from language models with gradient-based methods. We use discrete distributions given by language models to define densities and develop an algorithm based on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to sample from them. We name our gradient-based technique Structured Voronoi Sampling (SVS). In an experimental setup where the reference distribution is known, we show that the empirical distribution of SVS samples is closer to the reference distribution compared to alternative sampling schemes. Furthermore, in a controlled generation task, SVS is able to generate fluent and diverse samples while following the control targets significantly better than other methods.

paragraphs: Gradient-based methods can help steer generated text toward desired properties, but the paper identifies a shortage of principled foundations for this use. Structured Voronoi Sampling, or SVS, takes the discrete distribution supplied by a language model and uses it to define densities suitable for gradient-based sampling.

The resulting algorithm is based on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. The methodological contribution is a route from a language model's discrete probabilities to a sampling procedure grounded in those probabilities. This matters because successful control alone does not establish that a sampler accurately represents the distribution it is intended to follow.

The authors test distributional fidelity in a setting where the reference distribution is known. The empirical distribution produced by SVS is closer to that reference than those produced by alternative schemes. In a separate controlled-generation task, SVS produces fluent and diverse text while following the control targets significantly better than competing methods. Together, the experiments support both more faithful sampling and useful control of generated text in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SVS builds a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler from language-model probabilities and improves evaluated distributional fidelity and text control.

title: Structured Voronoi Sampling

abstract: Peer review assignment algorithms aim to match research papers to suitable expert reviewers, working to maximize the quality of the resulting reviews. A key challenge in designing effective assignment policies is evaluating how changes to the assignment algorithm map to changes in review quality. In this work, we leverage recently proposed policies that introduce randomness in peer-review assignment—in order to mitigate fraud—as a valuable opportunity to evaluate counterfactual assignment policies. Specifically, we exploit how such randomized assignments provide a positive probability of observing the reviews of many assignment policies of interest. To address challenges in applying standard off-policy evaluation methods, such as violations of positivity, we introduce novel methods for partial identification based on monotonicity and Lipschitz smoothness assumptions for the mapping between reviewer-paper covariates and outcomes. We apply our methods to peer-review data from two computer science venues: the TPDP'21 workshop (95 papers and 35 reviewers) and the AAAI'22 conference (8,450 papers and 3,145 reviewers). We consider estimates of (i) the effect on review quality when changing weights in the assignment algorithm, e.g., weighting reviewers' bids vs. textual similarity (between the review's past papers and the submission), and (ii) the "cost of randomization", capturing the difference in expected quality between the perturbed and unperturbed optimal match. We find that placing higher weight on text similarity results in higher review quality and that introducing randomization in the reviewer-paper assignment only marginally reduces the review quality. Our methods for partial identification may be of independent interest, while our off-policy approach can likely find use in evaluating a broad class of algorithmic matching systems.

paragraphs: Changing how papers are assigned to reviewers may change review quality, but evaluating an alternative policy requires reasoning about assignments that were not made. This paper uses randomness already introduced into reviewer assignment to mitigate fraud. Because randomized policies can select many different reviewer-paper matches, their resulting reviews provide evidence about alternative assignment policies.

It finds higher review quality when textual similarity receives more weight, and only a marginal quality reduction from randomization. The findings inform these assignment choices, while the partial-identification approach may also be useful for other algorithmic matching systems.
summary.tldr: Randomized reviewer assignments enable counterfactual policy evaluation, with reported evidence favoring text similarity and finding a small quality cost from randomization.

title: Counterfactual Evaluation of Peer-Review Assignment Policies

abstract: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) algorithms can perform planning at multiple levels of abstraction. Empirical results have shown that state or temporal abstractions might significantly improve the sample efficiency of algorithms. Yet, we still do not have a complete understanding of the basis of those efficiency gains nor any theoretically grounded design rules. In this paper, we derive a lower bound on the sample complexity for the considered class of goal-conditioned HRL algorithms. The proposed lower bound empowers us to quantify the benefits of hierarchical decomposition and leads to the design of a simple Q-learning-type algorithm that leverages hierarchical decompositions. We empirically validate our theoretical findings by investigating the sample complexity of the proposed hierarchical algorithm on a spectrum of tasks (hierarchical $n$-rooms, Gymnasium's Taxi). The hierarchical $n$-rooms tasks were designed to allow us to dial their complexity over multiple orders of magnitude. Our theory and algorithmic findings provide a step towards answering the foundational question of quantifying the improvement hierarchical decomposition offers over monolithic solutions in reinforcement learning.

This paper studies the sample complexity of a particular class of goal-conditioned hierarchical algorithms to make that benefit more precise.

The authors derive a lower bound on the number of samples required within the considered class. The bound helps quantify the benefit of hierarchical decomposition and informs a simple Q-learning-type algorithm that uses such decompositions. This links a theoretical account of learning requirements to an algorithmic design, rather than leaving hierarchy solely as an empirical choice.

The n-rooms construction allows task complexity to vary over multiple orders of magnitude, supporting evaluation across a wide range of difficulty. The findings provide a step toward quantifying how hierarchical decomposition improves sample requirements relative to monolithic learning within the studied framework.
summary.tldr: A sample-complexity lower bound helps quantify hierarchical reinforcement-learning benefits and guides a simple hierarchy-aware Q-learning algorithm.

title: Sample Complexity of Goal-Conditioned Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We present a novel framework for 3D object-centric representation learning. Our approach effectively decomposes complex scenes into individual objects from a single image in an unsupervised fashion. This method, called \underline{s}lot-guided \underline{V}olumetric \underline{O}bject \underline{R}adiance \underline{F}ields~(sVORF), composes volumetric object radiance fields with object slots as a guidance to implement unsupervised 3D scene decomposition. Specifically, sVORF obtains object slots from a single image via a transformer module, maps these slots to volumetric object radiance fields with a hypernetwork and composes object radiance fields with the guidance of object slots at a 3D location. Moreover, sVORF significantly reduces memory requirement due to small-sized pixel rendering during training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by showing top results in scene decomposition and generation tasks of complex synthetic datasets (e.g., Room-Diverse). Furthermore, we also confirm the potential of sVORF to segment objects in real-world scenes (e.g., the LLFF dataset). We hope our approach can provide preliminary understanding of the physical world and help ease future research in 3D object-centric representation learning.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene as a collection of objects requires separating its contents while representing their spatial structure. This paper introduces sVORF, an unsupervised framework that decomposes complex scenes into individual objects from a single image. It combines object-centered representations with volumetric radiance fields to build a three-dimensional account of the scene.

A transformer first extracts object slots from the image. A hypernetwork maps those slots to volumetric object radiance fields, and the slots then guide how those fields are combined at a three-dimensional location. This connects the image's object representations with the volumetric components used to represent and render the scene.

The training procedure also uses small-sized pixel rendering to substantially reduce memory requirements. Experiments report top results for decomposition and generation on complex synthetic datasets, including Room-Diverse. Results on LLFF additionally demonstrate potential for object segmentation in real-world scenes. The evidence therefore combines strong synthetic-scene results with an initial indication of real-world usefulness, supporting further work on object-centered three-dimensional representation learning.
summary.tldr: sVORF uses object slots to construct and combine volumetric object radiance fields for unsupervised scene decomposition from a single image.

title: Slot-guided Volumetric Object Radiance Fields

abstract: The visual object category reports of artificial neural networks (ANNs) are notoriously sensitive to tiny, adversarial image perturbations. Because human category reports (aka human percepts) are thought to be insensitive to those same small-norm perturbations -- and locally stable in general -- this argues that ANNs are incomplete scientific models of human visual perception. Consistent with this, we show that when small-norm image perturbations are generated by standard ANN models, human object category percepts are indeed highly stable. However, in this very same "human-presumed-stable" regime, we find that robustified ANNs reliably discover low-norm image perturbations that strongly disrupt human percepts. These previously undetectable human perceptual disruptions are massive in amplitude, approaching the same level of sensitivity seen in robustified ANNs. Further, we show that robustified ANNs support precise perceptual state interventions: they guide the construction of low-norm image perturbations that strongly alter human category percepts toward specific prescribed percepts. In sum, these contemporary models of biological visual processing are now accurate enough to guide strong and precise interventions on human perception.

paragraphs: Small adversarial image changes can alter a neural network's object classification while appearing to leave human category judgments stable. That mismatch has been used to question neural networks as models of human vision. This paper examines whether the mismatch depends on which network generates the image perturbation.

Perturbations produced by standard networks do leave human object-category judgments highly stable in the tested small-norm regime. Robustified networks, however, find perturbations within that same regime that strongly disrupt human judgments. The resulting human sensitivity approaches the level observed in the robustified networks, challenging the presumed stability of human perception under these changes.

The authors also demonstrate targeted interventions: robustified networks guide image modifications that shift human category judgments toward specified percepts. The result goes beyond inducing arbitrary errors by showing control over the direction of a perceptual change. These findings support the use of such networks to design strong, precise interventions on human object perception in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: Robustified neural networks find small image perturbations that strongly and selectively change human object-category judgments.

title: Strong and Precise Modulation of Human Percepts via Robustified ANNs

abstract: Interpretable AI tools are often motivated by the goal of understanding model behavior in out-of-distribution (OOD) contexts. Despite the attention this area of study receives, there are comparatively few cases where these tools have identified previously unknown bugs in models. We argue that this is due, in part, to a common feature of many interpretability methods: they analyze model behavior by using a particular dataset. This only allows for the study of the model in the context of features that the user can sample in advance. To address this, a growing body of research involves interpreting models using feature synthesis methods that do not depend on a dataset. In this paper, we benchmark the usefulness of interpretability tools for model debugging. Our key insight is that we can implant human-interpretable trojans into models and then evaluate these tools based on whether they can help humans discover them. This is analogous to finding OOD bugs, except the ground truth is known, allowing us to know when a user's interpretation is correct. We make four contributions. (1) We propose trojan discovery as an evaluation task for interpretability tools and introduce a benchmark with 12 trojans of 3 different types. (2) We demonstrate the difficulty of this benchmark with a preliminary evaluation of 16 state-of-the-art feature attribution/saliency tools. Even under ideal conditions, given direct access to data with the trojan trigger, these methods still often fail to identify bugs. (3) We evaluate 7 feature-synthesis methods on our benchmark. (4) We introduce and evaluate 2 new variants of the best-performing method from the previous evaluation.

paragraphs: Interpretability tools are often intended to help discover unexpected model behavior, yet evaluating whether they actually uncover bugs is difficult. Dataset-based tools can only examine features represented in the examples available to the user. This paper develops a controlled debugging benchmark to assess whether interpretability tools help people identify known problematic behavior.

The authors implant human-interpretable trojans into models and ask whether tools help users discover them. Because the implanted behavior is known, the benchmark can check whether an interpretation is correct. It contains twelve trojans across three types, creating an evaluation task analogous to discovering unfamiliar bugs while retaining ground truth.

The paper also evaluates seven feature-synthesis methods, which can explore features without depending on a dataset, and introduces two variants of the strongest method in that evaluation. The contribution is both a debugging benchmark and evidence that access to relevant examples alone does not ensure successful interpretation.
summary.tldr: A benchmark of implanted model trojans tests whether interpretability tools help humans discover bugs and exposes frequent failures of attribution methods.

title: Red Teaming Deep Neural Networks with Feature Synthesis Tools

abstract: When training node embedding models to represent large directed graphs (digraphs), it is impossible to observe all entries of the adjacency matrix during training. As a consequence most methods employ sampling. For very large digraphs, however, this means many (most) entries may be unobserved during training. In general, observing every entry would be necessary to uniquely identify a graph, however if we know the graph has a certain property some entries can be omitted - for example, only half the entries would be required for a symmetric graph. In this work, we develop a novel framework to identify a subset of entries required to uniquely distinguish a graph among all transitively-closed DAGs. We give an explicit algorithm to compute the provably minimal set of entries, and demonstrate empirically that one can train node embedding models with greater efficiency and performance, provided the energy function has an appropriate inductive bias. We achieve robust performance on synthetic hierarchies and a larger real-world taxonomy, observing improved convergence rates in a resource-constrained setting while reducing the set of training examples by as much as 99%.

paragraphs: Learning embeddings for a large directed graph usually requires sampling its adjacency matrix because inspecting every entry is impractical. The paper asks whether known hierarchical structure can identify a smaller set of entries that still uniquely determines the graph. Its setting is transitively closed directed acyclic graphs, a structured class of hierarchical relations.

The authors develop a framework for finding the entries needed to distinguish one such graph from every other graph in that class. They provide an explicit algorithm that computes a provably minimal set. This turns training-example selection into a problem guided by what information is sufficient to identify the hierarchy, rather than relying only on general sampling.

Experiments show that embedding models can learn more efficiently and perform better with these selected entries, provided their energy function has an appropriate inductive bias. Tests on synthetic hierarchies and a larger real-world taxonomy show improved convergence under resource constraints, with training examples reduced by as much as 99%. The guarantee concerns minimal identifying information, while the training benefits additionally depend on a suitably structured model.
summary.tldr: A provably minimal identifying set for transitively closed DAGs enables more efficient embedding training when the model has an appropriate inductive bias.

title: Learning Representations for Hierarchies with Minimal Support

abstract: Code generation models have increasingly become integral to aiding software development. Although current research has thoroughly examined the correctness of the code produced by code generation models, a vital aspect that plays a pivotal role in greencomputing and sustainability efforts — the efficiency of the generated code — has often been neglected. This paper presents Effibench, a benchmark with 1,000 efficiency-critical coding problems to assess the efficiency of code generated by code generation models. EffiBench contains a diverse set of LeetCode coding problems. Each problem is paired with an executable human-written canonical solution, which obtains the SOTA efficiency on the LeetCode solution leaderboard. With EffiBench, we empirically examine the ability of 42 large language models (35 open-source and 7 closed-source) to generate efficient code. Our evaluation results demonstrate that the efficiency of the code generated by LLMs is generally worse than the efficiency of human-written canonical solutions. For example, GPT-4 generated code has an average \textbf{3.12} times execution time that of the human-written canonical solutions. In the most extreme cases, the execution time and total memory usage of GPT-4 code are \textbf{13.89} and \textbf{43.92} times that of the canonical solutions. The source code of EffiBench is released on https://github.com/huangd1999/EffiBench. We also provide the LeaderBoard in https://huggingface.co/spaces/EffiBench/effibench-leaderboard.

paragraphs: A generated program can produce the right answers while taking unnecessarily long or consuming excessive memory. EffiBench targets this distinction by evaluating the computational efficiency of code produced by language models. The paper connects this overlooked aspect of code generation to the resource demands relevant to green computing and sustainability.

The benchmark contains 1,000 efficiency-critical LeetCode problems. Each comes with an executable human-written reference solution that achieves leading efficiency on the corresponding LeetCode leaderboard. The authors use these references to evaluate 42 language models, comprising 35 open-source models and seven closed-source models.

Generated code is generally less efficient than the reference solutions in the reported evaluation. GPT-4 code, for example, takes 3.12 times as long on average. In the most extreme cases, its execution time and total memory use reach 13.89 and 43.92 times the reference values, respectively. These results identify a substantial resource-efficiency gap and show why correctness alone gives an incomplete picture of code-generation performance.
summary.tldr: EffiBench finds substantial runtime and memory-efficiency gaps between model-generated code and strong human-written reference solutions.

title: EffiBench: Benchmarking the Efficiency of Automatically Generated Code

abstract: We propose a novel approach for training large language models (LLMs) to adhere to objectives defined within a latent embedding space. Our method leverages reinforcement learning (RL), treating a pre-trained LLM as an environment. Our embedding-aligned guided language (EAGLE) agent is trained to iteratively steer the LLM's generation towards optimal regions of the latent embedding space, w.r.t. some predefined criterion. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the EAGLE agent using the MovieLens 25M and Amazon Review datasets to surface content gaps that satisfy latent user demand. We also demonstrate the benefit of using an optimal design of a state-dependent action set to improve EAGLE's efficiency. Our work paves the way for controlled and grounded text generation using LLMs, ensuring consistency with domain-specific knowledge and data representations.

paragraphs: Some text-generation objectives are expressed through a latent embedding space: a representation in which a predefined criterion identifies desirable regions. This paper develops a way to guide a language model toward those regions. The aim is to connect generated language with objectives encoded in domain-specific knowledge and data representations.

The proposed EAGLE agent learns through reinforcement learning, treating a pretrained language model as its environment. It repeatedly steers the model's generation according to the embedding-space objective. This formulation gives the agent a defined target for control and makes generation an iterative process directed toward satisfying that target.

The authors demonstrate EAGLE on MovieLens 25M and Amazon Review data, using it to surface content gaps that satisfy latent user demand. They also show that an optimally designed, state-dependent set of available actions improves efficiency. Together, these demonstrations support embedding-based objectives as a practical means of guiding generation, with the action design helping the agent pursue those objectives more efficiently.
summary.tldr: EAGLE uses reinforcement learning to steer language-model generation toward objectives defined in a latent embedding space.

title: Embedding-Aligned Language Models

abstract: Deep neural networks, costly to train and rich in intellectual property value, areincreasingly threatened by model extraction attacks that compromise their confiden-tiality. Previous attacks have succeeded in reverse-engineering model parametersup to a precision of float64 for models trained on random data with at most threehidden layers using cryptanalytical techniques. However, the process was identifiedto be very time consuming and not feasible for larger and deeper models trained onstandard benchmarks. Our study evaluates the feasibility of parameter extractionmethods of Carlini et al. [1] further enhanced by Canales-Martínez et al. [2] formodels trained on standard benchmarks. We introduce a unified codebase thatintegrates previous methods and reveal that computational tools can significantlyinfluence performance. We develop further optimisations to the end-to-end attackand improve the efficiency of extracting weight signs by up to 14.8 times com-pared to former methods through the identification of easier and harder to extractneurons. Contrary to prior assumptions, we identify extraction of weights, notextraction of weight signs, as the critical bottleneck. With our improvements, a16,721 parameter model with 2 hidden layers trained on MNIST is extracted withinonly 98 minutes compared to at least 150 minutes previously. Finally, addressingmethodological deficiencies observed in previous studies, we propose new ways ofrobust benchmarking for future model extraction attacks.

paragraphs: This paper examines how feasibly an attacker can reconstruct a neural network’s parameters with high numerical fidelity. Earlier cryptanalytic methods had recovered parameters for small networks trained on random data, but their computational expense raised questions about applicability to networks trained on standard benchmarks. The study revisits those methods in that more practical setting.

The authors combine earlier attacks into a unified codebase and show that computational tools substantially affect performance. They also improve the overall attack, including a procedure that distinguishes neurons whose weight signs are easier or harder to recover. This accelerates sign extraction by up to 14.8 times. Their analysis identifies weight extraction itself, rather than sign extraction, as the main bottleneck.

With these improvements, they extract a two-hidden-layer MNIST model containing 16,721 parameters in 98 minutes, compared with at least 150 minutes previously. This is a concrete feasibility result for the studied model. The paper also proposes more robust benchmarking methods to address methodological weaknesses in previous extraction studies and make future comparisons more informative.
summary.tldr: An improved model-extraction implementation speeds parameter recovery and identifies weight extraction, rather than sign recovery, as the central bottleneck.

title: Beyond Slow Signs in High-fidelity Model Extraction

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a learning paradigm that enables collaborative training of models using decentralized data. Recently, the utilization of pre-trained weight initialization in FL has been demonstrated to effectively improve model performance. However, the evolving complexity of current pre-trained models, characterized by a substantial increase in parameters, markedly intensifies the challenges associated with communication rounds required for their adaptation to FL. To address these communication cost issues and increase the performance of pre-trained model adaptation in FL, we propose an innovative model interpolation-based local training technique called ``Local Superior Soups.''Our method enhances local training across different clients, encouraging the exploration of a connected low-loss basin within a few communication rounds through regularized model interpolation. This approach acts as a catalyst for the seamless adaptation of pre-trained models in in FL.We demonstrated its effectiveness and efficiency across diverse widely-used FL datasets.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets participants train collaboratively while keeping their data decentralized. Starting from pretrained weights can improve the resulting model, but increasingly large pretrained models make repeated communication more burdensome. This paper focuses on adapting those models effectively when only a few communication rounds are available.

Local Superior Soups changes the training performed at individual clients through regularized model interpolation. Interpolation combines model weights, and the regularization encourages exploration within a connected region of low loss. The intended effect is to improve local training in a way that supports merging the participating models during adaptation. This makes the local optimization process central to addressing the communication problem.

The authors evaluate the approach across diverse, widely used federated-learning datasets and report effectiveness and efficiency. The stated contribution is a local training technique that helps pretrained models adapt within a small number of communication rounds. Its significance lies in coordinating how clients explore useful model weights, so that stronger local training can contribute to collaborative performance under communication constraints.
summary.tldr: Local Superior Soups uses regularized weight interpolation to improve pretrained-model adaptation with few federated communication rounds.

title: Local Superior Soups: A Catalyst for Model Merging in Cross-Silo Federated Learning

abstract: This paper proposes the RePAIR dataset that represents a challenging benchmark to test modern computational and data driven methods for puzzle-solving and reassembly tasks. Our dataset has unique properties that are uncommon to current benchmarks for 2D and 3D puzzle solving. The fragments and fractures are realistic, caused by a collapse of a fresco during a World War II bombing at the Pompeii archaeological park. The fragments are also eroded and have missing pieces with irregular shapes and different dimensions, challenging further the reassembly algorithms. The dataset is multi-modal providing high resolution images with characteristic pictorial elements, detailed 3D scans of the fragments and meta-data annotated by the archaeologists. Ground truth has been generated through several years of unceasing fieldwork, including the excavation and cleaning of each fragment, followed by manual puzzle solving by archaeologists of a subset of approx. 1000 pieces among the 16000 available. After digitizing all the fragments in 3D, a benchmark was prepared to challenge current reassembly and puzzle-solving methods that often solve more simplistic synthetic scenarios. The tested baselines show that there clearly exists a gap to fill in solving this computationally complex problem.

paragraphs: RePAIR provides a benchmark for reconstructing genuinely broken objects using fragments of a fresco that collapsed during a World War II bombing at Pompeii. Its pieces have irregular shapes and sizes, erosion, and missing material. These properties make the reconstruction task substantially different from simplified synthetic puzzles with clean, complete pieces.

The dataset combines high-resolution images of painted surfaces, detailed three-dimensional scans, and metadata annotated by archaeologists. Ground truth comes from years of excavation, cleaning, and manual reconstruction. Archaeologists assembled a subset of approximately 1,000 pieces from roughly 16,000 available fragments, and all fragments were digitized in three dimensions.

The benchmark uses this material to assess current computational and data-driven reassembly methods. Tested baselines reveal a clear gap in solving the real reconstruction problem. The dataset’s importance lies in making archaeological damage and incomplete evidence part of the evaluation itself. Methods must contend with the visual and geometric irregularities found in actual fragments, rather than succeeding only under the cleaner conditions of synthetic puzzle construction.
summary.tldr: RePAIR benchmarks real-world reassembly using damaged fresco fragments, multimodal scans, and archaeologist-established partial ground truth.

title: Re-assembling the past: The RePAIR dataset and benchmark for real world 2D and 3D puzzle solving

abstract: Adam has been shown to outperform gradient descent on large language models by a larger margin than on other tasks, but it is unclear why. We show that a key factor in this performance gap is the heavy-tailed class imbalance found in language tasks. When trained with gradient descent, the loss of infrequent words decreases more slowly than the loss of frequent ones. This leads to a slow decrease on the average loss as most samples come from infrequent words. On the other hand, Adam and sign-based methods are less sensitive to this problem. To establish that this behavior is caused by class imbalance, we show empirically that it can be reproduced across architectures and data types, on language transformers, vision CNNs, and linear models. On a linear model with cross-entropy loss, we show that class imbalance leads to imbalanced, correlated gradients and Hessians that have been hypothesized to benefit Adam. We also prove that, in continuous time, gradient descent converges slowly on low-frequency classes while sign descent does not.

paragraphs: Adam's advantage over gradient descent is unusually large in language modeling. This paper identifies heavy-tailed class imbalance as a key contributor: word frequencies vary greatly, and gradient descent reduces the loss for uncommon words more slowly than for common ones. Because infrequent words collectively account for many samples, their slow progress can hold back the average loss.

The authors show empirically that this behavior also appears in vision convolutional networks and linear models, alongside language transformers. Reproducing it across these settings supports class imbalance as the underlying explanation rather than attributing the effect only to language-model architecture. Adam and methods based on gradient signs are less sensitive to the imbalance.

For a linear model trained with cross-entropy loss, the analysis connects imbalance to uneven, correlated gradients and loss curvature, properties previously hypothesized to favor Adam. A continuous-time proof further shows slow gradient-descent convergence on low-frequency classes without the corresponding slowdown for sign descent. The result provides both experimental and restricted theoretical support for class imbalance as one important cause of the optimizer performance gap.
summary.tldr: Heavy-tailed word-frequency imbalance helps explain Adam's advantage because gradient descent learns low-frequency classes more slowly.

title: Heavy-Tailed Class Imbalance and Why Adam Outperforms Gradient Descent on Language Models

abstract: This paper presents OmniJARVIS, a novel Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model for open-world instruction-following agents in Minecraft. Compared to prior works that either emit textual goals to separate controllers or produce the control command directly, OmniJARVIS seeks a different path to ensure both strong reasoning and efficient decision-making capabilities via unified tokenization of multimodal interaction data. First, we introduce a self-supervised approach to learn a behavior encoder that produces discretized tokens for behavior trajectories $\tau = \{o_0, a_0, \dots\}$ and an imitation learning policy decoder conditioned on these tokens. These additional behavior tokens will be augmented to the vocabulary of pretrained Multimodal Language Models. With this encoder, we then pack long-term multimodal interactions involving task instructions, memories, thoughts, observations, textual responses, behavior trajectories, etc into unified token sequences and model them with autoregressive transformers. Thanks to the semantically meaningful behavior tokens, the resulting VLA model, OmniJARVIS, can reason (by producing chain-of-thoughts), plan, answer questions, and act (by producing behavior tokens for the imitation learning policy decoder). OmniJARVIS demonstrates excellent performances on a comprehensive collection of atomic, programmatic, and open-ended tasks in open-world Minecraft. Our analysis further unveils the crucial design principles in interaction data formation, unified tokenization, and its scaling potentials. The dataset, models, and code will be released at https://craftjarvis.org/OmniJARVIS.

This lets planning and action generation operate within the same sequence-modeling framework while a policy decoder carries out the selected behavior.

The authors first learn a behavior encoder through self-supervision and train an imitation-learning decoder conditioned on the resulting discrete tokens. They add those tokens to a pretrained multimodal model's vocabulary. Instructions, memories, observations, textual responses, reasoning text, and behavior trajectories can then be assembled into long interaction sequences and modeled autoregressively.

The resulting agent can answer questions, generate plans and reasoning, and act by emitting behavior tokens for the decoder. Evaluations report excellent performance across atomic, programmatic, and open-ended Minecraft tasks. The accompanying analysis examines interaction-data construction, unified tokenization, and scaling potential. The contribution is a concrete connection between multimodal reasoning and executable behavior through learned tokens that carry behavioral meaning.
summary.tldr: OmniJARVIS combines language, vision, and learned behavior tokens to support reasoning and action in open-world Minecraft tasks.

title: OmniJARVIS: Unified Vision-Language-Action Tokenization Enables Open-World Instruction Following Agents

abstract: LiDAR-based 3D object detection has made impressive progress recently, yet most existing models are black-box, lacking interpretability. Previous explanation approaches primarily focus on analyzing image-based models and are not readily applicable to LiDAR-based 3D detectors. In this paper, we propose a feature factorization activation map (FFAM) to generate high-quality visual explanations for 3D detectors. FFAM employs non-negative matrix factorization to generate concept activation maps and subsequently aggregates these maps to obtain a global visual explanation. To achieve object-specific visual explanations, we refine the global visual explanation using the feature gradient of a target object. Additionally, we introduce a voxel upsampling strategy to align the scale between the activation map and input point cloud. We qualitatively and quantitatively analyze FFAM with multiple detectors on several datasets. Experimental results validate the high-quality visual explanations produced by FFAM. The code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FFAM-B9AF}.

paragraphs: LiDAR-based detectors identify objects in three-dimensional point clouds, but their internal decisions can be difficult to interpret. Explanation methods developed for image models do not readily transfer to these detectors. FFAM is designed to produce visual explanations that connect a 3D detector’s internal features with its point-cloud input.

The method first uses non-negative matrix factorization to produce concept activation maps, then combines them into a global explanation. For an individual detected object, it refines that global map using the gradient associated with the target object’s features. This provides both an overall view of the detector’s activations and an explanation focused on a particular detection.

FFAM also introduces voxel upsampling to match the activation map’s scale to the input point cloud, allowing the explanation to be spatially aligned with the data being inspected. The authors evaluate it qualitatively and quantitatively across multiple detectors and datasets, reporting high-quality visual explanations. The contribution is an explanation procedure tailored to the representations and spatial structure of LiDAR detection.
summary.tldr: FFAM combines feature factorization, object-specific gradients, and voxel upsampling to visually explain LiDAR-based 3D detections.

title: FFAM: Feature Factorization Activation Map for Explanation of 3D Detectors

abstract: Rectified flow and reflow procedures have significantly advanced fast generation by progressively straightening ordinary differential equation (ODE) flows under the assumption that image and noise pairs, known as coupling, can be approximated by straight trajectories with constant velocity. However, we observe that the constant velocity modeling and reflow procedures have limitations in accurately learning to couple with flow crossing, leading to suboptimal few-step generation. To overcome the limitations, we introduce the Constant Acceleration Flow (CAF), a novel framework based on a simple constant acceleration equation. Additionally, we propose two techniques to improve estimation accuracy: initial velocity conditioning for the acceleration model and a reflow process for the initial velocity. Our comparative studies show that CAF not only outperforms rectified flow with reflow procedures in terms of speed and accuracy but also demonstrates substantial improvements in preserving coupling for fast generation.

To overcome the limitations, we introduce the Constant Acceleration Flow (CAF), a novel framework based on a simple constant acceleration equation. Additionally, we propose two techniques to improve estimation accuracy: initial velocity conditioning for the acceleration model and a reflow process for the initial velocity. paragraphs: Flow-based generation connects noise and images through trajectories described by differential equations. Rectified flow and reflow speed up generation by progressively straightening these trajectories, treating the connection between each noise sample and image as approximately constant-velocity motion. This paper argues that such modeling has difficulty accurately learning the intended pairings when flows cross.

Constant Acceleration Flow replaces the constant-velocity description with a simple constant-acceleration equation. It also introduces two techniques intended to improve estimation: conditioning the acceleration model on initial velocity, and applying a reflow process to the initial velocity. Together, these changes address both the form of the trajectory and how its starting motion is estimated.

Comparative studies report improvements over rectified flow with reflow in speed and accuracy, alongside better preservation of the noise–image coupling. That last finding concerns whether the learned process maintains the intended pairing between its starting noise and resulting image. The results support constant acceleration as a useful alternative for fast generation with few steps.
summary.tldr: Constant Acceleration Flow improves reported generation speed, accuracy, and noise–image pairing preservation by changing how generative trajectories are modeled.

title: Constant Acceleration Flow

abstract: Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) is a powerful and theoretically sound methodology for sequential decision-making. However, it is not directly applicable to Reinforcement Learning (RL) due to the inaccessibility of explicit action-value functions. We address this challenge by introducing a novel approach based on learning a world model of the environment using conditional mean embeddings. Leveraging tools from operator theory we derive a closed-form expression of the action-value function in terms of the world model via simple matrix operations. Combining these estimators with PMD leads to POWR, a new RL algorithm for which we prove convergence rates to the global optimum. Preliminary experiments in finite and infinite state settings support the effectiveness of our method.

Leveraging tools from operator theory we derive a closed-form expression of the action-value function in terms of the world model via simple matrix operations. Combining these estimators with PMD leads to POWR, a new RL algorithm for which we prove convergence rates to the global optimum. paragraphs: Policy Mirror Descent offers a theoretically grounded method for sequential decisions, but applying it directly in reinforcement learning requires action-value functions that are not explicitly available. These functions describe the value of taking actions. The paper addresses this obstacle by learning a world model that can supply the needed estimates.

The world model uses conditional mean embeddings to represent the environment. Tools from operator theory then yield a closed-form expression for the action-value function in terms of that learned model. The expression uses simple matrix operations, providing a concrete computational connection between an environment representation and the quantities required for policy improvement.

Combining these estimators with Policy Mirror Descent produces an algorithm called POWR. The authors prove convergence rates to the global optimum and report preliminary experiments in both finite and infinite state settings that support its effectiveness. The contribution links world-model learning to policy optimization through an explicit value-function calculation, with theoretical convergence analysis and initial empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: POWR uses an operator-based world model to estimate action values for Policy Mirror Descent, with proven convergence rates.

title: Operator World Models for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Drawing upon recent advances in language model alignment, we formulate offline Reinforcement Learning as a two-stage optimization problem: First pretraining expressive generative policies on reward-free behavior datasets, then finetuning these policies to align with task-specific annotations like Q-values. This strategy allows us to leverage abundant and diverse behavior data to enhance generalization and enable rapid adaptation to downstream tasks using minimal annotations. In particular, we introduce Efficient Diffusion Alignment (EDA) for solving continuous control problems. EDA utilizes diffusion models for behavior modeling. However, unlike previous approaches, we represent diffusion policies as the derivative of a scalar neural network with respect to action inputs. This representation is critical because it enables direct density calculation for diffusion models, making them compatible with existing LLM alignment theories. During policy fine-tuning, we extend preference-based alignment methods like Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align diffusion behaviors with continuous Q-functions. Our evaluation on the D4RL benchmark shows that EDA exceeds all baseline methods in overall performance. Notably, EDA maintains about 95\% of performance and still outperforms several baselines given only 1\% of Q-labelled data during fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Efficient Diffusion Alignment, or EDA, separates learning how to act from learning which actions suit a particular task. It first trains a generative policy on behavior data without rewards. It then adjusts that policy using task-specific Q-values, which score actions. This organization allows diverse behavior data to support policy learning before task annotations are available.

The technical contribution is a particular representation of the diffusion policy: it is expressed as the derivative of a scalar neural network with respect to action inputs. This enables direct density calculation, connecting the policy to alignment theories developed for language models. The authors then extend preference-based methods such as Direct Preference Optimization to alignment with continuous Q-functions.

On the D4RL benchmark, EDA achieves better overall performance than all evaluated baselines. With only 1% of the Q-labeled data during fine-tuning, it retains about 95% of its performance and still exceeds several baselines. These results support the usefulness of separating broad behavior learning from annotation-efficient task adaptation.
summary.tldr: EDA learns diffusion policies from reward-free behavior data, then aligns them with Q-values to achieve strong continuous-control performance with few annotations.

title: Aligning Diffusion Behaviors with Q-functions for Efficient Continuous Control

abstract: Recent advancements in 3D perception have led to a proliferation of network architectures, particularly those involving multi-modal fusion algorithms. While these fusion algorithms improve accuracy, their complexity often impedes real-time performance. This paper introduces VeXKD, an effective and Versatile framework that integrates Cross-Modal Fusion with Knowledge Distillation. VeXKD applies knowledge distillation exclusively to the Bird's Eye View (BEV) feature maps, enabling the transfer of cross-modal insights to single-modal students without additional inference time overhead. It avoids volatile components that can vary across various 3D perception tasks and student modalities, thus improving versatility. The framework adopts a modality-general cross-modal fusion module to bridge the modality gap between the multi-modal teachers and single-modal students. Furthermore, leveraging byproducts generated during fusion, our BEV query guided mask generation network identifies crucial spatial locations across different BEV feature maps in a data-driven manner, significantly enhancing the effectiveness of knowledge distillation. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes dataset demonstrate notable improvements, with up to 6.9\%/4.2\% increase in mAP and NDS for 3D detection tasks and up to 4.3\% rise in mIoU for BEV map segmentation tasks, narrowing the performance gap with multi-modal models.

paragraphs: Combining multiple modalities can improve 3D perception, but complex fusion architectures can make real-time operation harder. VeXKD transfers knowledge from multimodal teachers to single-modal students. Its objective is to capture some benefits of cross-modal learning without adding inference-time overhead to the student.

The framework confines knowledge distillation to bird’s-eye-view feature maps, avoiding components that vary across perception tasks and student modalities. A modality-general fusion module helps bridge the gap between teacher and student representations. A query-guided mask-generation network then uses byproducts of fusion to identify important spatial locations, making the distillation process sensitive to where useful information appears.

The authors report increases of up to 6.9% in mAP and 4.2% in NDS for detection, and up to 4.3% in mIoU for segmentation. These improvements narrow the gap between single-modal and multimodal models. The findings support feature-map-level distillation as a versatile way to transfer cross-modal knowledge while preserving the student’s inference efficiency.
summary.tldr: VeXKD distills multimodal knowledge through bird’s-eye-view features to improve single-modal 3D perception without additional inference overhead.

title: VeXKD: The Versatile Integration of Cross-Modal Fusion and Knowledge Distillation for 3D Perception

abstract: Humans draw to facilitate reasoning: we draw auxiliary lines when solving geometry problems; we mark and circle when reasoning on maps; we use sketches to amplify our ideas and relieve our limited-capacity working memory. However, such actions are missing in current multimodal language models (LMs). Current chain-of-thought and tool-use paradigms only use text as intermediate reasoning steps. In this work, we introduce Sketchpad, a framework that gives multimodal LMs a visual sketchpad and tools to draw on the sketchpad. The LM conducts planning and reasoning according to the visual artifacts it has drawn. Different from prior work, which uses text-to-image models to enable LMs to draw, Sketchpad enables LMs to draw with lines, boxes, marks, etc., which is closer to human sketching and better facilitates reasoning. \name can also use specialist vision models during the sketching process (e.g., draw bounding boxes with object detection models, draw masks with segmentation models), to further enhance visual perception and reasoning. We experiment on a wide range of math tasks (including geometry, functions, graph, chess) and complex visual reasoning tasks. Sketchpad substantially improves performance on all tasks over strong base models with no sketching, yielding an average gain of 12.7% on math tasks, and 8.6% on vision tasks. GPT-4o with Sketchpad sets a new state of the art on all tasks, including V*Bench (80.3%), BLINK spatial reasoning (83.9%), and visual correspondence (80.8%). We will release all code and data.

The LM conducts planning and reasoning according to the visual artifacts it has drawn. Sketchpad can also call specialist vision models, using object detection to draw bounding boxes or segmentation to draw masks. These capabilities connect perception with the sketching process, allowing the model’s evolving visual workspace to incorporate information extracted from the image.

GPT-4o with Sketchpad achieves state-of-the-art results on all evaluated tasks, including 80.3% on V*Bench, 83.9% on BLINK spatial reasoning, and 80.8% on visual correspondence. summary.tldr: Sketchpad lets multimodal models draw and inspect visual reasoning aids, improving performance across the evaluated math and vision tasks.

title: Visual Sketchpad: Sketching as a Visual Chain of Thought for Multimodal Language Models

abstract: Controllability, temporal coherence, and detail synthesis remain the most critical challenges in video generation. In this paper, we focus on a commonly used yet underexplored cinematic technique known as Frame In and Frame Out. Specifically, starting from image-to-video generation, users can control the objects in the image to naturally leave the scene or provide breaking new identity references to enter the scene, guided by a user-specified motion trajectory. To support this task, we introduce a new dataset that is curated semi-automatically, an efficient identity-preserving motion-controllable video Diffusion Transformer architecture, and a comprehensive evaluation protocol targeting this task. Our evaluation shows that our proposed approach significantly outperforms existing baselines.
