paragraphs: Image-to-video generation becomes more demanding when a scene’s cast must change during the clip. This paper focuses on Frame In and Frame Out: making an object leave the visible scene or introducing a new subject using an identity reference. Users specify a motion trajectory to guide these entrances and exits.

The task connects several difficult requirements. The movement must follow the requested path, the subject’s identity must remain recognizable, and the video must remain coherent over time while synthesizing detail. The authors introduce an efficient video Diffusion Transformer designed for identity preservation and motion control. Its purpose is to support these changes in scene contents within an image-to-video generation framework.

The contribution also includes a semi-automatically curated dataset and an evaluation protocol tailored to the task. The reported evaluation finds that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing baselines. Together, these components make entrances and exits a concrete generation problem with dedicated training material, a model architecture, and a way to assess performance, rather than treating them only as incidental motion.
summary.tldr: Frame In-N-Out enables trajectory-controlled entrances and exits in image-to-video generation while preserving subject identity.

title: Frame In-N-Out: Unbounded Controllable Image-to-Video Generation

abstract: Recent advances in reasoning-centric language models have highlighted reinforcement learning (RL) as a promising method for aligning models with verifiable rewards. However, it remains contentious whether RL truly expands a model’s reasoning capabilities or merely amplifies high-reward outputs already latent in the base model’s distribution, and whether continually scaling up RL compute reliably leads to improved reasoning performance. In this work, we challenge prevailing assumptions by demonstrating that prolonged RL (ProRL) training can uncover novel reasoning strategies that are inaccessible to base models, even under extensive sampling. We introduce ProRL, a novel training methodology that incorporates KL divergence control, reference policy resetting, and a diverse suite of tasks. Our empirical analysis reveals that RL-trained models consistently outperform base models across a wide range of pass@$k$ evaluations, including scenarios where base models fail entirely regardless of the number of attempts. We further show that reasoning boundary improvements correlates strongly with task competence of base model and training duration, suggesting that RL can explore and populate new regions of solution space over time. These findings offer new insights into the conditions under which RL meaningfully expands reasoning boundaries in language models and establish a foundation for future work on long-horizon RL for reasoning. We will release model weights and data to support further research.

paragraphs: Does reinforcement learning teach new reasoning strategies, or mainly make an existing model produce its better answers more often? ProRL investigates this question through prolonged training. Its methodology combines control of KL divergence, resetting the reference policy, and a diverse collection of tasks to support extended reinforcement learning.

The authors compare trained and base models across pass-at-k evaluations, which examine success when multiple attempts are allowed. The trained models consistently perform better, including on cases where base models fail throughout extensive sampling. These observations support the paper's argument that prolonged reinforcement learning can uncover strategies unavailable to the base models in the tested sampling conditions.

The extent of improvement is strongly correlated with the base model's competence on a task and with training duration. The authors interpret this as evidence that reinforcement learning can gradually explore additional regions of the solution space. The findings identify circumstances in which extended training meaningfully broadens observed reasoning capability, rather than establishing that additional reinforcement-learning compute always produces the same benefit.
summary.tldr: ProRL provides empirical evidence that prolonged reinforcement learning can uncover reasoning strategies beyond those found by extensive base-model sampling.

title: ProRL: Prolonged Reinforcement Learning Expands Reasoning Boundaries in Large Language Models

abstract: The Koopman operator provides a principled framework for analyzing nonlinear dynamical systems through linear operator theory. Recent advances in dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) have shown that trajectory data can be used to identify dominant modes of a system in a data-driven manner. Building on this idea, deep learning methods such as VAMPnet and DPNet have been proposed to learn the leading singular subspaces of the Koopman operator. However, these methods require backpropagation through potentially numerically unstable operations on empirical second moment matrices, such as singular value decomposition and matrix inversion, during objective computation, which can introduce biased gradient estimates and hinder scalability to large systems. In this work, we propose a scalable and conceptually simple method for learning the top-$k$ singular functions of the Koopman operator for stochastic dynamical systems based on the idea of low-rank approximation. Our approach eliminates the need for unstable linear-algebraic operations and integrates easily into modern deep learning pipelines. Empirical results demonstrate that the learned singular subspaces are both reliable and effective for downstream tasks such as eigen-analysis and multi-step prediction.

paragraphs: The Koopman operator offers a way to analyze nonlinear dynamics using linear operator theory. Data-driven methods learn important structures of this operator from system trajectories. Some deep learning approaches estimate its leading singular subspaces, but their training objectives require differentiation through matrix decompositions or inversions involving empirical second moments.

Those operations can be numerically unstable, introduce biased gradient estimates, and hinder scaling to larger systems. The paper proposes learning the top-k singular functions through a low-rank approximation formulation. Its central design choice removes the problematic linear-algebra operations from the learning objective, producing a method intended to fit naturally into modern deep learning workflows for stochastic dynamical systems.

Empirical results show that the learned singular subspaces are reliable and useful for subsequent eigen-analysis and prediction over multiple steps. This connects the training reformulation to the downstream purposes of learning the operator. The contribution is therefore both computational and representational: a simpler route to learning dominant operator structure that retains practical value for analyzing and predicting the tested systems.
summary.tldr: A low-rank learning formulation estimates leading Koopman singular functions without unstable matrix operations, supporting downstream analysis and prediction.

title: Efficient Parametric SVD of Koopman Operator for Stochastic Dynamical Systems

abstract: Heterogeneous hypergraph is a kind of structural data that contains multiple types of nodes and multiple types of hyperedges. Each hyperedge type corresponds to a specific multi-ary relation (called hyper-relation) among subsets of nodes, which goes beyond traditional pair-wise relations in simple graphs. Existing representation learning methods for heterogeneous hypergraphs typically learn embeddings for nodes and hyperedges based on graph neural networks. Although achieving promising performance, they are still limited in capturing more complex structural features and richer semantics conveyed by the composition of various hyper-relations. To fill this research gap, in this work, we propose the concept of hyper-meta-path for heterogeneous hypergraphs, which is defined as the composition of a sequence of hyper-relations. Besides, we design an attention-based heterogeneous hypergraph neural network (HHNN) to automatically learn the importance of hyper-meta-paths. By exploiting useful ones, HHNN is able to capture more complex structural features to boost the model's performance, as well as leverage their conveyed semantics to improve the model's interpretability. Extensive experiments show that HHNN can achieve significantly better performance than state-of-the-art baselines, and the discovered hyper-meta-paths bring good interpretability for the model predictions. To facilitate the reproducibility of this work, we provide our dataset as well as anonymized source code at: https://github.com/zhengziyu77/HHNN.

paragraphs: A heterogeneous hypergraph contains several kinds of nodes and relationships, with each relationship able to connect a group of nodes. This richer structure can represent interactions that go beyond pairs. The paper argues that existing representation-learning methods still struggle to capture the complex structure and meaning created when several types of these group relationships are composed.

The authors introduce hyper-meta-paths to describe such compositions as sequences of hyper-relations. They also design HHNN, an attention-based heterogeneous hypergraph neural network that learns which paths matter. Using informative paths gives the model access to structural patterns assembled from multiple relationships, while their associated meanings provide a way to interpret its predictions.

Extensive experiments report significantly better performance than state-of-the-art baselines, together with useful interpretability from the discovered paths. The contribution therefore combines a language for describing richer hypergraph structure with a model that learns to use it. The reported findings support the value of considering compositions of group relationships when learning representations and explaining predictions.
summary.tldr: HHNN learns useful compositions of hypergraph relationships to improve both prediction performance and interpretability.

title: Defining and Discovering Hyper-meta-paths for Heterogeneous Hypergraphs

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to preserve model performance under distribution shifts. Yet, most existing methods rely on entropy minimization for confident predictions. This paper re-examines the sufficiency of entropy minimization by analyzing its dual relationship with energy. We view energy as a proxy for likelihood, where lower energy indicates higher observability under the learned distribution. We uncover that entropy and energy are tightly associated, controlled by the model’s confidence or ambiguity, and show that simultaneous reduction of both is essential. Importantly, we reveal that entropy minimization alone neither ensures energy reduction nor supports reliable likelihood estimation, and it requires explicit discriminative guidance to reach zero entropy. To combat these problems, we propose a twofold solution. First, we introduce a likelihood-based objective grounded in energy-based models, which reshape the energy landscape to favor test samples. For stable and scalable training, we adopt sliced score matching—a sampling-free, Hessian-insensitive approximation of Fisher divergence. Second, we enhance entropy minimization with a cross-entropy that treats the predicted class as a target to promote discriminability. By counterbalancing entropy and energy through the solution of multi-objective optimization, our unified TTA, ReTTA, outperforms existing entropy- or energy-based approaches across diverse distribution shifts.

paragraphs: ReTTA revisits the practice of adapting a model to shifted test data by making its predictions more confident. The resulting contribution connects confidence-focused adaptation with an explicit objective for how well test data fit the model.
summary.tldr: ReTTA balances prediction entropy with an energy-based likelihood objective to improve adaptation under distribution shifts.

title: Rethinking Entropy in Test-Time Adaptation: The Missing Piece from Energy Duality

abstract: Graph condensation (GC) is an emerging technique designed to learn a significantly smaller graph that retains the essential information of the original graph. This condensed graph has shown promise in accelerating graph neural networks while preserving performance comparable to those achieved with the original, larger graphs. Additionally, this technique facilitates downstream applications like neural architecture search and deepens our understanding of redundancies in large graphs. Despite the rapid development of GC methods, particularly for node classification, a unified evaluation framework is still lacking to systematically compare different GC methods or clarify key design choices for improving their effectiveness. To bridge these gaps, we introduce GC4NC, a comprehensive framework for evaluating diverse GC methods on node classification across multiple dimensions including performance, efficiency, privacy preservation, denoising ability, NAS effectiveness, and transferability. Our systematic evaluation offers novel insights into how condensed graphs behave and the critical design choices that drive their success. These findings pave the way for future advancements in GC methods, enhancing both performance and expanding their real-world applications. The code is available at https://github.com/Emory-Melody/GraphSlim/tree/main/benchmark.

GC4NC provides a unified framework for comparing condensation methods across several dimensions. This broadens evaluation beyond whether a condensed graph supports accurate classification in a single setting.

The authors report that their systematic assessment yields insights into condensed graph behavior and the design choices associated with successful methods. The contribution is an evaluation framework for examining several practical properties together, making the strengths of condensation methods easier to compare. Its publicly available code also provides a common basis for subsequent evaluations and development of methods intended for broader applications.
summary.tldr: GC4NC evaluates graph condensation methods across accuracy, efficiency, privacy, denoising, architecture search, and transferability.

title: GC4NC: A Benchmark Framework for Graph Condensation on Node Classification with New Insights

abstract: We introduce PurpCode, the first post-training recipe for training safe code reasoning models towards generating secure code and defending against malicious cyberactivities. PurpCode trains a reasoning model in two stages: (i) Rule Learning, which explicitly teaches the model to reference cybersafety rules to generate vulnerability-free code and to avoid facilitating malicious cyberactivities; and (ii) Reinforcement Learning, which optimizes model safety and preserves model utility through diverse, multi-objective reward mechanisms. To empower the training pipelines with comprehensive cybersafety data, we conduct internal red-teaming to synthesize comprehensive and high-coverage prompts based on real-world tasks for inducing unsafe cyberactivities in the model. Based on PurpCode, we develop a reasoning-based coding model, namely PurpCode-32B, which demonstrates state-of-the-art cybersafety, outperforming various frontier models. Moreover, our alignment method decreases the model overrefusal rates in both general and cybersafety-specific scenarios, while preserving model utility in both code generation and common security knowledge.

paragraphs: PurpCode is a post-training approach for coding models that combines two safety goals: producing secure code and avoiding assistance with malicious cyberactivity. It also seeks to preserve useful coding and security capabilities. The approach explicitly trains reasoning around cybersafety rules, making those rules part of how the model learns to respond.

Training has two stages. Rule Learning teaches the model to reference safety rules when generating code and deciding how to handle harmful requests. Reinforcement Learning then uses multiple reward objectives to improve safety while retaining utility. The authors support this process with synthesized prompts developed through internal red-teaming and grounded in real-world tasks.

Using this recipe, they produce PurpCode-32B and report state-of-the-art cybersafety performance, exceeding various frontier models in their evaluation. They also report lower overrefusal rates in both general and cybersecurity-specific settings while preserving code-generation ability and common security knowledge. These findings matter because the stated gains combine stronger safety with fewer unnecessary refusals, rather than measuring safety solely through a model’s willingness to decline requests.
summary.tldr: PurpCode combines safety-rule learning and multi-objective reinforcement learning to improve coding-model cybersafety while reducing overrefusal.

title: PurpCode: Reasoning for Safer Code Generation

abstract: 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) faces persistent challenges due to coarse scene-level observations and logically inconsistent annotations, which introduce ambiguities that compromise data quality and hinder effective model supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce Refer-Judge, a novel framework that harnesses the reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to identify and mitigate toxic data. At the core of Refer-Judge is a Jury-and-Judge Chain-of-Thought paradigm, inspired by the deliberative process of the judicial system. This framework targets the root causes of annotation noise: jurors collaboratively assess 3DVG samples from diverse perspectives, providing structured, multi-faceted evaluations. Judges then consolidate these insights using a Corroborative Refinement strategy, which adaptively reorganizes information to correct ambiguities arising from biased or incomplete observations. Through this two-stage deliberation, Refer-Judge significantly enhances the reliability of data judgments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework not only achieves human-level discrimination at the scene level but also improves the performance of baseline algorithms via data purification. Code is available at https://github.com/Hermione-HKX/Refer_Judge.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional visual grounding depends on reliable connections between scene observations and annotations. Refer-Judge targets data whose ambiguity or logical inconsistency weakens that supervision. Here, toxic data refers to problematic training examples arising from coarse observations and annotation noise, which can make it unclear what a model should learn from a sample.

The framework uses multimodal language models in a two-stage process inspired by juries and judges. Jurors examine samples from different perspectives and produce structured assessments. Judges combine these assessments using Corroborative Refinement, which adaptively reorganizes the information to address ambiguity caused by biased or incomplete observations. The design makes multiple perspectives part of the data-quality decision.

Experiments report human-level discrimination at the scene level and improved performance for baseline algorithms after data purification. These are complementary findings: the framework can identify problematic examples, and its judgments can improve the supervision supplied to other models. The paper’s contribution is therefore a reasoning-based approach to cleaning 3D grounding data, with measured benefits for both judgment reliability and downstream model performance.
summary.tldr: Refer-Judge combines multiple model assessments to identify unreliable 3D grounding data and improve downstream training through purification.

title: Jury-and-Judge Chain-of-Thought for Uncovering Toxic Data in 3D Visual Grounding

abstract: In this paper, we address the challenges associated with merging low-rank adaptations of large neural networks. With the rise of parameter-efficient adaptation techniques, such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), model fine-tuning has become more accessible. While fine-tuning models with LoRA is highly efficient, existing merging methods often sacrifice this efficiency by merging fully-sized weight matrices. We propose the Core Space merging framework, which enables the merging of LoRA-adapted models within a common alignment basis, thereby preserving the efficiency of low-rank adaptation while substantially improving accuracy across tasks. We further provide a formal proof that projection into Core Space ensures no loss of information and provide a complexity analysis showing the efficiency gains. Extensive empirical results demonstrate that Core Space significantly improves existing merging techniques and achieves state-of-the-art results on both vision and language tasks while utilizing a fraction of the computational resources. Codebase is available at https://github.com/apanariello4/core-space-merging.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation makes fine-tuning large networks more manageable by representing model changes compactly. Combining several adapted models can undermine that advantage, however, when merging methods operate on full-sized weight matrices. This paper addresses that mismatch: adaptation may be inexpensive, while the subsequent merging step needlessly returns to a much larger representation.

The proposed Core Space framework places the low-rank adaptations into a common alignment basis and performs merging there. This shared representation makes the adaptations compatible for combination while retaining the computational benefits of their compact form. The authors formally prove that projection into Core Space loses no information and analyze the resulting computational savings.

Experiments show that Core Space improves existing merging techniques across vision and language tasks, achieving reported state-of-the-art results with a fraction of the computational resources. The information-preservation result concerns the projection itself; the accuracy gains come from empirical evaluation. The contribution therefore combines a justified compact representation with evidence that it is useful for practical model merging.
summary.tldr: Core Space merges low-rank model adaptations in a shared compact representation, improving measured accuracy while reducing computation.

title: Accurate and Efficient Low-Rank Model Merging in Core Space

abstract: As a new paradigm of visual content generation, autoregressive text-to-image models suffer from slow inference due to their sequential token-by-token decoding process, often requiring thousands of model forward passes to generate a single image. To address this inefficiency, we propose Speculative Jacobi-Denoising Decoding (SJD2), a framework that incorporates the denoising process into Jacobi iterations to enable parallel token generation in autoregressive models. Our method introduces a next-clean-token prediction paradigm that enables the pre-trained autoregressive models to accept noise-perturbed token embeddings and predict the next clean tokens through low-cost fine-tuning. This denoising paradigm guides the model towards more stable Jacobi trajectories. During inference, our method initializes token sequences with Gaussian noise and performs iterative next-clean-token-prediction in the embedding space. We employ a probabilistic criterion to verify and accept multiple tokens in parallel, and refine the unaccepted tokens for the next iteration with the denoising trajectory. Experiments show that our method can accelerate generation by reducing model forward passes while maintaining the visual quality of generated images.

To address this inefficiency, we propose Speculative Jacobi-Denoising Decoding (SJD2), a framework that incorporates the denoising process into Jacobi iterations to enable parallel token generation in autoregressive models. Our method introduces a next-clean-token prediction paradigm that enables the pre-trained autoregressive models to accept noise-perturbed token embeddings and predict the next clean tokens through low-cost fine-tuning. This denoising paradigm guides the model towards more stable Jacobi trajectories. During inference, our method initializes token sequences with Gaussian noise and performs iterative next-clean-token-prediction in the embedding space. We employ a probabilistic criterion to verify and accept multiple tokens in parallel, and refine the unaccepted tokens for the next iteration with the denoising trajectory. Experiments show that our method can accelerate generation by reducing model forward passes while maintaining the visual quality of generated images.

paragraphs: Autoregressive text-to-image models generate images through sequential token prediction, which can require thousands of model evaluations. Speculative Jacobi-Denoising Decoding, or SJD2, aims to reduce that work by generating multiple tokens in parallel. It combines iterative Jacobi decoding with a denoising process that helps stabilize the sequence of predictions.

The method first applies low-cost fine-tuning so a pretrained model can accept noisy token embeddings and predict the next clean tokens. At inference, it initializes token sequences with Gaussian noise and repeatedly updates them in embedding space. A probabilistic verification rule decides which proposed tokens can be accepted together. Tokens that are not accepted are refined along the denoising trajectory for another iteration.

Experiments show that SJD2 can reduce the number of forward passes and accelerate generation while maintaining image quality. The contribution is a coordinated adaptation of training and decoding: the model learns to work with noisy intermediate representations, and the inference procedure uses that ability to make and refine parallel token proposals.
summary.tldr: SJD2 combines denoising fine-tuning with parallel speculative decoding to reduce autoregressive image-generation passes while preserving reported visual quality.

title: Speculative Jacobi-Denoising Decoding for Accelerating Autoregressive Text-to-image Generation

abstract: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly improved 2D visual understanding, prompting interest in their application to complex 3D reasoning tasks. However, it remains unclear whether these models can effectively capture the detailed spatial information required for robust real-world performance, especially cross-view consistency, a key requirement for accurate 3D reasoning. Considering this issue, we introduce Viewpoint Learning, a task designed to evaluate and improve the spatial reasoning capabilities of MLLMs. We present the Viewpoint-100K dataset, consisting of 100K object-centric image pairs with diverse viewpoints and corresponding question-answer pairs. Our approach employs a two-stage fine-tuning strategy: first, foundational knowledge is injected to the baseline MLLM via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on Viewpoint-100K, resulting in significant improvements across multiple tasks; second, generalization is enhanced through Reinforcement Learning using the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm on a broader set of questions. Additionally, we introduce a hybrid cold-start initialization method designed to simultaneously learn viewpoint representations and maintain coherent reasoning thinking. Experimental results show that our approach significantly activates the spatial reasoning ability of MLLM, improving performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain reasoning tasks. Our findings highlight the value of developing foundational spatial skills in MLLMs, supporting future progress in robotics, autonomous systems, and 3D scene understanding.

paragraphs: Understanding individual images does not by itself establish that a multimodal model can reason consistently about an object seen from different viewpoints. Actial addresses this spatial reasoning problem through Viewpoint Learning, a task intended both to evaluate and improve these abilities. Cross-view consistency is central because three-dimensional reasoning requires reconciling changing appearances.

Supervised fine-tuning first develops foundational spatial knowledge using this dataset. Reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization then uses a broader collection of questions to improve generalization. A hybrid cold-start initialization is designed to support both viewpoint representations and coherent reasoning.

Experiments report improvements on reasoning tasks within and outside the training domain, with supervised fine-tuning already improving multiple tasks. These results support explicitly developing foundational spatial skills rather than assuming they follow automatically from strong two-dimensional understanding. The work points toward applications in robotics, autonomous systems, and scene understanding without claiming to have validated every such application.
summary.tldr: Actial develops spatial reasoning through viewpoint-focused supervised training followed by reinforcement learning, improving both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.

title: Actial: Activate Spatial Reasoning Ability of Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: In daily life, people often move through spaces to find objects that meet their needs, posing a key challenge in embodied AI. Traditional Demand-Driven Navigation (DDN) handles one need at a time but does not reflect the complexity of real-world tasks involving multiple needs and personal choices. To bridge this gap, we introduce Task-Preferenced Multi-Demand-Driven Navigation (TP-MDDN), a new benchmark for long-horizon navigation involving multiple sub-demands with explicit task preferences. To solve TP-MDDN, we propose AWMSystem, an autonomous decision-making system composed of three key modules: BreakLLM (instruction decomposition), LocateLLM (goal selection), and StatusMLLM (task monitoring). For spatial memory, we design MASMap, which combines 3D point cloud accumulation with 2D semantic mapping for accurate and efficient environmental understanding. Our Dual-Tempo action generation framework integrates zero-shot planning with policy-based fine control, and is further supported by an Adaptive Error Corrector that handles failure cases in real time. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both perception accuracy and navigation robustness.

Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in perception accuracy and navigation robustness. The paper contributes both a task setting that makes multiple demands and preferences explicit and an integrated system for coordinating interpretation, mapping, planning, control, and monitoring over extended navigation.
summary.tldr: TP-MDDN benchmarks navigation with multiple preferred demands, and AWMSystem combines task decomposition, spatial memory, planning, and error correction to address it.

title: TP-MDDN: Task-Preferenced Multi-Demand-Driven Navigation with Autonomous Decision-Making

abstract: We study the problem of aligning a generative model's response with a user's preferences. Recent works have proposed several different formulations for personalized alignment; however, they either require a large amount of user preference queries or require that the preference be explicitly specified as a text input. In this paper, we propose a novel inference-time personalized alignment method, UserAlign, that elicits the user's preferences with a few queries as pairwise response comparisons. In particular, UserAlign builds on the theoretical framework of best-arm identification in logistic bandits and selects a personalized response from a fixed pool of the model's generated responses. The key idea is to consider the user's feedback consistent and noise-free, and incorporate it into the theoretical framework to identify the best response quickly. Experimental results across several tasks, involving personalized text and image generation, showcase the effectiveness of UserAlign in achieving personalized alignment.

paragraphs: Personalizing generated content requires learning what a particular user prefers. Existing approaches can demand many preference questions or require users to express their preferences directly in text. UserAlign instead asks for a few comparisons between pairs of responses and uses those choices to select a personalized output at inference time.

The method builds on best-arm identification in logistic bandits, a framework for finding the best candidate through informative feedback. Its candidates form a fixed pool of responses already generated by the model. UserAlign incorporates the assumption that the user's feedback is consistent and noise-free to identify the preferred response quickly.

That assumption is central to how the method uses a small number of comparisons, and the selected answer is limited to the available response pool. Experiments across personalized text and image generation tasks demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to turn lightweight comparative feedback into response selection, reducing the need for either extensive questioning or an explicit written description of the user's preferences.
summary.tldr: UserAlign selects personalized responses from a fixed candidate pool using a few pairwise comparisons under consistent, noise-free feedback.

title: Inference-Time Personalized Alignment with a Few User Preference Queries

abstract: There has been great progress in improving numerical weather prediction and climate models using machine learning. However, most global models act at a kilometer-scale, making it challenging to model individual clouds and factors such as extreme precipitation, wind gusts, turbulence, and surface irradiance. Therefore, there is a need to move towards higher-resolution models, which in turn require high-resolution real-world observations that current instruments struggle to obtain. We present Cloud4D, the first learning-based framework that reconstructs a physically consistent, four–dimensional cloud state using only synchronized ground‐based cameras. Leveraging a homography-guided 2D‐to‐3D transformer, Cloud4D infers the full 3D distribution of liquid water content at 25 m spatial and 5 s temporal resolution. By tracking the 3D liquid water content retrievals over time, Cloud4D additionally estimates horizontal wind vectors. Across a two-month deployment comprising six skyward cameras, our system delivers an order-of-magnitude improvement in space-time resolution relative to state-of-the-art satellite measurements, while retaining single-digit relative error ($<10\\%$) against collocated radar measurements.

Moving to finer scales requires measurements that capture how clouds vary across space and time, which existing instruments struggle to provide at the needed resolution.

summary.tldr: Cloud4D uses synchronized ground cameras to reconstruct cloud water content over time and estimate horizontal winds at fine resolution.

title: Cloud4D: Estimating Cloud Properties at a High Spatial and Temporal Resolution

abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting have shown remarkable potential for novel view synthesis. However, most existing large-scale scene reconstruction methods rely on the divide-and-conquer paradigm, which often leads to the loss of global scene information and requires complex parameter tuning due to scene partitioning and local optimization. To address these limitations, we propose MixGS, a novel holistic optimization framework for large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. MixGS models the entire scene holistically by integrating camera pose and Gaussian attributes into a view-aware representation, which is decoded into fine-detailed Gaussians. Furthermore, a novel mixing operation combines decoded and original Gaussians to jointly preserve global coherence and local fidelity. Extensive experiments on large-scale scenes demonstrate that MixGS achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality and competitive speed, while significantly reducing computational requirements, enabling large-scale scene reconstruction training on a single 24GB VRAM GPU.

paragraphs: Large-scale 3D scene reconstruction with Gaussian splatting often divides a scene into separate pieces and optimizes them locally. That can lose information about the scene as a whole and introduce complicated choices about partitioning and tuning. MixGS takes a holistic approach, seeking to preserve global organization while still reconstructing fine details needed for rendering.

The framework combines camera pose information with Gaussian attributes in a view-aware representation. It then decodes that representation into detailed Gaussians. A mixing operation combines these decoded Gaussians with the original ones, allowing both forms to contribute to reconstruction. This is the mechanism the paper uses to jointly support global coherence and local fidelity.

Experiments on large scenes report state-of-the-art rendering quality, competitive speed, and substantially reduced computational requirements. The authors demonstrate training on a single GPU with 24 GB of video memory. The practical significance is that optimizing a scene holistically can be compatible with a constrained GPU memory budget, while delivering strong rendering results in the evaluated large-scale settings.
summary.tldr: MixGS combines original and decoded Gaussians in a holistic scene representation, enabling high-quality large-scale reconstruction on a single 24 GB GPU.

title: Holistic Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction via Mixed Gaussian Splatting

abstract: Reinforcement learning with outcome-based feedback faces a fundamental challenge: when rewards are only observed at trajectory endpoints, how do we assign credit to the right actions? This paper provides the first comprehensive analysis of this problem in online RL with general function approximation. We develop a provably sample-efficient algorithm achieving $\widetilde{O}({C_{\rm cov} H^3}/{\varepsilon^2})$ sample complexity, where $C_{\rm cov}$ is the coverability coefficient of the underlying MDP. By leveraging general function approximation, our approach works effectively in large or infinite state spaces where tabular methods fail, requiring only that value functions and reward functions can be represented by appropriate function classes. Our results also characterize when outcome-based feedback is statistically separated from per-step rewards, revealing an unavoidable exponential separation for certain MDPs. For deterministic MDPs, we show how to eliminate the completeness assumption, dramatically simplifying the algorithm. We further extend our approach to preference-based feedback settings, proving that equivalent statistical efficiency can be achieved even under more limited information. Together, these results constitute a theoretical foundation for understanding the statistical properties of outcome-based reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: When reinforcement learning receives a reward only at the end of a trajectory, it must determine which earlier actions contributed to the outcome. This paper analyzes that credit-assignment problem for online learning with general function approximation, including large or infinite state spaces.

The authors develop an algorithm with sample complexity scaling, up to logarithmic factors, as C_cov H³/ε², where C_cov measures the underlying decision process's coverability. The approach uses function classes capable of representing the relevant value and reward functions. The theory also identifies settings where endpoint feedback is fundamentally less informative: certain decision processes exhibit an unavoidable exponential statistical gap compared with receiving rewards at each step.

They also extend the approach to preference feedback, proving equivalent statistical efficiency in that setting. The paper thus provides both a route to efficient learning and a characterization of cases where the form of feedback imposes an inherent cost.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sample-efficient algorithms for outcome-based reinforcement learning while proving that some environments impose an exponential cost relative to per-step rewards.

title: Outcome-Based Online Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms and Fundamental Limits

abstract: Language models (LMs) are increasingly being deployed to perform autonomous data analyses. However, their data awareness—the ability to recognize, reason over, and appropriately handle data artifacts such as missing values, outliers, and logical inconsistencies—remains underexplored. These artifacts are especially common in real-world tabular data and, if mishandled, can significantly compromise the validity of analytical conclusions. To address this gap, we present RADAR, a benchmark for systematically evaluating data-aware reasoning on tabular data. We develop a framework to simulate data artifacts via programmatic perturbations to enable targeted evaluation of model behavior. RADAR comprises 2,980 table-query pairs, grounded in real-world data spanning 9 domains and 5 data artifact types. In addition to evaluating artifact handling, RADAR systematically varies table size to study how reasoning performance holds when increasing table size. Our evaluation reveals that, despite decent performance on tables without data artifacts, frontier models degrade significantly when data artifacts are introduced, exposing critical gaps in their capacity for robust, data-aware analysis. Designed to be flexible and extensible, RADAR supports diverse perturbation types and controllable table sizes, offering a valuable resource for advancing tabular reasoning.

Missing values, outliers, and logical inconsistencies can change which conclusions are justified. RADAR evaluates this form of data awareness: whether models notice, reason about, and appropriately handle artifacts in tabular data.

summary.tldr: RADAR reveals substantial weaknesses in language models' handling of imperfect tables through controlled tests of data artifacts and table size.

title: RADAR: Benchmarking Language Models on Imperfect Tabular Data

abstract: Recent advances in large-scale neural recordings have enabled accurate decoding of behavior and cognitive states, yet decoding anatomical regions remains underexplored, despite being crucial for consistent targeting in multiday recordings and effective deep brain stimulation. Current approaches typically rely on external anatomical information, from atlas-based planning to post hoc histology, which are limited in precision, longitudinal applicability, and real-time feedback. In this work, we develop a self-supervised learning framework, Lfp2vec, to infer anatomical regions directly from the neural signal in vivo. We adapt an audio-pretrained transformer model by continuing self-supervised training on a large corpus of unlabeled local-field-potential (LFP) data, then fine-tuning for anatomical region decoding. Ablations show that combining out-of-domain initialization with in-domain self-supervision outperforms training from scratch. We demonstrate that our method achieves strong zero-shot generalization across different labs and probe geometries, and outperforming state-of-the-art self-supervised models on electrophysiology data. The learned embeddings form anatomically coherent clusters and transfer effectively to downstream tasks like disease classification with minimal fine-tuning. Altogether, our approach enables zero-shot prediction of brain regions in novel subjects, demonstrates that LFP signals encode rich anatomical information, and establishes self-supervised learning on raw LFP as a foundation to learn representations that can be tuned for diverse neural decoding tasks. Code to reproduce our results is found in the github repository at https://github.com/tianxiao18/lfp2vec.

title: Self supervised learning for in vivo localization of microelectrode arrays using raw local field potential

abstract: Despite their impressive performance across a wide range of tasks, Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) remain prone to hallucination. In this study, we propose a comprehensive intervention framework aligned with the transformer’s causal architecture in LVLMs, integrating the effects of different intervention paths on hallucination. We find that hallucinations in LVLMs do not arise from a single causal path, but rather from the interplay among image-to-input-text, image-to-output-text, and text-to-text pathways. For the first time, we also find that LVLMs rely on different pathways depending on the question–answer alignment format. Building on these insights, we propose simple yet effective methods to identify and intervene on critical hallucination heads within each pathway, tailored to discriminative and generative formats. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently reduces hallucinations across diverse alignment types.

The authors find that hallucination involves interactions among multiple pathways: image information reaching input text, image information reaching output text, and text influencing text. This motivates an intervention framework that considers their combined effects.

A second finding is that the pathways a model relies on vary with the question-answer alignment format. The authors therefore tailor their interventions to discriminative and generative formats. Within each pathway, their methods identify attention heads that are important to hallucination and intervene on those heads. This links the correction strategy to both the model’s internal causal organization and the format of the task.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks show consistent hallucination reductions across diverse alignment types. The findings suggest that effective intervention benefits from accounting for how different information routes interact and how task formatting changes their roles. The stated outcome is a reduction in hallucination across evaluated formats, supported by methods that target critical heads along the relevant pathways.
summary.tldr: Targeting hallucination-related attention heads across multiple information pathways reduces vision-language hallucinations across different question-answer formats.

title: Intervene-All-Paths: Unified Mitigation of LVLM Hallucinations across Alignment Formats

abstract: Old-photo face restoration poses significant challenges due to compounded degradations such as breakage, fading, and severe blur. Existing pre-trained diffusion-guided methods either rely on explicit degradation priors or global statistical guidance, which struggle with localized artifacts or face color. We propose Self-Supervised Selective-Guided Diffusion (SSDiff), which leverages pseudo-reference faces generated by a pre-trained diffusion model under weak guidance. These pseudo-labels exhibit structurally aligned contours and natural colors, enabling region-specific restoration via staged supervision: structural guidance applied throughout the denoising process and color refinement in later steps, aligned with the coarse-to-fine nature of diffusion. By incorporating face parsing maps and scratch masks, our method selectively restores breakage regions while avoiding identity mismatch. We further construct VintageFace, a 300-image benchmark of real old face photos with varying degradation levels. SSDiff outperforms existing GAN-based and diffusion-based methods in perceptual quality, fidelity, and regional controllability. Code link: https://github.com/PRIS-CV/SSDiff.

Such damage can be highly localized, making global guidance poorly suited to deciding which facial regions need repair. The paper also identifies natural face color as a challenge for existing diffusion-guided restoration methods.

A pretrained diffusion model first generates pseudo-reference faces under weak guidance. Their aligned contours and natural colors provide supervision for restoration. Structural guidance operates throughout denoising, while color refinement is introduced later, matching diffusion's coarse-to-fine progression. Face-parsing maps and scratch masks direct the restoration toward damaged regions, with the aim of avoiding identity mismatch.

The authors also introduce VintageFace, a benchmark containing 300 real old face photographs with different degradation levels. They report improvements over GAN-based and diffusion-based methods in perceptual quality, fidelity, and regional controllability. The central contribution is to combine generated reference information with selective, staged guidance, allowing structure, color, and localized damage to receive different treatment during restoration.
summary.tldr: SSDiff uses generated face references and region-specific, staged diffusion guidance to restore damaged old photographs.

title: Self-Supervised Selective-Guided Diffusion Model for Old-Photo Face Restoration

abstract: Latent action models (LAMs) aim to learn action-relevant changes from unlabeled videos by compressing changes between frames as latents. However, differences between video frames can be caused by \textit{controllable changes} as well as exogenous noise, leading to an important concern -- do latents capture the changes caused by actions or irrelevant noise? This paper studies this issue analytically, presenting a linear model that encapsulates the essence of LAM learning, while being tractable. This provides several insights, including connections between LAM and principal component analysis (PCA), desiderata of the data-generating policy, and justification of strategies to encourage learning controllable changes using data augmentation, data cleaning, and auxiliary action-prediction. We also provide illustrative results based on numerical simulation, shedding light on the specific structure of observations, actions, and noise in data that influence LAM learning.

paragraphs: Latent action models compress changes between video frames into hidden representations intended to capture action-relevant information. The difficulty is that frame differences also include changes caused by external noise. This paper asks when the learned representation captures controllable changes and when it instead reflects variation unrelated to an agent’s actions.

The authors build a tractable linear model that captures the central learning problem. Their analysis connects latent action learning to principal component analysis and identifies desirable properties of the policy that generates the data. These connections help explain why the structure of the observed variation and the way actions are collected matter for what the representation learns.

The analysis also provides justification for strategies intended to favor controllable changes, including data augmentation, data cleaning, and auxiliary action prediction. Numerical simulations illustrate how the structure of observations, actions, and noise influences learning. The contribution is an analytical account supported by illustrative simulations, giving a basis for reasoning about action relevance within the studied linear setting.
summary.tldr: A tractable linear analysis explains how latent action models can capture controllable changes or irrelevant noise and motivates strategies to favor action-relevant learning.

title: What Do Latent Action Models Actually Learn?

abstract: Directly generating 3D meshes, the default representation for 3D shapes in the graphics industry, using auto-regressive (AR) models has become popular these days, thanks to their sharpness, compactness in the generated results, and ability to represent various types of surfaces. However, AR mesh generative models typically construct meshes face by face in lexicographic order, which does not effectively capture the underlying geometry in a manner consistent with human perception. Inspired by 2D models that progressively refine images, such as the prevailing next-scale prediction AR models, we propose generating meshes auto-regressively in a progressive coarse-to-fine manner. Specifically, we view mesh simplification algorithms, which gradually merge mesh faces to build simpler meshes, as a natural fine-to-coarse process. Therefore, we generalize meshes to simplicial complexes and develop a transformer-based AR model to approximate the reverse process of simplification in the order of level of detail, constructing meshes initially from a single point and gradually adding geometric details through local remeshing, where the topology is not predefined and is alterable. Our experiments show that this novel progressive mesh generation approach not only provides intuitive control over generation quality and time consumption by early stopping the auto-regressive process but also enables applications such as mesh refinement and editing.

paragraphs: ARMesh changes the order in which an autoregressive model builds a three-dimensional mesh. Existing approaches typically generate individual faces in a fixed lexicographic order, which does not closely follow the shape's geometric organization. This paper instead generates a simple shape first and progressively adds detail, making the sequence of predictions correspond to increasing geometric resolution.

The approach starts from mesh simplification: a process that merges faces to obtain simpler shapes. The authors train a transformer to approximate the reverse of that process. They generalize meshes to simplicial complexes so generation can begin with a single point, then add geometry through local remeshing. The connections within the shape are allowed to change rather than being fixed beforehand.

Experiments show that this progressive process provides a practical control over generation time and detail: stopping earlier yields an earlier level of refinement. The same approach also supports mesh refinement and editing. Its contribution is therefore both a different generation order and a representation that accommodates changing geometry and topology throughout that order.
summary.tldr: ARMesh generates meshes by reversing simplification, progressively adding detail while allowing topology changes and early stopping.

title: ARMesh: Autoregressive Mesh Generation via Next-Level-of-Detail Prediction

abstract: Meta-learning has achieved significant advancements, with generalization emerging as a key metric for evaluating meta-learning algorithms. While recent studies have mainly focused on training strategies, data-split methods, and tightening generalization bounds, they often ignore the impact of inner-levels on generalization. To bridge this gap, this paper focuses on several prominent meta-learning algorithms and establishes two generalization analytical frameworks for them based on their inner-processes: the Gradient Descent Framework (GDF) and the Proximal Descent Framework (PDF). Within these frameworks, we introduce two novel algorithmic stability definitions and derive the corresponding generalization bounds. Our findings reveal a trade-off of inner-levels under GDF, whereas PDF exhibits a beneficial relationship. Moreover, we highlight the critical role of the meta-objective function in minimizing generalization error. Inspired by this, we propose a new, simplified meta-objective function definition to enhance generalization performance. Many real-world experiments support our findings and show the improvement of the new meta-objective function.

paragraphs: Meta-learning involves an inner learning process within a broader training objective. This paper examines how those inner levels affect generalization, a factor the authors argue has received less attention than training strategies and data splits. The analysis covers several prominent meta-learning algorithms through frameworks organized around their inner update processes.

The authors establish a Gradient Descent Framework and a Proximal Descent Framework. They introduce two definitions of algorithmic stability and derive generalization bounds from them. Stability provides a way to connect the behavior of a learning procedure to its ability to perform beyond the data used during training.

The two frameworks produce different conclusions: inner levels involve a trade-off under gradient descent, while the proximal framework exhibits a beneficial relationship. The analysis also identifies the meta-objective as important for controlling generalization error. Motivated by this finding, the authors propose a simpler meta-objective. Experiments on real-world tasks support the theoretical findings and show improved performance with the proposed objective.
summary.tldr: The paper links meta-learning’s inner processes to generalization and uses the analysis to design a simpler, improved meta-objective.

title: On the Stability and Generalization of Meta-Learning: the Impact of Inner-Levels

abstract: Linear Mode Connectivity (LMC) is a notable phenomenon in the loss landscapes of neural networks, wherein independently trained models have been observed to be connected—up to permutation symmetries—by linear paths in parameter space along which the loss remains consistently low. This observation challenges classical views of non-convex optimization and has implications for model ensembling, generalization, and our understanding of neural loss geometry. Inspired by recent studies on LMC in standard neural networks, we systematically investigate this phenomenon within Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures—a class of models known for their scalability and computational efficiency, which combine traditional neural networks—referred to as experts—through a learnable gating mechanism. We begin by conducting a comprehensive analysis of both dense and sparse gating regimes, demonstrating that the symmetries inherent to MoE architectures are fully characterized by permutations acting on both the expert components and the gating function. Building on these foundational findings, we propose a matching algorithm that enables alignment between independently trained MoEs, thereby facilitating the discovery of LMC. Finally, we empirically validate the presence of LMC using our proposed algorithm across diverse MoE configurations—including dense, sparse, and shared-expert variants—under a wide range of model settings and datasets of varying scales and modalities. Our results confirm the existence of LMC in MoE architectures and offer fundamental insights into the functional landscape and optimization dynamics of deep learning models.

paragraphs: Independently trained neural networks can sometimes be connected by a straight line between their parameters while keeping loss low along the path. Seeing this linear mode connectivity may first require rearranging equivalent components so that they correspond. This paper investigates that phenomenon in mixture-of-experts models, where a learned gate combines or selects among expert networks.

The authors analyze both dense and sparse gating and characterize the architectures’ symmetries through permutations involving the experts and the gating function. This matters because equivalent arrangements can look different when compared parameter by parameter. They then introduce a matching algorithm that aligns independently trained models, making it possible to search for low-loss linear connections after accounting for those symmetries.

Experiments find linear mode connectivity across dense, sparse, and shared-expert configurations, using varied model settings and datasets spanning different scales and modalities. These results extend the empirical picture of connectivity to mixture-of-experts architectures. They also provide a symmetry-based method for studying how separately trained expert systems relate within parameter space.
summary.tldr: A symmetry-aware matching algorithm reveals low-loss linear connections between independently trained mixture-of-experts models across diverse evaluated configurations.

title: On Linear Mode Connectivity of Mixture-of-Experts Architectures

abstract: The area under the ROC curve (AUC) is a widely used performance measure in machine learning. Increasingly, however, in several applications, ranging from ranking and biometric screening to medical diagnosis, performance is measured not in terms of the full area under the ROC curve, but instead, in terms of the partial area under the ROC curve between two specified false positive rates. In this paper, we develop a structural SVM framework for directly optimizing the partial AUC between any two false positive rates. Our approach makes use of a cutting plane solver along the lines of the structural SVM based approach for optimizing the full AUC developed by Joachims (2005). Unlike the full AUC, where the combinatorial optimization problem needed to find the most violated constraint in the cutting plane solver can be decomposed easily to yield an efficient algorithm, the corresponding optimization problem in the case of partial AUC is harder to decompose. One of our key technical contributions is an efficient algorithm for solving this combinatorial optimization problem that has the same computational complexity as Joachims’ algorithm for optimizing the usual AUC. This allows us to efficiently optimize the partial AUC in any desired false positive range. We demonstrate the approach on a variety of real-world tasks.

paragraphs: A classifier can perform well across its full ROC curve while the application cares about only a particular range of false positive rates. Partial AUC measures performance within that range. This paper develops a structural SVM framework that directly targets partial AUC between any two specified false positive rates.

The framework uses a cutting plane solver, which repeatedly finds a constraint that the current solution violates most strongly. For full AUC, the required combinatorial search separates into manageable pieces. Restricting attention to partial AUC makes that decomposition harder, creating a computational obstacle to optimizing the measure that the application actually uses.

The paper's key technical result is an efficient algorithm for this constraint-search problem. Its computational complexity matches the corresponding algorithm for full AUC. This makes the proposed approach practical for a chosen false positive interval without increasing the complexity of that central subproblem. Demonstrations on several real-world tasks support its applicability; the abstract does not claim uniform performance gains.
summary.tldr: A structural SVM framework efficiently optimizes partial AUC over any specified false positive range.

title: A Structural SVM Based Approach for Optimizing Partial AUC

abstract: Analyzing data sets of billions of records has now become a regular task in many companies and institutions. In the statistical analysis of those massive data sets, sampling generally plays a very important role. In this work, we describe a scalable simple random sampling algorithm, named ScaSRS, which uses probabilistic thresholds to decide on the fly whether to accept, reject, or wait-list an item independently of others. We prove, with high probability, it succeeds and needs only O(\sqrtk) storage, where k is the sample size. ScaSRS extends naturally to a scalable stratified sampling algorithm, which is favorable for heterogeneous data sets. The proposed algorithms, when implemented in MapReduce, can effectively reduce the size of intermediate output and greatly improve load balancing. Empirical evaluation on large-scale data sets clearly demonstrates their superiority.

paragraphs: Sampling is an important part of analyzing datasets containing billions of records, but constructing the sample must itself remain manageable. The paper introduces ScaSRS, a scalable algorithm for simple random sampling. It makes decisions as records are encountered, using probabilistic thresholds to determine whether each item should be accepted, rejected, or temporarily wait-listed.

These decisions are made independently of other items. The authors prove that, with high probability, the algorithm succeeds and requires storage on the order of the square root of the requested sample size. The approach also extends naturally to stratified sampling, which samples across groups and is useful when the dataset contains heterogeneous populations.

In a MapReduce implementation, the algorithms reduce intermediate output and improve load balancing. These benefits address the distributed computation needed to create samples, in addition to the sampling procedure itself. Evaluations on large datasets demonstrate the reported superiority of the proposed algorithms, supporting their usefulness for sampling at scales where storage and workload distribution matter.
summary.tldr: ScaSRS uses probabilistic accept, reject, and wait-list decisions to enable scalable random and stratified sampling with low storage requirements.

title: Scalable Simple Random Sampling and Stratified Sampling

abstract: The performance of machine learning methods is heavily dependent on the choice of data representation. In real world applications such as scene recognition problems, the widely used low-level input features can fail to explain the high-level semantic label concepts. In this work, we address this problem by proposing a novel patch-based latent variable model to integrate latent contextual representation learning and classification model training in one joint optimization framework. Within this framework, the latent layer of variables bridge the gap between inputs and outputs by providing discriminative explanations for the semantic output labels, while being predictable from the low-level input features. Experiments conducted on standard scene recognition tasks demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, comparing to the state-of-the-art scene recognition methods.

In this work, we address this problem by proposing a novel patch-based latent variable model to integrate latent contextual representation learning and classification model training in one joint optimization framework. Within this framework, the latent layer of variables bridge the gap between inputs and outputs by providing discriminative explanations for the semantic output labels, while being predictable from the low-level input features. paragraphs: The paper addresses a representation problem in scene recognition: low-level image features may not adequately explain high-level scene labels. A classifier therefore needs a useful connection between what the image measurements capture and what the output category means. The authors propose learning that connection through a patch-based latent variable model.

The model jointly trains a contextual representation and a classifier within one optimization framework. Its latent variables form an intermediate layer between input features and output labels. This layer has two linked requirements: it should help discriminate among semantic labels, and it should remain predictable from the low-level features available in the image.

Joint learning makes the representation's role in classification part of the training problem itself. The latent layer is useful insofar as it connects observable image information with the semantic distinctions the classifier must make. Experiments on standard scene recognition tasks demonstrate the approach's effectiveness in comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. These results provide empirical support for the proposed way of bridging low-level inputs and high-level outputs.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained patch-based latent representation connects low-level image features with semantic scene labels.

title: Latent Semantic Representation Learning for Scene Classification

abstract: Variational Bayesian (VB) approximations anchor a wide variety of probabilistic models, where tractable posterior inference is almost never possible. Typically based on the so-called VB mean-field approximation to the Kullback-Leibler divergence, a posterior distribution is sought that factorizes across groups of latent variables such that, with the distributions of all but one group of variables held fixed, an optimal closed-form distribution can be obtained for the remaining group, with differing algorithms distinguished by how different variables are grouped and ultimately factored. This basic strategy is particularly attractive when estimating structured low-dimensional models of high-dimensional data, exemplified by the search for minimal rank and/or sparse approximations to observed data. To this end, VB models are frequently deployed across applications including multi-task learning, robust PCA, subspace clustering, matrix completion, affine rank minimization, source localization, compressive sensing, and assorted combinations thereof. Perhaps surprisingly however, there exists almost no attendant theoretical explanation for how various VB factorizations operate, and in which situations one may be preferable to another. We address this relative void by comparing arguably two of the most popular factorizations, one built upon Gaussian scale mixture priors, the other bilinear Gaussian priors, both of which can favor minimal rank or sparsity depending on the context. More specifically, by reexpressing the respective VB objective functions, we weigh multiple factors related to local minima avoidance, feature transformation invariance and correlation, and computational complexity to arrive at insightful conclusions useful in explaining performance and deciding which VB flavor is advantageous. We also envision that the principles explored here are quite relevant to other structured inverse problems where VB serves as a viable solution.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian inference makes difficult posterior calculations manageable by approximating a distribution with simpler factors. A key design choice is how latent variables are grouped: each group can be updated while the others remain fixed. This paper examines how that choice affects methods seeking sparse or low-rank explanations of high-dimensional observations.

The authors compare two popular constructions, based on Gaussian scale mixture priors and bilinear Gaussian priors. Both can encourage sparsity or low rank, depending on the setting. By rewriting their variational objectives, the paper makes their behavior easier to analyze and compares local-minimum avoidance, sensitivity to feature transformations and correlations, and computational complexity.

The purpose is to explain why different variational factorizations behave differently and help determine which is advantageous in a particular setting. This is relevant across the structured estimation applications discussed in the abstract, including matrix completion and robust principal component analysis. The authors also suggest that the principles may extend to other structured inverse problems, presenting that broader relevance as a prospect.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes two common variational Bayesian factorizations to explain their trade-offs in sparse and low-rank estimation.

title: Analysis of Variational Bayesian Factorizations for Sparse and Low-Rank Estimation

abstract: Multivariate loss functions are extensively employed in several prediction tasks arising in Information Retrieval. Often, the goal in the tasks is to minimize expected loss when retrieving relevant items from a presented set of items, where the expectation is with respect to the joint distribution over item sets. Our key result is that for most multivariate losses, the expected loss is provably optimized by sorting the items by the conditional probability of label being positive and then selecting top k items. Such a result was previously known only for the F-measure. Leveraging on the optimality characterization, we give an algorithm for estimating optimal predictions in practice with runtime quadratic in size of item sets for many losses. We provide empirical results on benchmark datasets, comparing the proposed algorithm to state-of-the-art methods for optimizing multivariate losses.

paragraphs: Many information-retrieval tasks evaluate a selected set of items through a multivariate loss. The quality of the decision therefore depends on the set-level outcome. This paper studies how to minimize expected loss when retrieving relevant items from a presented set, with expectation taken over the joint distribution of item sets.

The main result shows that, for most multivariate losses, an optimal prediction can be obtained by ordering items according to their conditional probability of a positive label and selecting the top k. A result of this kind had previously been known for F-measure. The characterization reduces the structure of the optimal decision to a probability ranking and a choice of how many items to retrieve.

Using this characterization, the authors develop an algorithm for estimating optimal predictions in practice. For many losses, its runtime is quadratic in the number of items in the set. They also present benchmark comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, connecting the theoretical decision rule to an implementable prediction procedure.
summary.tldr: For most multivariate losses, optimal retrieval ranks items by conditional relevance probability and selects an appropriate top-k subset.

title: Optimal Classification with Multivariate Losses

abstract: We show that DBSCAN can estimate the connected components of the $\lambda$-density level set $\{ x : f(x) \ge \lambda\}$ given $n$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown density $f$. We characterize the regularity of the level set boundaries using parameter $\beta > 0$ and analyze the estimation error under the Hausdorff metric. When the data lies in $\mathbb{R}^D$ we obtain a rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/(2\beta + D)})$, which matches known lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. When the data lies on an embedded unknown $d$-dimensional manifold in $\mathbb{R}^D$, then we obtain a rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/(2\beta + d\cdot \max\{1, \beta \})})$. Finally, we provide adaptive parameter tuning in order to attain these rates with no a priori knowledge of the intrinsic dimension, density, or $\beta$.

paragraphs: The paper gives a statistical analysis of DBSCAN as a method for recovering connected high-density regions. Its target is the set of locations where an unknown density is at least a chosen threshold, lambda. Given independent, identically distributed samples, the goal is to estimate the connected components of that set.

The analysis measures geometric estimation error using Hausdorff distance and describes boundary regularity through a parameter beta greater than zero. For data in D-dimensional Euclidean space, the error rate is n^(-1/(2 beta + D)), up to logarithmic factors. This matches known lower bounds to that same qualification, providing a precise statistical justification for the method in this setting.

When observations instead lie on an unknown embedded manifold of dimension d, the rate becomes n^(-1/(2 beta + d max{1, beta})), again up to logarithmic factors. The authors also provide adaptive tuning that attains these rates without prior knowledge of intrinsic dimension, density, or beta. The results connect DBSCAN's recovery accuracy to boundary structure and the dimension on which the data actually lies.
summary.tldr: DBSCAN can recover connected density regions with quantified error rates and adaptive tuning, including when data lies on an unknown manifold.

title: Density Level Set Estimation on Manifolds with DBSCAN

abstract: We provide new theoretical insights on why over-parametrization is effective in learning neural networks. For a $k$ hidden node shallow network with quadratic activation and $n$ training data points, we show as long as $ k \ge \sqrt{2n}$, over-parametrization enables local search algorithms to find a globally optimal solution for general smooth and convex loss functions. Further, despite that the number of parameters may exceed the sample size, using theory of Rademacher complexity, we show with weight decay, the solution also generalizes well if the data is sampled from a regular distribution such as Gaussian. To prove when $k\ge \sqrt{2n}$, the loss function has benign landscape properties, we adopt an idea from smoothed analysis, which may have other applications in studying loss surfaces of neural networks.
