paragraphs: Static analysis reasons about program behavior without executing the program. Its precision depends partly on how it represents objects in memory. Traditional analyses use fixed rules for these representations, which can be restrictive for JavaScript’s varied object structures. ABSINT-AI introduces a language-model agent that helps choose an appropriate abstraction for each object.

The agent draws on cues such as object names and access patterns, allowing the analysis to adapt without encoding each cue as a handcrafted rule. Its authority is carefully bounded: it chooses within an interface and never directly changes program state. Ablations also report a 25% advantage over non-agentic model predictions, indicating that interaction with the analysis environment contributes materially to the results.
summary.tldr: ABSINT-AI lets a bounded language-model agent adapt object representations, reducing static-analysis false alarms while preserving formal guarantees.

title: ABSINT-AI: Agentic Heap Abstractions for Abstract Interpretation

abstract: Graph neural networks are widely used for node classification, but they remain vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts in node features and graph structure. Prior work established that methods trained with standard supervised learning (SL) objectives tend to capture spurious signals from either features and/or structure, leaving the model fragile under distributional changes. To address this, we propose TIDE, a novel and effective Tri-Component Information Decomposition framework that explicitly decomposes information into feature-specific, structure-specific and joint components. TIDE aims to preserve only the label-relevant part of the joint information while filtering out spurious feature- and structure-specific information, thereby enhancing the separation between in-distribution (ID) and OOD nodes. Beyond the framework, we provide theoretical and empirical analyses showing that an information bottleneck objective is preferable to standard SL for graph OOD detection, with higher ID confidence and a greater entropy gap between ID and OOD data. Extensive experiments across seven datasets confirm the efficacy of Tide, achieving up to a 34% improvement in FPR95 over strong baselines while maintaining competitive ID accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/DannyW618/TIDE.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks classify nodes using both node features and graph structure, but either source can carry misleading signals that fail under distribution shifts. TIDE examines this problem by separating information into three components: information specific to features, information specific to structure, and information shared jointly by the two.

The framework aims to retain the label-relevant portion of joint information while filtering spurious information specific to either source. The authors provide theoretical and empirical analyses favoring an information bottleneck objective over standard supervised learning for this detection task. Their analysis links it to higher confidence on familiar nodes and a larger entropy gap between familiar and out-of-distribution nodes.

Across seven datasets, TIDE reports up to a 34% improvement in FPR95 over strong baselines while maintaining competitive accuracy on in-distribution nodes. The results support explicitly controlling which feature–structure information is retained when learning to distinguish unfamiliar nodes. They connect the representation objective to both detection quality and preservation of ordinary node-classification performance.
summary.tldr: TIDE separates feature, structure, and joint information to improve detection of out-of-distribution graph nodes.

title: What Information Matters? Graph Out-of-Distribution Detection via Tri-Component Information Decomposition

abstract: We find multilayer perceptrons and transformers both universally learn an instantiation of the same divide-and-conquer algorithm that requires only a logarithmic number of neural representations to solve dihedral multiplication. Clustering neurons based on similar activation behaviour reveals remarkably clear structure: each neural representation corresponds to a Cayley graph. To our knowledge, this is the first work that fully characterizes and describes all neural representations that are learnable on a dataset, while prior work on group multiplications studied neuron-level behavior, or preliminarily investigated cluster behavior. Thus, we can understand the algorithm networks universally learn at three levels of abstraction: 1) Neurons activate on coset or approximate coset structure of the dihedral group. 2) Groups of neurons together form neural representations that act to divide the dataset into different subproblems, being Cayley graphs, where the equivalence class of the answer is computed. 3) The global algorithm then linearly combines each neural representation (subproblem) together at the logits. This work provides the community with a deep case study and a well-understood toy model for interpretability, and makes progress toward proving the conjecture that networks trained via stochastic gradient methods divide and conquer all group multiplication tasks.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how neural networks solve dihedral multiplication, a structured mathematical task involving group operations. The authors find that both multilayer perceptrons and transformers learn versions of the same divide-and-conquer algorithm. That algorithm needs only a logarithmic number of neural representations, making the task a compact setting for examining how internal features combine into a complete computation.

Collections of neurons form representations corresponding to Cayley graphs and divide the dataset into subproblems. Each representation computes an equivalence class of the answer, and the network combines these partial results linearly at its output logits.

The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first complete characterization of all neural representations learnable on a dataset. Its significance lies in connecting neuron behavior, representation structure, and the overall algorithm within one interpretable example. The work also advances a broader conjecture about divide-and-conquer learning for group multiplication, without claiming to prove that conjecture for every group.
summary.tldr: The paper traces how perceptrons and transformers solve dihedral multiplication through shared divide-and-conquer representations organized as Cayley graphs.

title: Deep neural networks divide and conquer dihedral multiplication

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across decentralized clients, but its performance often degrades under non-IID data distributions, particularly in the presence of data skew. Existing approaches mitigate this issue by estimating client skew via kernel density estimation over neighboring model updates, which preserves privacy and reduces communication costs. However, such approaches suffer from two fundamental limitations: bias toward skewed majority clients due to fixed neighborhood structures, and vulnerability to noise-induced perturbation in kernel space. To address these challenges, we propose FedVeer, a skew-aware FL framework based on self-adaptive kernel density estimation with k-free neighborhoods. FedVeer dynamically determines the neighborhood size via max-margin learning to mitigate majority-client bias, and further incorporates Kalman filtering to stabilize margin estimation under noisy updates, with a high-probability theoretical guarantee on margin deviation. Extensive experiments on realworld datasets demonstrate that FedVeer consistently outperforms four baselines, achieving up to 6.36% accuracy improvement and reducing noiseinduced degradation by up to 6.01%.

The paper identifies two problems with that approach: fixed neighborhoods can favor a skewed majority, and noisy updates can disturb the estimates in the kernel representation used for density estimation.

It uses max-margin learning to determine these neighborhoods and reduce majority-client bias. Kalman filtering stabilizes margin estimation when updates are noisy. The authors also provide a high-probability theoretical bound on margin deviation, connecting the stabilization mechanism to a formal guarantee.

The largest reported accuracy improvement is 6.36%, and the largest reduction in noise-induced degradation is 6.01%. These are best reported gains across the experiments. The results support adapting both the neighborhood structure and its noise handling when estimating skew from client updates.
summary.tldr: FedVeer estimates client skew with adaptive neighborhoods and filtered margins to improve federated learning under uneven and noisy updates.

title: FedVeer: Self-Adaptive Skew Estimation for Robust Federated Learning

abstract: Despite their strong performance on reasoning tasks, Large reasoning models (LRMs) often suffer from overthinking, producing unnecessarily long outputs and incurring high end-to-end latency, a significant limitation to their real-world deployment. To address overthinking, early-exit mechanisms have been proposed to terminate reasoning before typical completion, showing that this approach can effectively shorten generation length with minimal impact on accuracy. However, their reliance on probing mechanisms introduces a detection overhead that limits their end-to-end latency gains and compromises their generalizability across diverse problems. Inspired by the use of hidden states in speculative decoding, we propose SpecExit, a novel framework that predicts both future tokens and an early-exit signal directly from a lightweight draft model without probing overhead. Our method offers significant improvements, achieving up to 66% generation length reduction and 2.5$\times$ end-to-end speedup compared with the speculative decoding baseline, without compromising accuracy. Our method leverages the inherent signals from hidden states to provide effective early-exit signals, suggesting broader use of hidden states for efficient reasoning. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecExit-B802.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can spend time generating more reasoning than a problem requires. Early-exit methods try to stop this process sooner, but checking whether to stop can introduce its own computational overhead. SpecExit targets the resulting gap between reducing output length and actually reducing end-to-end response time.

The framework uses a lightweight draft model to predict both upcoming tokens and an early-exit signal. It draws that signal directly from hidden states, avoiding the probing overhead associated with the early-exit approaches discussed in the paper. Token prediction and the decision to stop reasoning are therefore handled within the same speculative framework.

Compared with a speculative-decoding baseline, the authors report up to a 66% reduction in generation length and a 2.5-times end-to-end speedup without compromising accuracy in their evaluations. The distinction between these measurements is central: shorter outputs are useful, but the system also needs to finish sooner after accounting for detection costs. The findings suggest that hidden states can provide useful signals for more efficient reasoning.
summary.tldr: SpecExit predicts tokens and stopping signals with a lightweight draft model, reporting up to 2.5-times faster reasoning without accuracy loss.

title: SpecExit: Accelerating Large Reasoning Model via Speculative Exit

abstract: This paper introduces EPS3D, a new end-to-end feed-forward framework for open-vocabulary 3D panoptic segmentation. Unlike existing methods relying on additional preprocessing, we design an end-to-end architecture, with a distillation-based training strategy on diverse 3D scenes to predict 3D-aware semantic and instance features from multi-view images, improving 3D consistency and avoiding error accumulation. We further propose a mutual enhancement module to enforce inherent semantic-instance consistency. By aligning semantics within instances (Ins2Sem) and refining instance features with semantic guidance (Sem2Ins), we achieve more coherent 3D scene understanding. Ultimately, EPS3D outperforms SOTA baselines on two benchmarks (e.g., +13% mIoU for semantics on Replica) with high efficiency (e.g., 1s per scene), supporting tasks like robotic manipulation and 3D scene editing.

Unlike existing methods relying on additional preprocessing, we design an end-to-end architecture, with a distillation-based training strategy on diverse 3D scenes to predict 3D-aware semantic and instance features from multi-view images, improving 3D consistency and avoiding error accumulation. We further propose a mutual enhancement module to enforce inherent semantic-instance consistency. By aligning semantics within instances (Ins2Sem) and refining instance features with semantic guidance (Sem2Ins), we achieve more coherent 3D scene understanding. Ultimately, EPS3D outperforms SOTA baselines on two benchmarks (e.g., +13% mIoU for semantics on Replica) with high efficiency (e.g., 1s per scene), supporting tasks like robotic manipulation and 3D scene editing.

paragraphs: Understanding a 3D scene requires identifying both what things are and which observations belong to the same individual object. EPS3D addresses these semantic and instance-level tasks together in an open-vocabulary setting. It uses an end-to-end feed-forward framework that predicts 3D-aware features from multiple images of a scene.

Training uses distillation across diverse 3D scenes to improve consistency and avoid error accumulation associated with additional preprocessing. A mutual enhancement module then connects semantic and instance information in both directions. Instance groupings help align semantic predictions within an object, while semantic guidance refines the features used to distinguish object instances.

The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on two benchmarks, including a 13% semantic mIoU improvement on Replica, alongside an example processing time of one second per scene. These results suggest that explicitly coordinating object identity and category information can improve coherent 3D interpretation efficiently. The framework is presented as supporting applications such as robotic manipulation and 3D scene editing, where both kinds of information are useful.
summary.tldr: EPS3D jointly predicts and reconciles semantic and instance features from multi-view images for efficient open-vocabulary 3D scene segmentation.

abstract: We discuss the problem of fitting an implicit shape model to a set of points sampled from a co-dimension one manifold of arbitrary topology. The method solves a non-convex optimisation problem in the embedding function that defines the implicit by way of its zero level set. By assuming that the solution is a mixture of radial basis functions of varying widths we attain the globally optimal solution by way of an equivalent eigenvalue problem, without using or constructing as an intermediate step the normal vectors of the manifold at each data point. We demonstrate the system on two and three dimensional data, with examples of missing data interpolation and set operations on the resultant shapes.
originalAbstract: We discuss the problem of fitting an implicit shape model to a set of points sampled from a co-dimension one manifold of arbitrary topology. The method solves a non-convex optimisation problem in the embedding function that defines the implicit by way of its zero level set. By assuming that the solution is a mixture of radial basis functions of varying widths we attain the globally optimal solution by way of an equivalent eigenvalue problem, without using or constructing as an intermediate step the normal vectors of the manifold at each data point. We demonstrate the system on two and three dimensional data, with examples of missing data interpolation and set operations on the resultant shapes.

paragraphs: The paper fits an implicit shape to points sampled from a manifold whose dimension is one less than the surrounding space. Such a shape is described by a function whose zero-valued locations define the boundary. This formulation allows the method to address shapes of arbitrary topology through the function used to represent them.

The fitting problem is nonconvex in that function. The authors assume that the solution is a mixture of radial basis functions with varying widths, then turn the optimization into an equivalent eigenvalue problem. Under this representation assumption, they obtain a globally optimal solution. The method does not require normal vectors at the sample points, including as an intermediate construction.

Demonstrations use both two-dimensional and three-dimensional data. Examples include interpolation across missing data and set operations on the resulting shapes. These applications illustrate the usefulness of the implicit representation beyond fitting the observed points. The main technical result connects a particular function representation with an eigenvalue formulation that makes the stated global solution attainable.
summary.tldr: Assuming a mixture of varying-width radial basis functions, implicit shape fitting becomes an eigenvalue problem with a globally optimal solution.

title: Implicit surface modelling as an eigenvalue problem

abstract: This paper investigates compression of 3D objects in computer graphics using manifold learning. Spectral compression uses the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian of an object’s topology to adaptively compress 3D objects. 3D compression is a challenging application domain: object models can have > 105 vertices, and reliably computing the basis functions on large graphs is numerically challenging. In this paper, we introduce a novel multiscale manifold learning approach to 3D mesh compression using diffusion wavelets, a general extension of wavelets to graphs with arbitrary topology. Unlike the “global” nature of Laplacian bases, diffusion wavelet bases are compact, and multiscale in nature. We decompose large graphs using a fast graph partitioning method, and combine local multiscale wavelet bases computed on each subgraph. We present results showing that multiscale diffusion wavelets bases are superior to the Laplacian bases for adaptive compression of large 3D objects.

Spectral compression uses the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian of an object’s topology to adaptively compress 3D objects. 3D compression is a challenging application domain: object models can have > 105 vertices, and reliably computing the basis functions on large graphs is numerically challenging. In this paper, we introduce a novel multiscale manifold learning approach to 3D mesh compression using diffusion wavelets, a general extension of wavelets to graphs with arbitrary topology. Unlike the “global” nature of Laplacian bases, diffusion wavelet bases are compact, and multiscale in nature. We decompose large graphs using a fast graph partitioning method, and combine local multiscale wavelet bases computed on each subgraph. We present results showing that multiscale diffusion wavelets bases are superior to the Laplacian bases for adaptive compression of large 3D objects.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compress large three-dimensional meshes using the connections between their vertices. Spectral compression represents an object's geometry using basis functions derived from its graph Laplacian. Computing these functions reliably becomes numerically challenging when an object contains more than one hundred thousand vertices, motivating a different representation.

The proposed method uses diffusion wavelets, which extend wavelets to graphs with arbitrary connectivity. Their basis functions are compact and operate at multiple scales, unlike the global Laplacian bases discussed in the paper. This gives the compression method a representation organized around local structure at different levels of detail.

To work with large meshes, the authors partition the graph using a fast method, compute local multiscale bases on the resulting subgraphs, and combine them. Their reported results show that diffusion wavelet bases outperform Laplacian bases for adaptive compression of large three-dimensional objects. The contribution combines a different kind of representation with a strategy for constructing it on large graphs.
summary.tldr: Local, multiscale diffusion wavelet bases improve adaptive compression of large 3D meshes in the reported comparisons with Laplacian bases.

title: Adaptive mesh compression in 3D computer graphics using multiscale manifold learning

abstract: We show how variational Bayesian inference can be implemented for very large generalized linear models. Our relaxation is proven to be a convex problem for any log-concave model. We provide a generic double loop algorithm for solving this relaxation on models with arbitrary super-Gaussian potentials. By iteratively decoupling the criterion, most of the work can be done by solving large linear systems, rendering our algorithm orders of magnitude faster than previously proposed solvers for the same problem. We evaluate our method on problems of Bayesian active learning for large binary classification models, and show how to address settings with many candidates and sequential inclusion steps.

We provide a generic double loop algorithm for solving this relaxation on models with arbitrary super-Gaussian potentials. By iteratively decoupling the criterion, most of the work can be done by solving large linear systems, rendering our algorithm orders of magnitude faster than previously proposed solvers for the same problem. We evaluate our method on problems of Bayesian active learning for large binary classification models, and show how to address settings with many candidates and sequential inclusion steps.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational cost of variational Bayesian inference for very large generalized linear models. The authors introduce a relaxation of the inference problem and prove that it is convex whenever the model is log-concave. That condition specifies the scope of the convexity guarantee and gives the approximation a useful optimization structure.

They provide a general double-loop algorithm for models with arbitrary super-Gaussian potentials. The algorithm repeatedly separates coupled parts of the objective, allowing most computation to be performed by solving large linear systems. This reformulation is the central efficiency mechanism: it turns much of the inference workload into a recurring type of numerical problem.

The authors report speed improvements of orders of magnitude over previously proposed solvers for the same problem. They evaluate the method through Bayesian active learning with large binary classification models, including settings with many candidates and sequential inclusion steps. The work therefore links an optimization guarantee under a stated model condition with a computational strategy for demanding inference and selection tasks.
summary.tldr: A variational inference relaxation is convex for log-concave models and admits a solver that shifts most computation to large linear systems.

title: Convex variational Bayesian inference for large scale generalized linear models

abstract: Link prediction is addressed as an output kernel learning task through semi-supervised Output Kernel Regression. Working in the framework of RKHS theory with vector-valued functions, we establish a new representer theorem devoted to semi-supervised least square regression. We then apply it to get a new model (POKR: Penalized Output Kernel Regression) and show its relevance using numerical experiments on artificial networks and two real applications using a very low percentage of labeled data in a transductive setting.
originalAbstract: Link prediction is addressed as an output kernel learning task through semi-supervised Output Kernel Regression. Working in the framework of RKHS theory with vector-valued functions, we establish a new representer theorem devoted to semi-supervised least square regression. We then apply it to get a new model (POKR: Penalized Output Kernel Regression) and show its relevance using numerical experiments on artificial networks and two real applications using a very low percentage of labeled data in a transductive setting.

paragraphs: The paper formulates link prediction as an output-kernel learning problem. It uses semi-supervised Output Kernel Regression to address prediction when only a small portion of the available data is labeled. This places the relationships represented on the output side of the regression model at the center of the proposed approach.

The mathematical foundation uses reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces with vector-valued functions. Within that framework, the authors establish a new representer theorem for semi-supervised least-squares regression. They then use the theorem to derive Penalized Output Kernel Regression, or POKR, connecting the theoretical result directly to a model for the link-prediction task.

Numerical experiments cover artificial networks and two real applications, using a very low proportion of labeled data. The evaluation is transductive, so the reported relevance concerns predictions within that setting. The paper’s contribution combines a new regression theorem with an application model and empirical evidence that output-kernel learning can be useful for link prediction under sparse supervision.
summary.tldr: POKR derives a semi-supervised output-kernel model for link prediction and demonstrates relevance with very little labeled data in transductive experiments.

title: Semi-supervised Penalized Output Kernel Regression for Link Prediction

abstract: In this paper we study output coding for multi-label prediction. For a multi-label output coding to be discriminative, it is important that codewords for different label vectors are significantly different from each other. In the meantime, unlike in traditional coding theory, codewords in output coding are to be predicted from the input, so it is also critical to have a predictable label encoding. To find output codes that are both discriminative and predictable, we first propose a max-margin formulation that naturally captures these two properties. We then convert it to a metric learning formulation, but with an exponentially large number of constraints as commonly encountered in structured prediction problems. Without a label structure for tractable inference, we use overgenerating (i.e., relaxation) techniques combined with the cutting plane method for optimization. In our empirical study, the proposed output coding scheme outperforms a variety of existing multi-label prediction methods for image, text and music classification.

In the meantime, unlike in traditional coding theory, codewords in output coding are to be predicted from the input, so it is also critical to have a predictable label encoding. To find output codes that are both discriminative and predictable, we first propose a max-margin formulation that naturally captures these two properties. We then convert it to a metric learning formulation, but with an exponentially large number of constraints as commonly encountered in structured prediction problems. paragraphs: The paper studies output coding for multi-label prediction, where an input can have several labels at once. A useful encoding must satisfy two goals: distinct label combinations should have well-separated codewords, and those codewords should be predictable from the input. Separation alone is insufficient if the prediction model cannot reliably produce the resulting codes.

The authors introduce a maximum-margin formulation that captures both discrimination and predictability, then reformulate it as metric learning. This creates exponentially many constraints, a computational challenge familiar from structured prediction. Because the problem lacks a label structure that makes inference tractable, the method combines relaxation techniques with cutting-plane optimization.

Experiments on image, text, and music classification show the proposed coding scheme outperforming a variety of existing multi-label prediction methods. These results support designing codes around both label separation and learnability in the evaluated applications. The contribution includes an optimization strategy for handling the large constraint set, making the joint design objective computationally usable.
summary.tldr: Maximum Margin Output Coding learns multi-label codes that are both distinguishable and predictable, with reported gains across image, text, and music tasks.

title: Maximum Margin Output Coding
